By engaging key stakeholders in France's private sector, we can open new markets for Liberian products, especially in agriculture, which remains the backbone of our economy.” ; Said he is cognizant of the importance of improved relations with France, which was the second European nation after the United Kingdom to have officially recognized Liberia's sovereignty in 1852, and that he is aware France is part of the Group of Seven (G7) informal bloc of industrialized democracies

acts.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
acts.speech: Pointed to the importance of ensuring that economic gains benefit ordinary Liberians. “It's not just about bringing investments, but ensuring that those investments create jobs, improve livelihoods, and contribute to national development.”

acts.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
acts.speech: Spoke extensively about leveraging Liberia's membership in global bodies such as UNESCO and vowed to enhance Liberia's participation in education, culture, and scientific initiatives promoted by UNESCO, noting that these programs align with Liberia's national priorities; said he will ensure the Permanent Delegation of Liberia to UNESCO remains a consequential member of the organization. “UNESCO offers immense opportunities in education and cultural preservation. As a nation rich in culture and history, we must make our voice heard and access the support needed to improve our education system and preserve our heritage.”

acts.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
acts.speech: Acknowledged the existing cooperation between Liberia and France in various sectors, including the training of security forces and French language promotion, and pledged to strengthen these collaborations, particularly in addressing pressing challenges like climate change and sustainable development

acts.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
acts.speech: Highlighted his commitment to inclusive development, with a particular focus on youth empowerment and gender equity, and stressed the importance of giving young Liberians access to education, training, and opportunities abroad. “Investing in our youth is investing in our future. Through scholarships and exchange programs, we can equip the next generation of Liberians with the skills needed to drive our country forward.” ; “Gender equality is not just a moral imperative; it is a developmental necessity. Women must be given equal opportunities to contribute to Liberia's growth.”

acts.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
acts.speech: Committed to advocating for increased international support to address environmental challenges and noted that France, as a leader in global climate initiatives, can play a significant role in supporting Liberia's environmental sustainability efforts. “Climate change is a shared challenge that requires shared solutions. We will work closely with France to secure resources and expertise to protect our forests, preserve biodiversity, and promote renewable energy.”

acts.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
acts.speech: Highlighted his readiness to bring his extensive experience in governance and policy implementation to bear in his new role. “I am fully prepared to serve Liberia with diligence and integrity. If confirmed, I will dedicate myself to achieving measurable results for the Liberian people.” ; Expressed gratitude for the trust placed in him by President Joseph N. Boakai and reiterated his commitment to putting Liberia's interests above all else: “This nomination is not just an honor; it is a call to serve. I am committed to working tirelessly to ensure that Liberia's voice is heard, our partnerships are strengthened, and our people reap the benefits of these efforts.” ; “Our success will not be measured by words but by actions and outcomes. Together, we can build a Liberia that is respected internationally and thriving domestically.”

acts.speaker: Members of the Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs
acts.speech: Commended Dr. Yorlay for his clear vision and readiness to serve as Liberia's top diplomat in France

acts.speaker: Senator Abraham Darius Dillon, Chair of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee
acts.speech: Described Yorlay as “a nominee with a wealth of experience and a strong sense of patriotism.”

title: ‘They’re inviting a movement to the main stage’: Kendrick Lamar’s road to the Super Bowl

acts.speaker: Kendrick Lamar, rapper (lyrics)
acts.speech: "I'm not sure why I'm infatuated with death?" ; "Maybe it's because I'm a dreamer and sleep is the cousin of death!"

acts.speaker: Kendrick Lamar, rapper
acts.speech: Reflected in an interview with Signed Media: "There was smoke everywhere and my dad had a bunch of stolen car rims [he had looted] in the back seat he took from the Compton Swap Meet." ; "My pops and my uncle were both involved in the Watts riots! LA is very sensitive and prideful of its people. We literally burned down our old neighbourhoods because of our anger over Rodney King."

acts.speaker: 9th Wonder, North Carolina rap producer
acts.speech: "Kendrick Lamar is more like a documentarian than an MC. Kendrick chooses to rap about everything and everyone across the social strata. People might call it 'woke' or 'deep', but I think of it as straight-up reporting. Some rappers leave out a certain section of people in their lyrics, right? Well, Kendrick tries to rap from everyone's perspective."

acts.speaker: 9th Wonder, North Carolina rap producer
acts.speech: On how good kid, m.A.A.d city subverted gangsta rap cliches: "Some rappers do come from good homes with loving moms and dads! Not everyone comes from a hardback struggle, or has to be a bad kid just because they come from a bad place. Kendrick knows the power of telling simple American stories about ordinary people doing their best."

acts.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author of The Butterfly Effect: How Kendrick Lamar Ignited The Soul of Black America
acts.speech: "Sadly, there's still a segment of the [American] population that doesn't consider rap a viable genre in music, despite its popularity. Such thinking suggests racism and classism, but with Kendrick Lamar, he's the type of rapper who can make fans out of anyone. He's a rapper's rapper with a pop sensibility on stage. And while he's tremendous on his own, he's also had the benefit of guesting with bigger stars like Beyonce and Taylor Swift. I think Kendrick has done a great job over the years of making himself undeniable."

acts.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author
acts.speech: "Artists of Kendrick's stature don't usually rock the boat [and change their sound too radically] once they become famous. But he's done so with many of his releases, no matter how popular the previous albums were. He's encouraged others to take creative risks for their music. I think, more than anything, this courage has helped change popular music."

acts.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author
acts.speech: Predicts of the Super Bowl performance: "I would prepare for anything! If there's any message that could emanate from Kendrick's Super Bowl performance in New Orleans, I think it could be about the wildfires in Los Angeles and the city's resilience."

acts.speaker: Marcus J Moore, music journalist and author
acts.speech: "Sure, some of his core fans might see his Super Bowl performance as a sell-out move, but I would encourage those listeners to go back and revisit his 2022 album, Mr Morale & The Big Steppers, where he shot back against the notion of being a paragon of virtue." ; "Though listeners may want him to be the same artist and person he was on albums like good kid, m.A.A.d. city and To Pimp a Butterfly, they have to realise that was a decade ago, and if they want that guy, they have to play those albums."

acts.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
acts.speech: Believes the NFL's decision to have Lamar as a half-time performer is supposed to reflect the changing values of their brand and business itself, and says his selection "isn't a risk - it's a statement" ; "If previous Super Bowl performers like Prince, Beyonce and Madonna embodied pop ubiquity, Kendrick represents something just as powerful: cultural gravity. His music isn't always designed for casual singalongs but rather it's built for reflection, resistance and resonance. And in a moment when the NFL is still navigating its own complicated relationship with race, protest and black artistic expression, Kendrick isn't just an artist - they're inviting a movement to the main stage."

acts.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
acts.speech: On whether performing Not Like Us is a risk to advertisers: "The song has transcended the beef. It's fun, it's infectious and it's already been embraced far beyond the hip-hop world. Instead of just a diss track, it's a cultural jolt - one that taps into regional pride, black joy and the communal energy that makes music feel alive. Brands love to co-opt hip-hop culture when it's convenient. They'll put rap lyrics on ad campaigns or with tweets; partner with artists for limited-edition sneakers' and drop hip-hop-inspired Super Bowl commercials - all while keeping a safe distance from the actual violent tensions that shape the genre."

acts.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
acts.speech: "The Super Bowl half-time show isn't just a performance - it's the single biggest branding opportunity in music. It's a 12-minute global ad for an artist's catalogue, cultural impact, and marketability, all broadcast to an audience of over 100 million people." ; "And here's the kicker: performers don't get paid! Instead, the exposure itself becomes the currency, often translating into massive streaming hikes, album sales and brand deals. Take Rihanna in 2023: her streams rose 640% after her performance, and Fenty Beauty reportedly pulled in more than $5 million in media impact value from that subtle but game-changing mid-show makeup touch up. But with the rewards come massive risks." ; "The Super Bowl is a high-stakes, zero-margin-for-error stage where the scrutiny is relentless, the expectations sky-high. If an artist miscalculates, whether it's the energy, the production or the cultural moment they're stepping into, the fallout can be brutal."

acts.speaker: Seb Joseph, marketing expert and editor at Digiday
acts.speech: Hopes to see Lamar perform Alright, believing the protest song's simple message of perseverance is needed now more than ever before: "At a time when history feels like it is repeating itself, when the same battles for justice and dignity are being fought yet again, Kendrick standing on that stage, leading millions in the chorus of 'We gon' be alright,' would be a powerful message. It would say: 'we're still here... and we're not going anywhere.'"

acts.speaker: Paul A Thompson, Pitchfork
acts.speech: Crowning Not Like Us the best song of 2024, wrote: "In the third verse, Kendrick casts Drake as a parasite who leeches off of younger, more inventive rappers in a quest for pyrrhic streaming statements. But by that point he's already turned the biggest pop star on the planet into a punchline."

acts.speaker: Drake, rapper
acts.speech: Denies Lamar's insinuation that he had relationships with underage women, and has taken legal action against record label Universal Music over the track Not Like Us.

source: AMAP (Agence Malienne de Presse et de Publicité)
title: Niafunké : Le préfet en guerre contre le désordre foncier - amap

acts.speaker: Modibo Kane Togo, Prefect of Niafunké
acts.speech: During the introductory meetings, the prefect insisted on communication — real communication — between colleagues and, above all, on transparency in the management of State affairs.

acts.speaker: Modibo Kane Togo, Prefect of Niafunké
acts.speech: Ordered that all constructions encroaching on the streets of Niafunké be listed, demolished and rectified "without qualms"; ordered the outright demolition of illegal market installations after traders failed to respect a two-month deadline they had set themselves; declared that letting toilet waste water flow directly into the streets, sometimes past mosques, is strictly forbidden and that offenders will answer before the law; announced that all blocked ditches will be cleared and cleaned within a week and that those using gutters to dump waste have been summoned by the sanitation service and will be handled by the police after a one-month grace period.

acts.speaker: Modibo Kane Togo, Prefect of Niafunké
acts.speech: "The situation is serious, since as of today, the town of Niafunké no longer has any unsold land. This is unacceptable. Future generations have done nothing to deserve this fate."

acts.speaker: Imam of the grand mosque of Niafunké
acts.speech: said, at the information meeting initiated by the prefect on Monday 10 March 2025: "We congratulate, support and encourage the prefect because everything he is doing benefits Niafunké."

acts.speaker: Another customary chief of Niafunké
acts.speech: stated that one must have the honesty to tell the truth in the face of history, because everyone is complicit in this situation. "In any case, there will be malcontents (those at fault), and also happy people, those who were wronged, without any defence," he said.

acts.speaker: Some native elders of Niafunké
acts.speech: say that the town's recent administrations are a disgrace.

acts.speaker: Residents of Niafunké
acts.speech: Frustrated for more than a decade, they show their support for the prefect at each of his visits; women, old people and young people punctuate his passage with chants of "Anga Ta", "Ambi Ko", "Tignè debi laban", "Prefect, free Niafunké for us"; after the meeting on rectifying the town's urban development plan, the inhabitants of Niafunké expressed their hope in prefect Togo's actions.

title: Malawi moves to sustain HIV gains - Nation Online

acts.speaker: Tione Chilambe, National Aids Commission (NAC) official
acts.speech: Said Malawi in its sustainability plan had expected donor support to reduce over time, but not as quickly as it has, especially around HIV prevention services: "We knew the money would eventually reduce, but not in such a sudden way."

acts.speaker: Tione Chilambe, National Aids Commission (NAC) official
acts.speech: Said that to keep services running the government responded by allocating K1 billion towards HIV treatment co-financing and setting aside K0.5 billion to hire and train more health workers.

acts.speaker: Unaids
acts.speech: Has warned that if the funding gap is not filled, there could be an additional six million HIV infections and four million Aids-related deaths globally by 2029.

acts.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, Unaids Executive Director
acts.speech: "We cannot let funding cuts wipe out the gains we've made."

acts.speaker: Musa Manganye, head of HIV treatment in South Africa
acts.speech: Said what matters is the budget line.

title: Accord de Paix entre la République Démocratique du Congo et le Rwanda

acts.speaker: Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Government of the Republic of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, preamble)
acts.speech: Reaffirming the mutual commitment to respect the Declaration of Principles signed by the Parties on 25 April 2025, based on mutual respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, national unity and the peaceful settlement of disputes; recognising the need for a negotiated political resolution - rather than a military solution - to the Parties' disputes; recognising the terms of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, the Charter of the United Nations and UN Security Council resolution 2773 (21 February 2025); taking note of the CONOPS of 31 October 2024 arising from the Luanda process and the communique of the second joint EAC-SADC Summit of 24 March 2025; conscious of the ongoing negotiations between the DRC and the AFC/M23 under the mediation of the State of Qatar in Doha; resolved to prevent a resumption of hostilities, to actively promote lasting peace, stability and integrated economic development throughout the region and to restore normal bilateral relations; determined to promote full respect for human rights and international humanitarian law; they hereby agree to be bound by the provisions that follow.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, Section 1: Territorial integrity and prohibition of hostilities)
acts.speech: The Parties agree to implement the Harmonised Plan for the neutralisation of the FDLR and the disengagement of forces/lifting of Rwanda's defensive measures (CONOPS) of 31 October 2024; agree that disputes shall be settled through processes established by the Agreement rather than through hostilities; agree to refrain from any act of aggression and not to commit, support or tolerate military incursions or other acts, direct or indirect, that threaten the peace and security of the other party or undermine its sovereignty or territorial integrity; agree to allow no military or other hostile activity against one another on or from their respective territories and to provide no support to such activities abroad; the prohibition of hostile acts applies without geographical restriction; the Parties take all possible measures to ensure that all armed groups in the conflict zone cease hostilities; the Parties facilitate the free movement of civilians, including humanitarian personnel, and must respect international humanitarian law.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, Section 2: Disengagement, disarmament and integration of non-state armed groups)
acts.speech: The Parties support the ongoing negotiations between the DRC and the AFC/M23 with the mediation of the State of Qatar in Doha and efforts to disarm and demobilise non-state armed groups; the Parties immediately and unconditionally cease all State support to non-state armed groups, except to the extent necessary to facilitate implementation of the agreement; they support the disengagement, disarmament and integration of non-state armed groups, including through the P-DDRCS; any eventual reintegration of combatants into the FARDC and the Congolese National Police is to be rigorous, individualised and conditional, case by case, on the basis of clear criteria including physical and moral fitness, respect for and absence of serious violations of international humanitarian law, and loyalty to the State and its institutions.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, Section 3: Joint Security Coordination Mechanism)
acts.speech: The Parties establish and agree to launch, within 30 days of entry into force, a joint security coordination mechanism between the DRC and Rwanda; the mechanism creates common operating procedures and reporting mechanisms to ensure transparency of the scale and scope of operations; it is governed by the irreversible and verifiable end of State support to the FDLR and associated armed groups and the total prohibition of any material, logistical, financial or other support to them; a commitment to identify, assess, locate and neutralise in accordance with the CONOPS of 31 October 2024; a commitment to build on already successful bilateral security cooperation arrangements in which operations are targeted, time-limited and aimed at a specific threat; and the protection of civilians and respect for international humanitarian law.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, Section 4: Refugees, internally displaced persons and humanitarian considerations)
acts.speech: The Parties, with the support of United Nations agencies, relevant humanitarian organisations and the international community, facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of refugees in a manner consistent with their international legal obligations and with the Tripartite Agreements on the voluntary repatriation of Congolese and Rwandan refugees signed in Kigali on 17 February 2010; recognise the need to end the conflict to allow internally displaced persons to return to their places of origin; and create conditions conducive to the delivery of emergency relief, guaranteeing humanitarian agencies free, safe, unhindered and unconditional access to vulnerable populations, with DRC local authorities responsible under the supervision of the DRC central government.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, Section 5: MONUSCO and other multilateral support)
acts.speech: The Parties facilitate and support MONUSCO's capacity to protect civilian populations and implement all elements of its mandate, including by respecting MONUSCO's freedom of movement and taking all appropriate measures to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel deployed in eastern DRC; commit to advancing the implementation of UN Security Council resolution 2773 (2025) and other relevant resolutions; and recognise that MONUSCO, as mandated by resolution 2765 (2024), plays an important role in local peace and security.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, Section 6: Regional economic integration framework)
acts.speech: The Parties agree to launch, within three months of entry into force, a multi-stage regional economic integration framework to be defined in a separate agreement, building on existing efforts such as the AfCFTA, ICGLR, COMESA and the EAC, in order to develop external trade and investment from the region's critical mineral supply chains and introduce greater transparency; under the framework the Parties launch and/or expand cooperation on shared priorities such as national park management, hydroelectric development, de-risking mineral supply chains, joint management of resources in Lake Kivu, and transparent, formalised end-to-end mineral value chains linking the two countries, in partnership where appropriate with the government and investors of the United States; they commit to explore options for linking the framework to other international or regional economic development initiatives; and they establish or use independent economic audit and anti-corruption mechanisms to monitor mineral supply chains, infrastructure projects and any future economic agreement.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Peace Agreement, Sections 7-9: Implementation, dispute settlement and final provisions)
acts.speech: Any dispute arising from implementation is to be resolved amicably between the Parties with the facilitation of the Joint Oversight Committee; the Parties hereby create a Joint Oversight Committee and invite, within three days, the African Union Facilitator, Qatar and the United States to sit on it; its mandate is to receive complaints of violations, take measures to remedy violations, monitor and examine accusations and resolve disputes, and it may appoint another representative or establish an ad hoc mechanism; its first meeting is to be held as soon as possible and no later than 45 days after entry into force, with the Parties considering holding it in Washington; the Agreement creates no obligation for non-Party States sitting on the Committee; the Agreement remains in force indefinitely unless otherwise agreed, may be terminated by either Party on sixty (60) days' written notice, may be amended by written agreement, and enters into force upon signature; signed at Washington in 2025 in duplicate in French and English, for the Government of the DRC and the Government of Rwanda, and attested by the Government of the United States of America.

acts.speaker: Government of the DRC and Government of Rwanda (Annex: Modalities of operation of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism)
acts.speech: The Parties reaffirm their commitment under the terms and obligations of the CONOPS of 31 October 2024 and incorporate it, save as otherwise provided; the JSCM is composed of at least three permanent representatives of each Party, including representatives of the armed forces, intelligence services and foreign affairs ministries; its mission is to identify, assess and locate the FDLR and affiliated groups so as to enable their neutralisation, and it is empowered to monitor implementation of the CONOPS, exchange intelligence and information, define the status and composition of the FDLR, establish and monitor their locations, verify information, coordinate with international actors, assess the threat and coordinate measures to neutralise them; the JSCM meets monthly, alternating between locations in the DRC and Rwanda, adopts terms of reference at its first meeting, drafts a single joint report after each monthly meeting and submits it at ministerial level; the Parties agree to invite the United States and Qatar to attend JSCM meetings as observers and the JSCM may invite other third States or organisations and jointly seek additional financial, logistical and technical support; the JSCM continues to operate until the completion of its mandate.

acts.speaker: Concept of Operations (CONOPS) of the Harmonised Plan for the neutralisation of the FDLR and the disengagement of forces/lifting of Rwanda's defensive measures, Luanda, 31 October 2024
acts.speech: States that the DRC and Rwanda have had tense relations for almost three decades which have provoked mutual accusations following the actions of armed groups in eastern DRC; that the African Union mandated the President of the Republic of Angola, His Excellency Joao Manuel Goncalves Lourenco, the AU Champion for peace and reconciliation in Africa, to facilitate dialogue between the DRC and Rwanda; sets out the political objectives (restoring a climate of confidence, creating a safe and secure environment, ensuring lasting peace and stability where human rights are respected, protecting all citizens of both countries and ending hate speech and verbal attacks), the strategic objectives (defeating the FDLR armed group and its auxiliaries, protecting the population and local infrastructure, ensuring the return of displaced persons and controlling natural resource extraction sites), the desired end state, the missions of the DRC (neutralise the FDLR, promote the repatriation of FDLR members to Rwanda, guarantee lasting peace and stability in the Great Lakes sub-region, protect the population and ensure the return of the displaced) and of Rwanda (disengage forces/lift the defensive measures it has put in place and ensure the social reintegration of demobilised and repatriated ex-FDLR combatants), and a four-phase plan of manoeuvre (preparation, conduct of operations, evaluation, stabilisation) with timelines running to D+120, neutralisation and the lifting of Rwanda's defensive measures to be completed within three months; logistical support is the responsibility of each country, which finances its own activities; and it lists the risks and constraints, including the stigmatisation of certain communities, the regionalisation of the conflict, FDLR reprisals against the population, and a lack of political will and mutual trust between Rwanda and the DRC.

title: Gov't confirms Tebelopele nationwide shutdown

acts.speaker: Christopher Nyanga, Ministry of Health spokesperson (Botswana)
acts.speech: Confirmed the cessation of operations at a few agencies, following their initial statement that the United States of America will withdraw from the World Health Organization, which would not affect the availability of ARVs: "There are multiple civil society organisations and non-governmental organisations operating in the health space that were directly affected by the decision to suspend support" ; He added that following this decision most CSOs and NGOs, especially arms performing functions in the HIV/AIDS prevention and treatment, have since closed for business like Tebelopele Voluntary Testing and Counselling centres across the country, "in compliance with the decision".

acts.speaker: Christopher Nyanga, Ministry of Health spokesperson (Botswana)
acts.speech: Nyanga assured citizens that despite the recent developments, government would still be able to meet the demands of such services.

acts.speaker: Ministry of Health of Botswana (statement)
acts.speech: The ministry has since then advised Batswana to opt for public health services as there is uncertainty as to how long this predicament will persist ; "The ministry also wishes to inform the public that all possible efforts will be made to avail lubricants, condoms and other preventive devices at both public and private facilities so that no gap is experienced" ; The ministry highlighted that to mitigate the situation it would ensure that there are ARVs available at post offices despite the discontinued services at the centres.

title: Suite à notre article sur la visite de Bolloré au port : les autorités portuaires réagissent

acts.speaker: Port authorities of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou
acts.speech: Said that Vincent Bolloré came to the port solely to see the progress of the quay and terminal construction works that his group is building there; the authorities remain doubtful about the reported extradition deal and believe that Vincent Bolloré made a purely professional visit that in no way went beyond the framework of his group's investments.

acts.speaker: Head of the communication service of the Port of Cotonou
acts.speech: Said Vincent Bolloré's visit is one of the routine visits he makes to Benin to check on the progress of the works, and that the port is currently awaiting further investment from the second MCC compact while it is urgent that the other works be completed quickly: "At the port with Vincent Bolloré, there was no talk of the arrest or extradition of Patrice Talon, and we think that elsewhere (the Marina) it was not discussed either." Added that the current Director General of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou, Kassim Traoré, is very preoccupied with resolving the urgent matters on the port platform and shares, like the Head of State, the dream of making the port one of the most modern and largest in the sub-region, in order to meet the demands of a growing clientele.

acts.speaker: Vincent Bolloré, CEO of the Bolloré group
acts.speech: Emphasised the importance of the financial component and the advantages that the port of Cotonou will be able to draw in the coming years from this financing, which will propel the port into the ranks of the modern ports of the world.

acts.speaker: La Nouvelle Tribune (the newspaper's own earlier article)
acts.speech: Had asserted that "Bolloré is not a philanthropist and in return he must expect something. Behind the scenes, we learn that Boni Yayi is said to have promised the PVI, the railways and Bénin Télécoms to Vincent Bolloré. In return, the latter was to help the government in its obsessive desire to arrest Talon."

title: Building a renewed social contract: Tackling youth unemployment and planning Ghana’s future

acts.speaker: Afrobarometer (most recent survey)
acts.speech: Found that unemployment consistently ranks as the top concern among Ghanaians, with 41 percent identifying it as their primary worry.

acts.speaker: The Ghana Compact for Political and Economic Transformation (document)
acts.speech: Highlights key challenges around the employment crisis, including a persistent skills mismatch, an educational system that operates in silos, and graduates ill-prepared for the workforce.

acts.speaker: KY Amoako, convenor of the Ghana Compact
acts.speech: Described the proposed National Convention as sending a much-needed powerful message of 'unity, resolve, and commitment to a prosperous, peaceful future'.

title: በቴክኖሎጂ እየተነጠቀ ያለው የንባብ ባህል - ሪፖርተር - Ethiopian Reporter - #1 Reliable News Source In Ethiopia

acts.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
acts.speech: Said the association, beginning from Sene 30, 2017 (Ethiopian calendar), has designated the rainy season (kiremt) as "Reading Day" and is working to develop the reading culture within society ; "Kiremt is when schools close. At this time it is necessary to make sure children do not spend their time in inappropriate places," explaining that the association's general assembly decided to make Sene 30 Reading Day so that children spend their time in reading, in knowledge and in enjoyment.

acts.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
acts.speech: Said that if a reading revolution is to come to Ethiopia the work must not be left to the Ethiopian Writers' Association alone, that at present the writer, the journalist, the politician, the religious father and other sections of society are not seen reading, and that almost everyone has turned his back on reading.

acts.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
acts.speech: "At present, with the spread of social media, most people spend the day glued to their mobile phones," adding that the parent therefore stays away from reading and the child, seeing this, also drifts away, and that if the parent does not explain the benefit of reading and cannot be a role model, the present and future generations will be a cause for concern ; "A parent who wants to lead children onto a good path, and a teacher who strives for a good student to emerge, must first read themselves if they want to have a reading child and student," since children imitate what they see.

acts.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
acts.speech: Said the Ministry of Education, being the ministry of knowledge, should take the lead in making reading a habit among children, that the Ministry of Culture and Sport is also expected to give attention to this, and that every well-intentioned Ethiopian who cares about tomorrow's generation should care about children's reading culture.

acts.speaker: Abera Adamu, President of the Ethiopian Writers' Association
acts.speech: Stated that the mass media bear great responsibility for growing children's reading culture, and that just as every European footballer's shoe size and the number of rooms in his house are broadcast on FM radio stations until European football seems Ethiopian, the same amount of work should be done to make reading a culture among Ethiopians.

acts.speaker: Sintayehu Tasew, children's book author
acts.speech: Said she has produced two children's books titled "Adey Sitnesa" and "Amoditna Gomaditna," and that the books have been distributed in schools and bookshops.

acts.speaker: Sintayehu Tasew, children's book author
acts.speech: "For children's reading culture to develop, the homework has first to be done at the level of the family. Because children accept and follow what they see, the family has a responsibility for the growth of children's reading habit," adding that even parents whose children have not yet reached reading age should have the habit of reading books to them, that parents should set aside a time of day even out of tight schedules, and that since children are becoming victims of technology the family must work hard so that children turn away from the phone and towards reading.

acts.speaker: Sintayehu Tasew, children's book author
acts.speech: "One cannot say a child is reading merely because he spent the day at school. Parents are expected to make their children work hard at reading today in order to see their child's bright and good tomorrow," expressing her belief that if books were made available at public gatherings, walks, bazaars and exhibitions — as tents are pitched and trading takes place during religious and public holidays — and if reading were preached there, the reading culture in Ethiopia would grow again.

acts.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
acts.speech: Explained that her ten-year-old child has so far read 245 books ; "I make my child read children's books and selected adult books," recalling that there had been a campaign at the German Cultural Centre called "When Ethiopia Reads, Germany Helps," that the writer and translator Yonas Tarekegn made great efforts to grow children's reading culture by inviting authors to schools and donating books, that she herself took part in this work, and that it contributed to the development of her child's reading culture.

acts.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
acts.speech: Said that if children are to become readers the parent must be a reader; that studies indicate parents should read books to children up to the age of ten, and that applying this to her own child made him successful ; "We should not have children read adult or children's books before we ourselves have read them first," explaining that during the coronavirus pandemic, when schools closed and children's books could not be found, she let her child read selected adult books, but only those she believed would add to his knowledge and assist his development.

acts.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
acts.speech: Explained that her child's habitual reading has made him successful in his academic studies, bold enough to ask about what he does not understand, and able to carry out tasks in a reasoned and accountable manner ; "When we gather at home and watch the news, we allow ideas to circulate. Although the news of the present time is full of war, the practice of watching is long-standing within the family," saying the discussions made her realise her child grieves at the crisis war brings and is an ardent seeker of peace, and that the substantial thoughts he raises about the war between Palestine and Israel come from reading books.

acts.speaker: Esete Taye, teacher at the modern school of the Meskaye Hizunan Medhanealem Monastery
acts.speech: Said children are a reflection of what they see, that parents should allocate time and develop the habit of reading with their children, and that because children resemble their family, parents are expected to be role models by reading books.

acts.speaker: Studies (cited)
acts.speech: Studies indicate that parents should read books to children up to the age of ten.

title: Ajuda chega a hospital no norte de Gaza após duas semanas de bloqueio

acts.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: "The WHO team and partners managed to reach Al Shifa hospital today [Thursday] and deliver 9,300 litres of fuel and medical supplies to care for a thousand trauma patients and one hundred kidney dialysis patients." ; Explained that Al Shifa has partially resumed services, which "means that fuel consumption is much higher and the need for medical supplies is increasing."

acts.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: In a post on the social network X, called for "sustained and safe access" in order to continue supplying medical materials, fuel, food and water to Al Shifa, which was Gaza's main hospital ; had appealed to Israel to authorise the entry of WHO staff and stressed that the main obstacle to the delivery of aid has not been the capacity of UN agencies, but rather the lack of access.

acts.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: "We insist once again that health must be protected and never be a target or militarised."

acts.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO) daily report
acts.speech: Revealed that it had had to cancel six missions to northern Gaza over the past two weeks, having failed to receive authorisation and security guarantees from Israel; the report detailed that missions to send emergency medical supplies to Gaza City's central pharmacy were denied on five occasions, and that the delivery of fuel needed to operate medical supply facilities was cancelled six times.

acts.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: Lamented new attacks on health facilities in Gaza, such as the one suffered on Wednesday by a Palestinian Red Crescent ambulance, in which four of the organisation's workers and two already-injured patients died.

acts.speaker: United Nations (UN)
acts.speech: Said on Thursday that only three of the 21 humanitarian aid missions to northern Gaza have been carried out since the beginning of January, because of delays at Israeli checkpoints and because many roads are impassable.

acts.speaker: Ministry of Health of Gaza
acts.speech: According to the ministry, Israeli attacks have caused 23,357 deaths and 59,410 injuries since the start of the conflict in the strip on 7 October.

title: Antigo Largo da Igreja no Centro Histórico da Praia: Um marco toponímico de outrora representativo da cultura religiosa local

acts.speaker: Edicts of the Secretariat-General of the Government of the Province of Cape Verde, 10 February 1876 (Official Bulletin no. 7/1876)
acts.speech: The document included a map of all the city's urban axes (squares, small squares, streets and alleys), presenting their names in two columns, the "old names" and the "modern names"; in its "modern" toponymy the space came to be called "largo do Sá da Bandeira."

acts.speaker: Luísa Reis Lima (1992, pp. 211-226), study
acts.speech: According to her interpretation, the tradition of naming streets, squares and small squares persisted over time in analogous situations across the Portuguese world.

acts.speaker: António Correia e Silva (1998, p. 53), study
acts.speech: Alludes to the "cemetery" adjacent to the Church, attesting to this location.

acts.speaker: Minutes of the session of 6 August 1874 of the Praia Council
acts.speech: Reported a plot behind the Town Hall, where at the time the Council's premises were to be enlarged; attention was drawn to the need to take into account the measurement of the graves in the foundation works to be carried out at that site.

acts.speaker: Chelmicki (1821, pp. 70-72), study
acts.speech: Identified the place, at the time, as an open site close to the church where the dead were buried.

acts.speaker: Santa Rita Vieira (1993, p. 26), study
acts.speech: Refers to the Hermitage in these terms: "(...) a hermitage in which the Holy Virgin was venerated under that invocation and which was still to be seen at the beginning of the eighteenth century at the foot of the hill of the site."

title: US, Germany launch $40m Coastal States Stability Mechanism programme

acts.speaker: Anne Witkowsky, US Assistant Secretary of State for Conflict and Stabilisation Operations
acts.speech: noted that the CSSM project marked an important step forward in its partnership with Ghana as they worked together to enhance resilience and security across coastal West Africa in the face of regional threats, as Ghana stood out as a leader in the region and the “United States is proud to support the country's security efforts”.

acts.speaker: Anne Witkowsky, US Assistant Secretary of State for Conflict and Stabilisation Operations
acts.speech: The CSSM, according to her, was part of a broader US Strategy to Prevent Conflict and Promote Stability (SPCPS) in coastal West Africa and beyond and reiterated that through the strategy, the US was seeking to enhance social cohesion, improve government responsiveness and support security. “Through these initiatives, we aim to create lasting impacts that contribute to a more secure and resilient Ghana and the region. When Africa succeeds, the world succeeds,” Ms Witkowsky said, further emphasising the importance of CSSM and the broader US commitment to promoting stability and preventing violent extremism in West Africa.

title: Lettre ouverte au président Assimi Goïta : La gestion du pouvoir soumise à rude épreuve

acts.speaker: Unidentified caller (suspected French intelligence agent), speaking to the author by WhatsApp
acts.speech: Asked the author what he was currently doing: "How are your affairs going?" "What are you doing at present?" "Where do you stand with your projects?" ; and offered: "We can help you with your project!" ; then specified: "The factory manufacturing irrigation pipes for precision agriculture. With my colleagues, we are going to organise a meeting to talk about it."

acts.speaker: Anonymous source who contacted the author three months later
acts.speech: Told the author that the group wanted to take advantage of his "not very glowing situation" and to request his help in their "subversive projects", in exchange guaranteeing him "lodging, a wife, money, exile"; but that they were in no way surprised by his reaction: "They knew they had a patriot in front of them; they found instead a chauvinist," concluded the source.

acts.speaker: General Charles de Gaulle (quotation often attributed to him)
acts.speech: "France has interests, France has no friends!"

acts.speaker: The only person to whom the author told the story (postscript)
acts.speech: "Why do you give up your interests for the benefit of those people when they profit from the Republic? Besides, you have not criticised this Transition regime, whereas we remember your salvos against all the past governments!"

acts.speaker: Abdou Karim Dramé, independent journalist/consultant, analyst of sustainable-development issues and innovations, researcher on accelerated growth strategies (open letter to President Assimi Goïta)
acts.speech: Wrote that he refused to collaborate with the "foreign agents", putting Mali's interests before his own, out of loyalty to the Fatherland of Mali ; argued that France resorts to all forms of subversion — support for separatist rebels, the instrumentalisation, financing and training of terrorist groups, political and economic interference — to install a regime favourable to it at the head of Mali, and that what is not normal is that Malians accept being plundered, robbed and dominated by France ; estimated Mali's development financing needs at 20 billion US dollars over the next five years and urged the country to turn to the major sovereign wealth funds and investment capital.

title: Lesotho shocked by Trump's remarks that 'nobody has heard of the country'

acts.speaker: Government of Lesotho
acts.speech: says it is shocked by US President Donald Trump saying that “nobody has ever heard of” the southern African nation.

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
acts.speech: “Eight million dollars to promote LGBTQI+ in the African nation of Lesotho, which nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said, made while addressing the US Congress as he listed cuts to what he said was wasteful expenditure.

acts.speaker: Spokesperson for Lesotho’s foreign affairs department (unnamed)
acts.speech: told the BBC that Lesotho enjoyed “warm and cordial” relations with the US.

acts.speaker: US government
acts.speech: According to the US government, the two countries traded goods worth $240m (£187m) in 2024, mostly exports from Lesotho to the US, in particular textiles and clothing.

acts.speaker: Lejone Mpotjoane, Lesotho’s Foreign Affairs Minister
acts.speech: said it was “shocking” to hear a head of state “refer to another sovereign state in that manner” ; “To my surprise, ‘the country that nobody has heard of’ is the country where the US has a permanent mission” ; “Lesotho is a member of the UN and of a number of other international bodies. And the US has an embassy here and [there are] a number of US organisations we’ve accommodated here in Maseru.”

acts.speaker: Lesotho officials (unnamed)
acts.speech: dismissed Trump’s remarks as “off the cuff” and a “political statement”, adding that they were “uncalled-for” given the good relations between the two nations.

acts.speaker: Kutloano Pheko, Lesotho foreign affairs spokesperson
acts.speech: “We maintain very warm and cordial relations with the US. They’ve got a mission in Maseru and we also have [one] in Washington,” Mr Pheko told the BBC ; was unable to confirm Trump’s comments on the funding that went to LGBTQ organisations, saying that as the money went directly to them, they would be best placed to comment.

acts.speaker: Lejone Mpotjoane, Lesotho’s Foreign Affairs Minister
acts.speech: confirmed that the country had been affected by Trump’s sudden decision to pause aid funding to countries around the world, but declined to criticise this decision, saying it was the US’s “prerogative to cut aid if they want to”.

acts.speaker: Lesotho health ministry
acts.speech: told South African publication GroundUp in February that Lesotho is among those countries that benefited from Pepfar, with TB and HIV programmes among those receiving the critical funds.

title: Malawi needs more banks, parties missing the point

acts.speaker: Richard Werner, economist known for his theory of credit creation
acts.speech: argues that banks are not intermediaries that lend out deposits, as commonly believed; instead, banks create money through the process of credit creation – when a bank issues a loan, it simultaneously creates a deposit in the borrower’s account, effectively generating new money.

acts.speaker: Reserve Bank of Malawi
acts.speech: According to the Reserve Bank of Malawi, only about 30% of Malawians have access to formal banking services.

acts.speaker: World Bank data
acts.speech: According to World Bank data, countries like Germany and France have over 30 commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults, while Malawi lags far behind.

title: Tunisie : l’arrestation d’un député dans la flottille fait débat

acts.speaker: Group of Tunisian members of parliament of the Assembly of the Representatives of the People (ARP) (joint statement)
acts.speech: Forcefully denounced the "criminal abduction" of their colleague Mohamed Ali, arrested with other members of the global Soumoud flotilla as they were heading to Gaza to deliver humanitarian aid, describing the operation carried out by Israeli forces as a "flagrant violation of international law and humanitarian law." According to them, this arrest constitutes not only an infringement of freedom of movement and of humanitarian action, but also "a direct attack on a sovereign institution embodying the will of the Tunisian people."

acts.speaker: Group of Tunisian members of parliament of the Assembly of the Representatives of the People (ARP) (joint statement)
acts.speech: The parliamentarians demand the immediate and unconditional release of the deputy and of all those arrested aboard the vessel. They hold Israel "entirely responsible" for the safety of Tunisian citizens, considering that this act represents a provocation toward the Tunisian people as a whole.

acts.speaker: Group of Tunisian members of parliament of the Assembly of the Representatives of the People (ARP) (joint statement)
acts.speech: The signatories call for a firm national response and request that an extraordinary session of parliament be held. They also propose the establishment of an emergency commission to coordinate with the Tunisian authorities and international organisations with a view to securing the rapid release of the detainees. ; Finally, the deputies urge the international community, foreign parliaments and human rights organisations to condemn these "abuses" and to intervene to guarantee the protection of the flotilla's participants.

source: AMAP (Agence Malienne de Presse et de Publicité)
title: Koulouba : le chef de l'Etat malien reçoit le ministre des Affaires étrangères de la Mauritanie - amap

acts.speaker: Mohamed Salem Ould Merzoug, Mauritanian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Cooperation and Mauritanians Abroad
acts.speech: "The two heads of state have this shared desire to consolidate, diversify and strengthen this relationship in the interest of the two peoples and for the benefit of the whole sub-region" ; expressed his satisfaction at having a perfect identity of views with the Malian side on all the questions addressed.

acts.speaker: Mohamed Salem Ould Merzoug, Mauritanian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Cooperation and Mauritanians Abroad
acts.speech: Recalled that the majority of African migratory movements take place within the continent: "80% of African migrants remain in Africa, within the framework of traditional migrations that are often beneficial to local economies and to social cohesion" ; expressed his keen concern at the worrying rise of irregular immigration orchestrated by human trafficking networks: "In 2024, more than 500 bodies of young Africans were recovered off our coasts, and more than 100 since the beginning of this year. It is a human tragedy that we must confront together" ; insisted on the need for a coordinated and anticipatory response based on cooperation between states: "It is imperative to combat these criminal networks and to encourage regular, safe and orderly migration, in strict respect of national legislation and bilateral agreements."

acts.speaker: Mohamed Salem Ould Merzoug, Mauritanian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Cooperation and Mauritanians Abroad
acts.speech: Reaffirmed the fraternal and hospitable character of relations between the two peoples regarding Malian nationals living in Mauritania: "A Malian who arrives in Mauritania is at home, just as a Mauritanian who goes to Mali is. Those who are in a regular situation live in complete peace. The difficulties mainly concern unregistered persons, which requires better organisation on both sides" ; "What we ask of people is to ensure that what we are preparing together is respected."

acts.speaker: Communique of the Malian presidency
acts.speech: States that the exchange "made it possible to address questions of common interest, notably the strengthening of bilateral cooperation and the concerted management of migratory flows."

acts.speaker: Mohamed Ould El-Ghazaouani, President of Mauritania
acts.speech: Sent a message to the President of the Transition, Army General Assimi Goita, carried by his Minister of Foreign Affairs.

title: Les États-Unis au Sahel : sécurité ou ressources ?

acts.speaker: Ulf Laessing, regional expert
acts.speech: Notes that Washington has already offered to eliminate certain extremist leaders on condition of obtaining access to the exploitation of natural resources.

acts.speaker: Troy Fitrell, US official
acts.speech: Declared, in Abidjan in May, that trade, and not aid, would be the pillar of the new American policy in Africa.

acts.speaker: Dorothy Shea, US official
acts.speech: Underscores at the UN that the destabilization of the region could directly affect American interests.

title: Experts warn HIV efforts at risk amid funding cuts

acts.speaker: HIV response researchers (experts addressing the press ahead of the IAS 2025 Conference)
acts.speech: Have sounded the alarm over recent global funding cuts, saying they have severely disrupted efforts to combat HIV, threatening life-saving research, prevention and treatment; presented scientific highlights from four studies selected from abstracts being showcased at the conference, revealing predictive modelling and real-world data from Africa and Latin America, indicating rising HIV acquisitions, stalled treatment and fragile health systems.

acts.speaker: Dr Beatriz Grinsztejn, IAS president
acts.speech: Said that, on one hand, the world is witnessing extraordinary scientific breakthroughs that could transform prevention and treatment and “even bring us closer to a cure” ; “On the other hand, these very advances are under threat from massive funding cuts that risk stalling clinical trials, slowing our progress and jeopardising the achievements we’ve fought so hard to attain.”

acts.speaker: Professor Kenneth Ngure, IAS president-elect
acts.speech: Said that the sudden cuts to United States (US) funding, announced earlier this year, have been “deeply felt” across the African continent by millions of people who rely on HIV prevention, testing and treatment services.

acts.speaker: Preprint modelling study presented by lead author Dr Jack Stone, Associate Professor in Infectious Disease Mathematical Modelling at the University of Bristol
acts.speech: Finds that HIV incidence and related deaths are expected to rise significantly in sub-Saharan Africa due to disruptions in funding for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) under Pepfar; suggests that the pause in PrEP funding from January 2025 — after PEPFAR-funded PrEP had been accessed by nearly 700,000 people across 28 sub-Saharan African countries, including Malawi, by late 2024 — could result in approximately 6,671 additional HIV acquisitions over one year, and a further 3,617 cases over the subsequent five years, with more than 2,900 of these additional cases projected among gay and bisexual men who have sex with men and over 2,000 among female sex workers.

acts.speaker: Dr Jack Stone, Associate Professor in Infectious Disease Mathematical Modelling at the University of Bristol
acts.speech: “It is crucial that funding is secured to continue and expand PrEP services in sub-Saharan Africa.”

acts.speaker: Zackie Achmat, founder of the Treatment Action Campaign and member of the Global HIV Treatment Coalition
acts.speech: Issued a call to action on the urgent need for debt refinancing to protect the HIV response in low- and middle-income countries: “You can’t end the Aids pandemic while African nations must choose between paying creditors and saving lives. As someone who has lived with HIV for more than half my life, I have seen the cost of political inaction.” ; “We fought for treatment when the world said it was impossible. Now, the convergence of crushing debt and funding cuts threatens everything we’ve built. We need urgent debt restructuring so African countries can invest in saving lives instead of servicing debt.”

title: US health aid cut hurts – Musokotwane

acts.speaker: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Zambian Finance and National Planning Minister
acts.speech: Says it has been tough dealing with the abruptness of the cut in the United States’ funding to the health sector, and that it would have been better to be told two years earlier; admitted that donor aid cannot last forever but criticised the manner of the withdrawal. “It’s been tough dealing with the abruptness of the cut. Of course, everyone knows that aid is not meant to last forever, and at some point we have to become less aid-dependent. But what’s been difficult is how suddenly it’s being implemented. It would have been better to be told two, three, or even four years ahead – but that didn’t happen.”

acts.speaker: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Zambian Finance and National Planning Minister
acts.speech: Noted that the tough US tariffs would hurt Zambia as an exporter of copper ; ruled out cutting ties with the US, insisting that “we will not disengage from US because of this. There are problems but we are hopeful this can be resolved.”

acts.speaker: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Zambian Finance and National Planning Minister
acts.speech: Has called for a fundamental shift in how the country approaches its mining sector, stressing the urgent need to increase mineral production, and reminded delegates that national prosperity hinges on growth in output – not the preservation of outdated systems. “If we are going to create environments that benefit many people, that only happens when we produce more and more.” ; “This country will not become wealthy if we keep producing copper in the same quantity as we did in 1964,” he warned.

title: Ali-Sabieh : Pour une implication accrue des tuteurs d’élèves dans la stratégie de renforcement de l’apprentissage de la lecture des apprenants à l’école de base

acts.speaker: Moussa Aden Miganeh, Prefect of the Ali-Sabieh region (representative of the public authorities in the region)
acts.speech: Underlined the importance of this workshop focused on the learning of reading in basic school. He made it known that the strengthening of reading must not stop at school and that support for it must continue into the family home with the guidance of parents.

acts.speaker: Charmake Hassan Allaleh, President of the Ali-Sabieh regional council
acts.speech: Said he was proud to host at the seat of his institution a workshop on a school subject that is nothing less than the key to teaching and learning, and that mastery of reading is essential in primary school. To this end, he stressed in his address, it is essential to make parents or guardians of pupils aware of the crucial importance for learners of knowing how to read and understand texts.

acts.speaker: Abdillahi Omar, coordinator of the literacy programme at the National Union of Djiboutian Women (UNFD)
acts.speech: Recalled the divine injunction given to the Prophet of Islam at the very beginning of his revelation: "Read, read, read in the name of the GOOD LORD" — a fine way of proclaiming the greatness, for a human being, of knowing how to read through religious texts. He recalled the two strands that this component seeks to improve: pupils' reading performance in basic education from the 1st to the 5th year in the country, through the involvement of community organisations such as parents' associations and school management committees.

acts.speaker: Ahmed Hamadou Ibrahim, regional inspector and head of service of the Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training (MENFOP)
acts.speech: Said he was enthusiastic about witnessing the assistance of public education partners in a field that is essential to learning and teaching. Reading is the key to learning well; it is a means for schoolchildren to learn. Involving pupils' guardians is a strategy that will certainly strengthen mastery of knowing how to read and understand.

acts.speaker: Head teachers of the basic schools
acts.speech: Set out the reading-strengthening activities implemented since the beginning of the current school year, including support classes scheduled outside normal class hours, each school putting in place extra hours of support classes for children with learning difficulties.

title: Children pay highest price of climate woes - Nation Online

acts.speaker: Mary Sapeza, 21, mother from Kwatani Village, Phalombe
acts.speech: “I only harvested two bags of maize last growing season and that lasted until May,” she says with exhaustion. “Now I do piecework to get daily food.” ; “Now weight has improved to 7.5 kilogrammes,” says Sapeza, proudly clutching her baby’s health passport.

acts.speaker: Beatrice Muchiri, 25, mother from Mwambeni Village, Phalombe
acts.speech: Says her 19-month-old daughter is also recovering from wasting fuelled by drought: “I have been coming here weekly, and she is getting better. Her appetite is back.”

acts.speaker: Lucy Ndiwo, Phalombe chief nutrition, HIV and Aids officer
acts.speech: “Our district experiences disasters which disrupt food production almost every year. This leaves families unable to feed themselves and malnutrition cases keep rising, especially among children and pregnant women.”

acts.speaker: 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Survey
acts.speech: According to the survey, 38.7 percent of children under five are stunted, 10 percent are underweight and two percent are wasted.

acts.speaker: Health workers
acts.speech: Say poor nutrition in the critical first 1 000 days of life causes irreversible damage to a child’s health, physical growth, learning and productivity.

acts.speaker: Rebecca Adda-Dontoh, United Nations resident coordinator in Malawi
acts.speech: Said the UN is committed to support Malawi’s health and nutrition agenda: “Malawi 2063 prioritises a healthy population as a cornerstone for national development. The SDGs echo the same. So, malnutrition is not just a health issue—it is a development bottleneck.” ; “We are not going anywhere. The UN will continue standing with Malawi, its people and its systems, to build resilience and secure a better future.”

title: FMI–Mali : À quoi serviront les 129 millions de dollars débloqués ? - Mali 24

acts.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
acts.speech: Announced on Wednesday 16 April the immediate disbursement of 129 million dollars, about 78.5 billion CFA francs, to support Mali in managing the consequences of the deadly floods of September and October 2024 ; according to the IMF, the floods caused significant damage to infrastructure, destroyed vast areas of farmland and undermined the livelihoods of thousands of families.

acts.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
acts.speech: Foresees that the funds will also serve to strengthen the country's resilience to climate shocks, through the implementation of adaptation policies, improved early-warning systems and investment in sustainable infrastructure ; requires reforms in return for the aid.

acts.speaker: Malian authorities
acts.speech: Committed to strengthening tax administration and broadening the tax base, in order to increase State revenue and guarantee a lasting economic recovery.

title: Industrial Corp Blooms with $100m Investment

acts.speaker: Aklilu Tadesse, CEO of the Industrial Parks Development Corporation (IPDC)
acts.speech: Aklilu said service delivery improvements have greatly increased the investment flow in the parks last year with 5,000 job opportunities expected to be open through this investment.

acts.speaker: International Trade Portal
acts.speech: According to the International Trade Portal, FDI inflows to Ethiopia increased to 4.2 billion dollars in 2021, up from 2.4 billion dollars the previous year.

title: Una Mtoto Mwenye Umri Kati ya Miaka Miwili na Sita? Haya Yatakusaidia Kumjengea Nidhamu - The Chanzo

acts.speaker: Dr Daniel Siegel, professor of psychology and author of the book The Whole-Brain Child
acts.speech: Stresses that when children make mistakes they need to be guided and not punished or shamed. This is where the concept of positive discipline comes in, by teaching children to control their emotions and behaviour in ways that build them up rather than hurt them.

acts.speaker: Research studies (cited)
acts.speech: Studies show that caning and shouting often cause fear and a discipline of fear rather than of understanding; these punishments can badly affect a child's mental health and self-confidence, increase aggressive behaviour, reduce the capacity for self-control, and weaken the relationship between parent and child.

acts.speaker: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
acts.speech: Has found that physical punishment can build a habit of cruelty in children when they become adults, because they learn to use violence and domination to resolve conflicts and challenges.

title: Youth Response for Social Change nullifies 320 child marriages in Machinga - Malawi24

acts.speaker: Triza Nyirenda, Communication Coordinator, Youth Response for Social Change
acts.speech: Said the organisation nullifies child marriages through a project called “Social Transformation for Ending Child Marriages,” implemented in six traditional authorities in Machinga with funding from USAID ; added that Youth Response nullifies child marriages in traditional authorities, among them Nyambi, Mizinga, Chikweo, Mchinguza and Paramount Chief Kawinga ; said out of the 320 girls, 65 of them were referred to learn vocational skills to sustain their livelihood, while the rest went back to school ; “From 2021 to this year, Youth Response for Social Change nullified 320 marriages in Machinga. This is an alarming figure.”

acts.speaker: Triza Nyirenda, Communication Coordinator, Youth Response for Social Change
acts.speech: Called on the government and other organisations to collaborate in ending child marriages so that girls can go back to school to continue with their education, and said there was a need to continue supporting the girls with educational materials once they return to school to ensure they concentrate on their education.

acts.speaker: Masautso Katemera, Inspector and Community Policing Coordinator, Machinga Police Station
acts.speech: Said child marriage is a concern in Machinga due to poverty and cultural practices ; said police continue to engage communities on the negative implications of child marriages, and commended Youth Response NGO for taking the lead in nullifying child marriages in Machinga.

title: Élection de Donald Trump : quel impact pour l'Afrique ? -

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
acts.speech: Has already promised to impose significant tariffs on foreign imports, but his position on the future of AGOA, which is due to be renewed next year, is unclear.

acts.speaker: Ronak Gopaldas, consultant at the Institute for Security Studies (ISS)
acts.speech: "Under a Trump administration, with its 'America First' mantra, trade policy would probably be insular and transactional. Given Trump's scepticism towards multilateral frameworks, the survival of AGOA could legitimately be under threat." ; Notes that while "Africa may not be among the priorities" of Trump, "his first administration pushed for trade deals with certain hand-picked African countries, which suggests a preference for bilateral engagement."

acts.speaker: General Michael Langley, head of the US military command for Africa (Africom)
acts.speech: In September, reported discussions with other African partners in order to "reset and recalibrate" American military assistance on the continent.

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
acts.speech: Has already criticised the billions of dollars spent by the United States on Ukraine.

acts.speaker: US State Department
acts.speech: According to the State Department, the United States is an important provider of aid to Africa, with $4 billion (3.7 billion euros) planned for 2024.

acts.speaker: Some South African media
acts.speech: Are already wondering whether the American programme of aid for the fight against HIV, called Pepfar, will continue.

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
acts.speech: Has described climate change as a hoax, and has pledged to roll back the environmental measures taken by his predecessor.

acts.speaker: Mohamed Adow, Kenyan activist and director of the NGO Power Shift Africa (statement)
acts.speech: "The world has experienced (the first) Trump presidency and the American withdrawal from the Paris agreement. His return (...) is a moment of profound apprehension in global climate diplomacy."

title: Le Sahel veut repenser sa coopération

acts.speaker: Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, Mali's Minister of Territorial Administration
acts.speech: Declared in his address that “it is essential to rethink international cooperation in the Sahel in depth in order to make it relevant in the face of contemporary realities,” and that the meeting is “a precious opportunity to share ideas, exchange experiences and build together a promising future for the States and the peoples of the Sahel.”

acts.speaker: Abdoulaye Diop, Mali's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation
acts.speech: Spoke of a reconfiguration of international cooperation, long based on development aid: “This reconfiguration begins on the basis of the three principles that we have put forward. Until now, cooperation with the countries of the Sahel, or cooperation with Mali, has been based on what is called development aid” ; “But one cannot develop on the basis of aid,” stating that it is necessary to leave this framework and enter into win-win partnership frameworks.

title: AVCA Announces Lagos To Host Largest Africa-Focussed Investment Event

acts.speaker: African Private Capital Association (AVCA)
acts.speech: Announced Lagos as the host city for the AVCA Annual Conference and Venture Capital Summit in 2025.

acts.speaker: Panellists at the 3rd Annual AVCA Venture Capital Summit
acts.speech: Took stock of the global decline of VC funding and explored a range of solutions to catalyse growth ; speakers marked the influence of rapidly emerging technologies shaping African innovation and driving the digital economy, creating new skills and increasing efficiency, such as artificial intelligence, blockchain and quantum computing.

acts.speaker: Andre Jr. Ayotte, Partner, Modus Capital
acts.speech: Speaking on the panel 'The DeepTech Potential in African Tech', highlighted how founders can apply technology to build companies solving problems at scale.

acts.speaker: Nick Allen, Managing Partner, Savant
acts.speech: Noted that gaps in Africa's tertiary education system have led to a lack of skilled graduates with sufficient engineering knowledge; added that in comparison to more developed markets such as Europe and the US, there is a lack of investors who understand how to finance deep tech in Africa.

acts.speaker: Khaled Ben Jilani, Senior Partner, AfricInvest
acts.speech: Raised the importance of active strategies to make businesses less capital intensive in order to anticipate new risks and navigate a lack of liquidity in the market.

acts.speaker: Steve Beck, Co-Founder and Managing Partner, Novastar Ventures
acts.speech: Expressed that private equity firms and development finance institutions (DFIs) with dedicated VC teams had stepped in to partially fill the funding gaps, particularly in the early stages.

title: Banjul salue la condamnation d'un ancien «Jungler» aux États-Unis

acts.speaker: Ministry of Justice of The Gambia (official statement)
acts.speech: Issued an official statement concerning the conviction of Michael Sang Correa, qualifying the conviction as an "important milestone" and a "significant victory in the global quest for justice for victims of human rights abuses" ; "This conviction sends a clear message: the perpetrators of human rights violations will find no refuge," the statement says, recalling the Gambian government's commitment to "preserving the rule of law and guaranteeing justice for all victims of former president Jammeh."

acts.speaker: Government of The Gambia
acts.speech: Expressed its "deep gratitude" to the American government for "its unwavering commitment to justice," particularly praising the team of prosecutors who handled the case.

acts.speaker: Ministry of Justice of The Gambia
acts.speech: Announced that it is working to establish an Office of the Special Prosecutor to begin trials concerning the crimes investigated by the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC).

acts.speaker: US indictment (acte d'accusation) in the Correa case
acts.speech: According to the indictment, the facts date back to the brutal repression carried out after the failed coup of 2006; alleged coup plotters were violently tortured at Mile 2 prison and at the headquarters of the National Intelligence Agency (NIA) in Banjul, by methods including beatings with military boots, pipes, electrical wires and sticks, as well as electrocutions, suffocation with plastic bags and even acid attacks.

acts.speaker: Brian A. Benczkowski, US Department of Justice assistant attorney general
acts.speech: When the case was opened, denounced Correa's "heinous acts of violence," aimed at extracting confessions through terror.

acts.speaker: Pharing Sanyang, former commander at the presidential palace in Banjul in 2006 (witness)
acts.speech: Testified that he still bears the scars of the abuse suffered after being accused of taking part in the attempted coup, and described Correa as "very aggressive" during the torture sessions aimed at extracting false confessions from him.

acts.speaker: Ebou Jarjue, former waiter at the presidential palace in Banjul, 2001-2008 (witness)
acts.speech: Testified that he was detained for more than nine months and then imprisoned at Mile II for four years, after being falsely accused of having tried to poison President Jammeh.

acts.speaker: Tamsir Jasseh, former director general of immigration of The Gambia (witness)
acts.speech: Testified that he was tortured and convicted on the basis of forced confessions for having helped a political opponent flee the country, despite his dual American nationality; he described Correa as "overzealous" and said that he "enjoyed himself" while torturing detainees.

title: Interview with the Director of the Department of Partnership with Africa of the Russian Foreign Ministry, T.E.Dovgalenko, RIA Novosti (February 20, 2025)

acts.speaker: T.E. Dovgalenko, Director of the Department of Partnership with Africa of the Russian Foreign Ministry
acts.speech: On the department's main areas of work: “Our task is to develop comprehensive relations with Africa and strengthen their truly strategic character. Today it is a dynamically developing continent. It is not only and not so much about the huge natural resources that are the key to the economic sovereignty of African countries, but also about the colossal human capital.” ; Building relations with the African Union, as well as regional and sub-regional associations of the continent, alliances of states, multilateral formats and mechanisms is another key area of the department's work.

acts.speaker: T.E. Dovgalenko, Director of the Department of Partnership with Africa of the Russian Foreign Ministry
acts.speech: On the impetus for Russian-African relations: “In recent years, Russian-African cooperation has reached a qualitatively new level. The first and second Russia–Africa summits, as well as the first ministerial conference of the Russia–Africa Partnership Forum last November, provided a powerful impetus for this. Together with our African friends, we are working on the practical implementation of the agreements reached, based on the Action Plan adopted at the summit in St. Petersburg.”

acts.speaker: T.E. Dovgalenko, Director of the Department of Partnership with Africa of the Russian Foreign Ministry
acts.speech: On trade: “The volume of trade and economic cooperation, which reached a record high of $24.5 billion in 2023, continues to grow. Work is underway on the implementation of major investment projects on the continent, including in the fields of energy, the creation of transport and logistics chains, the formation of a system of secure mutual settlements, high technologies, including space exploration and digital technologies.”

acts.speaker: T.E. Dovgalenko, Director of the Department of Partnership with Africa of the Russian Foreign Ministry
acts.speech: On the Sahel States Alliance: “The creation of the Sahel States Alliance Confederation is an important step in consolidating the efforts of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger to ensure national security and address socio-economic challenges. The most important goal of the association is to counter the terrorist threat in the Sahara-Sahel zone. The situation in the region is really difficult, including with the help of the West, which was directly involved in the destruction of Libyan statehood in 2011. Russia provides assistance both in strengthening counter-terrorism capabilities and increasing the combat capability of the national armed forces by sending military specialists and equipment, training military personnel and law enforcement officers, and in the socio-economic development of the countries of the region.”

acts.speaker: T.E. Dovgalenko, Director of the Department of Partnership with Africa of the Russian Foreign Ministry
acts.speech: On food aid: “Our country provides humanitarian assistance to the needy population of African countries both through bilateral channels and through international organizations. The United Nations World Food Program is a key multilateral channel for us to provide such assistance.
