acts.speech: According to the report, released in Washington in August 2025, Ghana is ineligible to receive U.S. foreign assistance under section 7012 of the Fiscal Year 2025 State, Foreign Operations and Related Programs Appropriations Act.

acts.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
acts.speech: explained that while Ghana met the income threshold for consideration, the legal prohibition automatically disqualified the country from compact eligibility because of debt default.

title: Somalia, Azerbaijan Explore Partnership in Investment and Green Energy

acts.speaker: Abdisalam Abdi Ali, Somali Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation
acts.speech: Appreciated Azerbaijan's role in strengthening ties and emphasized the importance of developing a partnership that delivers significant and enduring benefits to both countries.

acts.speaker: Ali Asadov, Prime Minister of Azerbaijan
acts.speech: Reaffirmed that Azerbaijan places great importance on strengthening relations with Somalia and expressed satisfaction with the mutual support the two countries continue to provide each other within international organizations.

title: Governor Mamo Takes a Swing at Inflation

acts.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE)
acts.speech: Candidly addressed the challenges the economy has been grappling with, particularly the inflation rate, which he admitted was aggravated by “uncharacteristically loose” fiscal and monetary policies over the past two years ; “These were deemed necessary to mitigate the impact of the war, drought, and the massive internal displacement,” the Governor said in a press conference at the Central Bank’s headquarters on Sudan Street. “But we’re seeing the consequences.”

acts.speaker: Mamo Mihretu, Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE)
acts.speech: Maintained that the rate would not decrease total borrowing but merely keep it from ballooning unnecessarily.

acts.speaker: Fiscal and monetary experts
acts.speech: Who have long argued for budget discipline and a tighter monetary stance, met the announcements with approval.

acts.speaker: Abdulmenan Mohammed (PhD), London-based financial analyst
acts.speech: Concurs with a general policy shift towards an interest-based monetary policy framework. He emphasised on political autonomy of the central bank as of first-order importance. Successfully moving past the reserve-prioritising central banking framework requires a simultaneous upgrade to the structural integrity of the institution. The mandatory treasury bond purchases of commercial banks imposed by the central bank contradicted a general orientation towards politically independent central banking, he argued ; “The central bank's independence is crucial for its effectiveness,” he told Fortune ; “It’s a return to a more sensible, stringent fiscal approach. However, while commendable, aiming for a 20pc inflation rate might be a tad optimistic.”

acts.speaker: Abdulmenan Mohammed (PhD), London-based financial analyst
acts.speech: Warns: “We could see a preference for certain customers, potentially leading to corrupt lending practices.”

acts.speaker: Tewodros Mekonen (PhD), macroeconomist with ties to the London School of Economics
acts.speech: Agrees that abandoning the reserve-based orientation in monetary policy requires credible institutions but asserts that development objectives in a poor country can be calibrated by maintaining the transparency of the central bank despite slight nudges from the government. He characterised the new trajectory of the Central Bank as a hybrid of interest and reserve-based monetary policy frameworks ; “While the measures are steps in the right direction, the federal government must exercise caution and avoid viewing the central bank as an open treasury,” he told Fortune.

acts.speaker: Tewodros Mekonen (PhD), macroeconomist with ties to the London School of Economics
acts.speech: Argued that despite credit growth over the years, most funds have been absorbed by the public sector through the state-owned behemoth, the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE) ; “The private sector has been crowded out of the credit market,” he said while indicating that governments are generally inefficient resource allocators.

acts.speaker: Tewodros Mekonen (PhD), macroeconomist with ties to the London School of Economics
acts.speech: Summed up the sentiment succinctly: “Consistent application of publicly stated policy garners trust in the market.”

acts.speaker: International community and multilateral financial institutions like the IMF
acts.speech: Have consistently advocated for a blend of interest and reserve-based monetary policy frameworks for countries like Ethiopia.

acts.speaker: Sisay Amare, head of the Ethiopian Pulses, Oilseeds & Spices Processors Exporters Association (EPOSPEO)
acts.speech: Welcomed the forex adjustment. “We’ve been advocating for a change in these,” he told Fortune. “This could mean an uptick in our foreign exchange accounts.” ; While recognising the role of a lower retention rate for exporters in declining forex inflow, he disclosed that too much of it would be spent on importing consumption goods: “Even if the forex surrender rate were zero, the import demand would not be met.”

acts.speaker: Gizat Worku, leading Ethiopian coffee export business figure
acts.speech: “This is an incentivising move. We’ve already stored export-ready coffee, promising good revenue ahead of the next harvest season.” ; Indicated that several levers and gears would need to be tweaked in productivity and efficiency to tackle the forex woes of a country largely reliant on agricultural produce for its forex earnings.

acts.speaker: Aklilu Wubet, president of Wegagen Bank
acts.speech: “Inflation has become a formidable challenge for the Ethiopian economy,” he told Fortune. “It’s imperative for banks to rally behind efforts to stabilise our economic landscape.” ; Had expected the move by the Central Bank to limit credit growth and increase interest rates on emergency loans to limit the money supply in the economy: “Excess credit might be fueling inflation.”

title: Trump celebrates 100 days in office with campaign-style rally

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
acts.speech: Promised Tuesday that he is just getting started, touting the "most successful first 100 days of any administration in the history of our country" ; told reporters he was on track to accomplish all of his second-term goals: "I think either we've done everything, or it's in the process of being done," Trump said before heading to his rally ; Trump said he missed the campaign trail.

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
acts.speech: Listing targets of his ire, said Joe Biden is "sleepy," the media is "fake," judges who oppose him are "communist," Democratic opponents are "radical left," and friendly countries have "abused us more so than foe on trade"; the president promised to conclude deals on trade, but provided little in the way of details.

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
acts.speech: Criticized Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell Tuesday as "not really doing a good job."

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
acts.speech: Claimed the pledge to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours was made "in jest."

acts.speaker: Jerome Powell, Federal Reserve chairman
acts.speech: Has warned that Trump's tariffs would likely reignite inflation.

acts.speaker: Donna Fitzsimons, 65-year-old merchandise seller at the Michigan rally venue
acts.speech: "He's amazing. Everybody's worried about tariffs. We don't care — look at everything else that's coming together too" ; "People don't realize it takes time to get where you need to go."

acts.speaker: Democratic National Committee
acts.speech: "Trump is to blame for the fact that life is more expensive, it's harder to retire, and a 'Trump recession' is at our doorstep," the Democratic National Committee said, calling the 100 days a "colossal failure."

acts.speaker: CNN
acts.speech: Reported that he made the 24-hour Ukraine pledge more than 50 times before taking office, and was even at pains to point out that he was being serious.

title: Africa will play a crucial role in the rising new world

acts.speaker: Patrice Lumumba (quoted epigraph)
acts.speech: “I prefer to die with my head unbowed, my faith unshakeable and with profound trust in the destiny of my country, rather than live under subjection and disregarding sacred principles. History will one day have its say, but it will not be the history that is taught in Brussels, Paris, Washington or in the United Nations. But the history which will be taught in the countries freed from imperialism and its puppets.”

acts.speaker: Declaration adopted following the second Russia-Africa summit in St Petersburg (document)
acts.speech: Africa is proclaimed as playing an “increasing global role and influence as one of the key pillars of a multipolar world.”

acts.speaker: Experts (demographic projections)
acts.speech: Estimate that by 2050, the continent’s population could reach 2.5 billion, meaning one in four people on Earth will be African.

acts.speaker: Informed Russian experts
acts.speech: According to informed Russian experts, African countries “support each other on the global stage and adopt common positions on many current international issues.”

acts.speaker: African experts
acts.speech: Lament that the West is unwilling “to recognize the right of the continent’s countries to set their own agenda” and that its policy toward opponents amounts to “punishing them for having their own interests”; some Africans openly call on “the EU and other U.S. allies not to impose their way of life and values on those who do not wish it.”

acts.speaker: African experts (on colonialism)
acts.speech: Believe that the foundations of the continent’s complex underdevelopment and the conflicts arising from territorial and ethno-religious divisions were largely laid by the predatory policies of colonizers.

acts.speaker: African experts (on Western aid)
acts.speech: Lament that, for example, the US Agency for International Development (USAID) predominantly promotes a political agenda rooted in neoliberal globalist ideology, prioritizing activities in Africa such as promoting “democracy, supporting civil society, and assisting in leadership elections.”

acts.speaker: Bernard Dadie, poet (Cote d'Ivoire) (quoted epigraph)
acts.speech: “God deliver us from Europe, which cares about our freedom.”

acts.speaker: Bai T. Moore, Liberian poet
acts.speech: Wrote in the 1950s, “Civilization is in full swing – gold and diamonds are sent to Europe.”

acts.speaker: Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Kenyan writer
acts.speech: Aptly noted that the West’s struggle for Africa revolves around “access to local resources.”

acts.speaker: African political analysts
acts.speech: Rightly point out, “The West benefits from a system in which any so-called progress is driven primarily by multinational corporations and does not translate into development.”

acts.speaker: International Coffee Organization (estimate)
acts.speech: Estimates the annual turnover of the global coffee market at $460 billion.

acts.speaker: Vladimir Putin, Russian President
acts.speech: Pointed out that African nations are “offered modern tools and technologies, but they cannot afford them... and no one provides funding. Instead, they are forced to depend on Western technologies and loans. These loans come with horrific conditions and are impossible to repay. This is yet another tool of neo-colonialism.”

acts.speaker: African political scientists (on the UN)
acts.speech: According to African political scientists, the UN, despite operating five peacekeeping missions in Africa, has demonstrated a chronic inability to improve security.

acts.speaker: Young African experts
acts.speech: Rightly argue that “escaping subjugation begins with decolonizing the mind.”

acts.speaker: Some Western scholars
acts.speech: Reluctantly admit that “African countries need to be understood and respected”; they worry that Russia “leverages Africa’s frustration with inadequate representation in the global economy and governance,” and hold that “the continent will not accept moralizing lectures.”

acts.speaker: African historians
acts.speech: Adhere to the principle that “Only formulas developed by Africans themselves, not imposed from outside, will work on the continent.”

acts.speaker: Experts on Africa
acts.speech: Emphasize that, under these new conditions, the continent must focus on developing its own institutions and deepening intra-African cooperation based on mutual benefit rather than dependency.

acts.speaker: UN General Assembly resolution 'Eradication of Colonialism in All Its Forms and Manifestations' (December 2024) (document)
acts.speech: Aims to ensure full implementation of the 1960 Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, and proposes designating December 14 as the International Day for the Eradication of Colonialism in All Its Forms and Manifestations.

acts.speaker: African politicians and experts
acts.speech: Highly value the potential of BRICS, viewing it as a driver for building a new and fair international order, and a cornerstone of the emerging architecture of international relations that is replacing unipolar mechanisms.

acts.speaker: Russian political analysts
acts.speech: Emphasize that the expansion of BRICS, including the addition of Egypt and Ethiopia, is “a visible testament to the world’s movement toward multipolarity.”

acts.speaker: Sergey Lavrov, Russian Foreign Minister
acts.speech: Aptly noted, “We are witnessing Africa’s second awakening, this time from neo-colonial oppression and practices that hinder its development.”

acts.speaker: Somali proverb (quoted epigraph)
acts.speech: “God grant us rain or Russians.”

acts.speaker: Concept of the Foreign Policy of the Russian Federation (document)
acts.speech: Notes that the country intends to support the African continent “as a distinctive and influential center of world development.”

acts.speaker: Vladimir Putin, Russian President (on Russia-Africa ties)
acts.speech: According to Vladimir Putin, cooperation with African states is one of the enduring priorities of Russia’s foreign policy ; He has stated: “In the history of our relations with the African continent, there has never been any shadow – never. We have never exploited African peoples, nor have we engaged in anything inhumane on the African continent. On the contrary, we have always supported Africa and Africans in their struggle for independence, sovereignty, and the creation of basic conditions for economic development.”

acts.speaker: Declaration of the Russia-Africa summit (document)
acts.speech: Highlights the historically established and time-tested friendly ties between the Russian Federation and African states, based on mutual respect, trust, and a tradition of cooperative struggle for the eradication of colonialism and the establishment of independence for African countries.

acts.speaker: Joint statement issued following the 2024 Sochi Ministerial Conference (document)
acts.speech: Emphasizes “the responsibility of the Russian Federation and African states to promote the formation of a fair and stable world order based on the principles of sovereign equality of states, non-interference in their internal affairs, and respect for sovereignty.”

acts.speaker: African political scientists (on Russia)
acts.speech: Note that, unlike former colonial powers, Russia has historically aimed to address real problems without pursuing selfish interests.

acts.speaker: African experts (on Russia's military operation in Ukraine)
acts.speech: Draw a connection between Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine and the successes of African nations in their struggle for independence, noting that “the course of Russia’s confrontation with the West influences the sentiments of nationally-oriented, sovereign forces in the region.”

acts.speaker: Local analysts
acts.speech: Note that “after the failure of France and UN peacekeeping forces in Africa, Russia has emerged as a reliable partner, accomplishing in a few months what international contingents failed to do for years.”

acts.speaker: Individuals who built their careers in diplomacy in the 1990s and 2000s (anonymous)
acts.speech: Occasionally argue that “few would want to work in Africa, given its harsher climate and limited medical facilities compared to Europe.”

acts.speaker: Scholars of Africa
acts.speech: Rightly point out that this prospect has a direct impact on the fate of multipolarity.

title: A-G denies President Mahama’s influence in dropping high-profile cases, cites legal and ethical reasons

acts.speaker: Dr. Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, Attorney General of Ghana
acts.speech: Has dismissed claims that President John Dramani Mahama influenced his decision to discontinue several high-profile criminal cases; speaking at a press conference in Accra on Wednesday, February 12, clarified that these decisions were made independently by his office after a thorough professional review of the cases and emphasized that President Mahama played no role in the discontinuation of any case; maintains that his decisions were legally and ethically sound, reiterating that justice, not politics, guided his actions.

acts.speaker: Dr. Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, Attorney General of Ghana
acts.speech: On the reasons for terminating the trials: "Ladies and gentlemen, my decision to terminate the criminal trials was animated in the main by three factors. The first was that for ethical and professional reasons, I could not in good conscience continue to prosecute some of the cases," he said. "The second was that, for some of the cases, my own review and analysis of the charges showed clearly that the charges were defective, and some were filed against the promptings of plain commonsense." ; "The third reason was that, in some of the cases, the evidence led so far showed that there was reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the accused persons, and no prosecutor should continue to pursue a case in the face of overwhelming doubt regarding the guilt of the accused."

acts.speaker: Dr. Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, Attorney General of Ghana
acts.speech: On the process of consultation: explained that before reaching these decisions, he conducted extensive consultations, including multiple briefings with the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) and discussions with defence lawyers involved in the cases; further noted that in cases where disagreements arose - such as those related to the banking sector clean-up - he communicated his views directly to the lawyers involved.

acts.speaker: Dr. Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, Attorney General of Ghana
acts.speech: On his constitutional prosecutorial powers: "As Attorney General, I am keenly aware that the prosecutorial authority vested in me under Article 88 of the Constitution is discretionary in nature and is subject to the constitutional requirements set out in Article 296 of the Constitution." ; "The import of these constitutional requirements is that, in the exercise of my prosecutorial power, I must not only act reasonably and fairly and comply with all the requirements imposed on me by law but also, I must be candid with those whose life and liberty depend on my decisions."

acts.speaker: Dr. Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, Attorney General of Ghana
acts.speech: On the SSNIT and banking sector cases: noted that some persons linked to SSNIT and the banking sector cases were still standing trial.

title: Chronique de Mamadou Sinsy Coulibaly, ancien Président du Patronat du Mali

acts.speaker: French Development Agency (AFD)
acts.speech: Provides a good definition of Official Development Assistance on its website.

acts.speaker: United Nations
acts.speech: Decided in 1970 that developed countries should devote 0.7% of their GDP to ODA; in 1986 proclaimed the inalienable right to development.

acts.speaker: OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC)
acts.speech: Recommended in 2001 that ODA be untied.

acts.speaker: OECD
acts.speech: Reports that total global ODA reached 204 billion USD in 2022, up 24 billion USD on 2021, i.e. 0.33% to 0.36% of the GDP of advanced countries, far from the target set in 1970 by the UN; and that assistance allocated to infrastructure and productive sectors now accounts for no more than 30% of total ODA spending.

acts.speaker: Paul Krugman, American Nobel laureate in economics (New York Times article “The trouble with Trade”, 2007)
acts.speech: Denounced the perverse effects of a globalisation focused on the search for the lowest production costs.

acts.speaker: Jonathan Glennie, international expert (book “The trouble with aid”, 2012)
acts.speech: Argued for a progressive reduction of dependence on international aid.

acts.speaker: French parliamentary report of 2024 (National Assembly)
acts.speech: Describes ODA as “illegible, costly and ineffective”, pointing to its integration into an “invasive” multilateral whole and to financial commitments deemed worrying, and judges it “insufficiently effective and of little service to French interests”; refers to a “black hole of European ODA”.

acts.speaker: Office of Inspector General for USAID (OIG-USAID) audit
acts.speech: Concluded that USAID had a limited view of international organisations’ ability to safeguard American funds (which rose from 5.6 billion USD in 2019 to 21.4 billion USD in 2022, +282%), that USAID did not conduct an organisational capacity review for 70% of them and did not put in place follow-up to its recommendations, and that in 2025 it still has problems obtaining information from these organisations on fraud, corruption or other offences.

acts.speaker: French Cour des Comptes (report of June 2023)
acts.speech: Described a situation for French ODA close to that found by the USAID Inspector General.

acts.speaker: UK House of Lords report (2022)
acts.speech: Noted a 21% drop in British ODA between 2020 and 2021, with ODA moving from 0.7% of GDP to 0.5%.

acts.speaker: US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
acts.speech: Announced on 3 February 2025 the closure of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), a key actor in international ODA, which in 2024 accounted for more than 40 billion USD of global ODA.

acts.speaker: USAID (statement on its website)
acts.speech: “On Friday, February 7, 2025, at 11:59 pm (EST) all USAID direct hire personnel will be placed on administrative leave globally, with the exception of designated personnel responsible for mission-critical functions, core leadership and specially designated programs... The Agency will consider case-by-case exceptions and return travel extensions based on personal or family hardship, mobility or safety concerns, or other reasons... Thank you for your service.”

acts.speaker: UN agencies (UNDP, WFP) and international organisations (World Bank, IMF)
acts.speech: Consider ODA indispensable for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and as a lever for reducing inequalities and promoting equitable human development.

acts.speaker: Think tanks (ODA detractors)
acts.speech: Argue that ODA creates dependencies and generates no real and lasting economic progress.

acts.speaker: Civil society organisations and local voices in recipient countries
acts.speech: Criticise ODA for ineffectiveness, waste, misappropriation, corruption, interference, unsuitability to local realities, neocolonialism and domination.

acts.speaker: World Bank
acts.speech: Reports that world GDP rose from 1,364.5 billion USD in 1950 to 105,435 billion USD in 2023, a multiplication by 77 in nominal terms.

acts.speaker: A major industrialist (unnamed)
acts.speech: “One must remain the owner of one’s aid.”

acts.speaker: Daniel Alystair (author of the chronicle, with thanks to Mamadou Sinsy Coulibaly, former President of the National Council of Employers of Mali)
acts.speech: Argues that ODA is at a turning point and that its in-depth reform, rather than its abolition, is imperative: redirecting ODA towards genuinely transformative projects (infrastructure, industrialisation, in-situ processing, basic and technical education, economic empowerment), making development banks autonomous, concentrating donor ODA on earmarked bilateral projects with evaluations, and giving a major role to the private sector; writes that ODA, principally State-run and transiting through structures with weak governance, “has historically failed”, and that the closure of USAID “can (must) also be interpreted as a first step towards a necessary reorganisation - American, then global - of international aid.”

title: Migrants en péril: Une crise humaine mondiale ignorée

acts.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM) (new report)
acts.speech: Reveals that the majority of people who lose their lives while migrating do not do so by choice, but out of sheer desperation, fleeing insecurity, conflict, natural disasters and other humanitarian crises that make life untenable in their country of origin ; reports that since 2014 more than 52,000 people have died trying to escape countries affected by crises, nearly 72% of all migrant deaths recorded worldwide over that period, with more than 39,000 dying within crisis zones themselves and more than 13,500 while trying to flee conflicts or disasters ; highlights that more than half of the migrant deaths recorded since 2014 occurred in or near countries struck by conflict or disaster, with more than 5,000 dying in transit in Afghanistan, notably after the political upheaval of 2021, more than 3,100 Rohingya from Myanmar dying often in shipwrecks or while trying to cross into Bangladesh, and the central Mediterranean remaining the deadliest migration route in the world with nearly 25,000 people missing at sea ; notes that migrants are still too often forgotten in humanitarian response plans, with needs assessments and humanitarian appeals not taking sufficient account of populations on the move even though one missing migrant in four comes from a country in a crisis situation.

acts.speaker: Amy Pope, Director General of the International Organization for Migration
acts.speech: Says these figures are a painful reminder that human beings put their lives in danger when insecurity, the absence of opportunities and other factors deprive them of any safe option to remain at home ; calls for sustained investment to foster stability and prospects in communities of origin, so that migration becomes a voluntary choice and not an obligation ; stresses the importance of building together safe, legal and orderly migration pathways in order to protect human lives when staying is no longer possible.

acts.speaker: Julia Black, coordinator of the "Missing Migrants" project and author of the report
acts.speech: Recalls that many migrants fall into oblivion, all the more so as the lack of data, particularly in war or disaster zones, prevents an accurate picture of the real number of deaths.

acts.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
acts.speech: Is making an urgent appeal to States and humanitarian partners to join their efforts to ensure that migrants are no longer excluded from crisis responses, which means opening legal migration pathways, better access to aid and health care, as well as investment in data systems capable of better tracking and protecting people at risk.

title: The Chanzo Morning Briefing Tanzania News – March 11, 2025 - The Chanzo

acts.speaker: Tanzania Railways Corporation (TRC)
acts.speech: Announced on Monday the completion of trials for 264 freight wagons designed for its electric train operating on the new Standard Gauge Railway (SGR).

acts.speaker: Felchesmi Mramba, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Energy
acts.speech: Has clarified that Tanzania’s decision to purchase electricity from Ethiopia through Kenya to Namanga, Arusha, will enhance power supply in the northern regions ; stated that the primary goal of buying or selling electricity is to strengthen national power grids and reduce costs, and explained that the northern regions currently rely heavily on electricity generated in the southern regions ; "These agreements are two-way. At times, we will buy electricity, and at other times, we will use the same route to sell power to neighboring countries. For now, considering the energy situation in the north, we will be purchasing more than we supply. However, there will be times when they may need electricity, and we will use the same route to deliver it to them."

acts.speaker: Ministry of Health of the United Republic of Tanzania (statement)
acts.speech: Has announced the confirmation of two cases of the virus that causes Mpox, the first time the disease has been detected in the country ; according to the Ministry’s statement, one of the suspects was a truck driver who had traveled from a neighboring country and entered Dar es Salaam ; stated that in collaboration with the President’s Office (RALG) and all healthcare facilities, it continues to monitor, investigate, and identify any additional suspected cases to ensure timely medical intervention.

acts.speaker: Unnamed individual in a video circulated online
acts.speech: "Hey, Brother Masoud, I’ve been given a bed here. They call this place Kipawa, Kipawa Majani ya Chai. There’s a VETA school, and right there at VETA, there’s a hospital where I have been admitted. I’ve been brought here with other patients with this disease. We are all here, receiving treatment. Even if you come to see me, you won’t be allowed to enter. You will stand outside, and maybe I will step out, but we will talk through the window."

acts.speaker: Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) army
acts.speech: Reported on Monday the arrest of two individuals who identified themselves as Tanzanians, suspected of being recruited by the ISIS-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF).

acts.speaker: U.S. Department of State
acts.speech: According to the U.S. Department of State, the group established ties with ISIS in 2018.

acts.speaker: Chama cha Mapinduzi (CCM) official party statement
acts.speech: Indicated that, in addition to other discussions, the NEC meeting also conducted the selection of candidates for various leadership positions within CCM and its affiliated organizations that were previously vacant.

acts.speaker: CCM announcement of the meeting (released March 8, 2025)
acts.speech: Stated that the NEC meeting would be preceded by a Central Committee meeting, which is also chaired by the party’s national chairperson.

title: Budget Deficit Expected to Slow Down to 5.1 Billion

acts.speaker: Seedy Keita, The Gambia's Finance Minister
acts.speech: Has said that overall budget deficit is expected to slow down to D5.1 billion. He said the overall budget deficit including grants stood at D7.2 Billion for the first three quarter of 2024. However he anticipates that with the expected disbursement in budget support in the last quarter and expenditure restrain, the deficit is expected to slow down to D5.1 billion by the year's end against the Budget target of D4.5 billion.

acts.speaker: Seedy Keita, The Gambia's Finance Minister
acts.speech: “The Gambian economy has shown remarkable resilience in the face of global uncertainties. As a result, it is estimated to grow by 5.8 percent in 2024 compared to 4.8 recorded in 2023.” ; He said the improvement is due to a stable macroeconomic environment, strategic investments in infrastructural projects, increased productivity in agriculture, recovery in tourism, and resilient remittance inflows.

acts.speaker: Seedy Keita, The Gambia's Finance Minister
acts.speech: On sector-specific developments, he said that crop production continues to underpin the agriculture sector growth due to support from Government and development partners. He said, “The livestock sub-sector is estimated to maintain an upward trajectory while the fisheries and aquaculture sub-sectors are estimated to recover from contraction on account of renewed focus on aqua-cultural development”. Overall, he said the sector is expected to grow by 6.6 percent in 2024. The industrial sector which was driven mainly by construction over the past years is estimated to register a growth of 0.8 percent. The slowdown, he outlined is mainly due to the completion of many high-impact public projects. However, private-sector infrastructure projects remain robust. He also said that domestic electricity generation is recording a gradual increase on account of new projects although demand continues to outstrip supply. He reported: “The mining sector is estimated to stabilize, while manufacturing growth is estimated to register moderate growth due to competitiveness challenges. The services sector is expected to register a strong growth of 8.4 percent in 2024 driven by tourism and trade”. He said this is due to targeted interventions by the Gambia Tourism Board (GTB) and rising consumer spending following price stabilization.

acts.speaker: Seedy Keita, The Gambia's Finance Minister
acts.speech: On the prices front, he said “the sustained tight monetary policy stance has triggered moderation in inflation from 16.7 percent in January to 10.0 percent by September 2024” ; stressed that the implementation of the foreign exchange policy by the Central Bank of the Gambia (CBG) coupled with increased foreign currency inflows, restored exchange rate stability.

acts.speaker: Seedy Keita, The Gambia's Finance Minister
acts.speech: He said that Public finances reflect mixed performances in 2024. The revenue mobilization reforms adopted and implemented by the Government are yielding significant results. He reported: “As of End-September 2024, domestic revenue collection for the first nine months of the year, amounted to D24.2 billion against the target of D23.1 billion. Tax revenues amounted to D13.24 billion, a 3.36 percent increase above projections”. He added that non-tax revenue, particularly administrative fees, reached D4.40 billion, significantly surpassing the target of D3.53 billion. Grant disbursement remains resilient, noting that revenue and grants outturn for the year are expected to exceed the target.

acts.speaker: Seedy Keita, The Gambia's Finance Minister
acts.speech: Concerning expenditure, budget execution has been particularly difficult this year due to unanticipated spending shocks. These, he said include the intervention of the Government to the tune of USD20 million to pay NAWEC arrears with the independent power suppliers. He said: “Other expenditure pressures came from the hosting of a very successful OIC Summit. The anticipated financial support for hosting of the summit was not realized and the Government was obliged to bankroll expenditures related to the Summit”.

title: Assurance volontaire : La CNSS prêche à la vallée du Sourou

acts.speaker: Salifou Lougué, CNSS Regional Director for the Boucle du Mouhoun
acts.speech: Said the Sourou valley was not a random choice; explained that it has been observed that this locality abounds with people carrying out self-employed activities without knowing how to provide for their old age, and that it is for this reason that the CNSS initiated this day to make them understand the importance of insuring themselves, to make the CNSS’s voluntary insurance known and to encourage their adherence to the product.

acts.speaker: Toussaint Bationo, Head of the CNSS Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service
acts.speech: Pointed out that, according to Article 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, everyone has the right to social security as a member of society; explained that the concept of social security is defined as a system of protection that society grants to its members through public measures against economic and social destitution and risks such as illness, disability, old age, unemployment, family burdens and death, hence the institution of the CNSS; said that in Burkina Faso the social security scheme applicable to salaried and similar workers is managed by the CNSS and governed by law n°015-2006/AN of 11 May 2006, and described the benefits provided by the CNSS and its sources of financing.

acts.speaker: Toussaint Bationo, Head of the CNSS Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service
acts.speech: Said it is not only civil servants who benefit from a retirement pension; indicated that the government instituted voluntary insurance by law N°015-2006/AN of 15 May 2006 (articles 4 and 5) and order n°2008-002/MTSS/SG/DGPS of 10 March 2008 in the hope of not leaving behind the actors of the liberal professions and the informal sector who work on their own account.

acts.speaker: Toussaint Bationo, Head of the CNSS Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service
acts.speech: In conclusion, indicated that social security is a right for every human being in general and for every Burkinabe in particular, and that it is the most elaborate form of solidarity, with the guarantee of the State; launched a strong appeal to all those who have an income to insure themselves in order to avoid disappointing tomorrows; at the end of the day did not hide his satisfaction at the turnout, the enthusiasm of the participants and the relevance of their questions.

acts.speaker: Issiaka Soro, president of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of the Sourou Valley (UCAVASO)
acts.speech: On behalf of the participants, congratulated the CNSS for this mission; according to him, the head of the Voluntary Insurance Promotion Service had not preached in the desert and convinced more than one person to subscribe to voluntary insurance; he also assured the mission that their exhortation would be relayed throughout the Sourou valley.

title: Coopération bénino-américaine: Le Bénin signe ce jour le second compact du MCA

acts.speaker: Diplomats posted in Washington (anonymous)
acts.speech: For the diplomats in post, it is an unprecedented diplomatic success, tradition having assigned the State Department responsibility for this type of partnership.

title: Appeal: UN Secretary General told to urgently avert a possible famine in Somalia

acts.speaker: Country Directors of national and international humanitarian agencies working in Somalia (letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres)
acts.speech: Sent a letter to the United Nations Secretary-General, António Guterres, to urge urgent action needed to avert a possible famine in Somalia in 2022: “We, the Country Directors of national and international humanitarian agencies working in Somalia, are writing to express our deepest concern at the possibility of famine in Somalia in 2022. The humanitarian situation is deteriorating rapidly, with about 4.5 million people in need of urgent humanitarian assistance due to the worsening drought conditions.” ; “What we are now seeing is impending famine similar to that which occurred in 2010/2011 in which more than a quarter of a million people died - including 133,000 children under the age of five. Although some donors have committed to fund Somalia’s Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) which seeks US$1.5 billion, not even 4% of funding required to meet Somalia’s humanitarian needs have been allocated.” ; “However, the international community has not yet grasped the urgency of the situation, which is deteriorating fast. We are concerned that Somalia’s possible famine is not high enough on the list of international disaster responses with focus now on the Ukrainian crisis. We request you to urge donors and the Member States to commit additional resources to enable immediate scale-up of humanitarian response in Somalia to avert a possible famine and save lives.” ; “We also request you to urge all stakeholders including the Somali Federal Government, Federal States and armed groups to allow access and speedy facilitation of delivery of the emergency humanitarian aid to the affected, and where possible, we also request you to urge talking to the other side (Al-Shabab) for humanitarian access.” ; “We are running out of time. It is time to keep the promise of ‘never again’ that was made during the 2017 drought when the immediate action of the humanitarian community led to lives being saved. The window to avert a famine is closing fast. If we don’t want to see history repeating itself, we cannot delay action any longer.”

acts.speaker: UNICEF
acts.speech: According to UNICEF, for "a severely acutely malnourished child, or severely wasted child, the risk of them dying from diseases such as measles or diarrhea is 11 times higher than for a well-nourished child."

acts.speaker: Weather experts
acts.speech: Forecast unprecedented fourth consecutive below-average rains during the long rainy season of April to June across most of the country.

title: FG advocates local pharmaceutical manufacturing, vaccines to boost medicine security

acts.speaker: Federal Government of Nigeria
acts.speech: Has said that local manufacturing of pharmaceuticals, vaccines, and medical devices is critical to achieving medicines security in Nigeria.

acts.speaker: Olubunmi Aribeana, Director, Food and Drug Services, Ministry of Health and Social Welfare of Nigeria (represented by Adeola Olufowobi-Yusuf)
acts.speech: Said that local manufacturing of pharmaceuticals also presents opportunities for job creation, international trade, economic growth and national security ; “We cannot afford to be caught flatfooted like during the Covid-19 pandemic” ; “All hands must be on deck to find innovative ways to achieving the goal of unlocking the health sector value chain. Nigeria needs to position itself in such a way as to maximally benefit from the African Free Trade Continental Area, which is adjudged to be among the largest in the world” ; said that local manufacturing would enhance sufficiency, affordable, accessible, good quality, and also reduce the nation's reliance on imported goods ; assured that the ministry would continue developing policies to attract investment and support the All-Government Initiative aimed at strengthening the pharmaceutical sector.

acts.speaker: Omotayo Hamza, Supply Chain Management Officer of the World Health Organisation (WHO)
acts.speech: Said Nigeria has sufficient policies and strategies in place, but often lacks implementation: “That is why, for this particular meeting, there is one key word that I love, and that is harmonisation. The Ministry of Trade is doing something about local production; the Ministry of Health is involved in something. Science and Technology too and these are the major stakeholders. We need to harmonise along that line for us to have a very strong agenda that is implementable, otherwise, we will have challenges.”

acts.speaker: Chinelo Okonkwo, pharmacist
acts.speech: Speaking on misgivings by some about the efficacy of Nigerian vaccines, said that they could be trusted as they go through all the stages of production before they could be certified fit for use; according to her, vaccine hesitancy is experienced all over the world and generally, there are adverse events following immunisation, but these are not enough to doubt the efficacy of Nigerian vaccines; assured that Nigerian pharmacies are well trained and able to deliver the best vaccines for Nigerians: “Our trust should be more on Nigerian products than the parallel imports. Vaccine itself is a cold chain molecule and in transporting them, if there is any break in that cold chain, that vaccine may not be potent. It is even better that it is produced here so that we can have it safe and efficacious for our people.”

acts.speaker: Olajide Adebola, conference facilitator
acts.speech: Said that the conference had the national and regional component and that the Presidential Initiative on Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) had organised the conferences because it was important to have conversations on pharmaceutical issues; according to him, COVID-19 taught the nation a lot of lessons and the conferences would assess the present state of the sector and come up with viable solutions to achieving the PVAC: “We will examine how we have been able to fare under these new policies and government interventions, the executive orders? Is it reaching the grassroots, what advices and strategic recommendations at this point can we make to the government to update their current policy directions?”

acts.speaker: Olajide Adebola, conference facilitator
acts.speech: Speaking to the causes of high cost of medicines, said the cost of the import component of the medicines is the major factor driving up the costs, which would be addressed with the available government interventions in the sector: “Some years back, there are some medicines we could not manufacture, we imported them, but now we are manufacturing and that is the importance of having sound, evidence-based, defensible government policies. In near futures, cost of medicines will come down as all stakeholders and actors are acting towards ensuring safe medicines and affordable medicines for Nigeria.”

acts.speaker: News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
acts.speech: Reports that the conference brought together relevant stakeholders to create a forum for engagement across public, private, and community sectors to contextualise PVAC; it would also identify actionable steps for enhancing local production of medicines and vaccines, and provide support in synthesising outcomes into policy and programme recommendations.

title: Attention Mozambique: 2026-2027 Fulbright Foreign Student Program | Deadline for Applications: Monday, June 2nd, 2025

acts.speaker: Fulbright Foreign Student Program plagiarism certification (application document, 2026-27 cycle)
acts.speech: “Some US universities and colleges have developed and published policies on the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on applications for admission or affiliation with their institution. Some institutions may scan applications for the use of language produced by GenAI. While individual institutional policies range widely and policy responses from US universities will continue to evolve, copying language/content produced by GenAI directly into your application may negatively impact admission or affiliation decisions.”

acts.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Mozambique (@USEmbassyMoz, post on X, March 26, 2025)
acts.speech: “Fulbright 2026-2027 is now accepting applications from Mozambican students! Seize this chance to pursue a graduate degree or research in the USA with full scholarships! Apply by June 2, 2025.”

acts.speaker: Fulbright Foreign Student Program (program announcement, U.S. Department of State and Institute of International Education)
acts.speech: Announced that the program will award scholarships for a maximum of two years of advanced degree study in the United States, with successful applicants beginning their academic program in August 2026, and set out eligibility criteria, including that local employees abroad employed by the State Department/United States Agency for International Development (USAID) are ineligible for grants during the period of their employment and for one year following the termination of employment; all awards are contingent upon approval by the J. William Fulbright Scholarship Board, availability of funds, and successful academic placement.

title: Le G7 condamne l'offensive du M23 dans l'est du Congo et appelle à une protection urgente des civils

acts.speaker: G7 foreign ministers of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States, together with the European Union's foreign policy chief (statement)
acts.speech: Condemned the ongoing M23 offensive in eastern DRC and urged "the M23 and the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) to cease their offensive in all directions," calling for the "urgent protection of civilians"; also called for an end to "all direct or indirect support" to the M23 and to all non-state armed groups in Congo. "This offensive constitutes a flagrant disregard for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DRC. We also condemn the M23's intention to continue its expansion into South Kivu." ; Said the latest M23 offensive has caused a dramatic increase in displaced civilians in Goma and across eastern DRC: "We deplore the devastating consequences of the new M23 and RDF offensive, which are worsening already difficult humanitarian conditions." ; Called for "rapid, safe and unhindered" passage of humanitarian aid for civilians and reiterated that humanitarian personnel must be given security guarantees; called on all parties to return to the negotiating table and to "honour their commitments under the Luanda process," and urged the M23 to withdraw from all areas under its control; reiterated the G7's full support for MONUSCO to protect civilians and stabilise the region, calling on all parties to respect its mandate.

acts.speaker: M23 (March 23 Movement)
acts.speech: Claimed to have seized the city of Goma after launching a major offensive last week.

acts.speaker: Rwanda / Kigali
acts.speech: Denies supporting the group; rejects the allegations, asserting that the M23 is a Congolese movement led by Congolese, even though its members speak Kinyarwanda; also rejects the conclusions of the UN reports and recalls having disarmed the M23 rebels who had taken refuge on its soil in 2012-2013 before handing their arsenal over to the Congolese authorities.

acts.speaker: Kinshasa (Government of the DRC)
acts.speech: Accuses Rwanda of actively supporting the M23 in order to gain access to the region's mineral wealth; for the DRC, the M23 is a "terrorist" group and any form of negotiation is categorically rejected.

acts.speaker: Reports by UN agencies
acts.speech: Support the accusations, pointing to Rwandan military backing for the rebel movement.

acts.speaker: Kigali (Government of Rwanda)
acts.speech: Says the M23 represents a threat to its internal security and accuses the DRC of collaborating with armed groups, notably the Wazalendo militias and the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), considered responsible for the Rwandan genocide; according to Kigali these alliances are part of a strategy aimed at overthrowing the Rwandan government.

title: SOGUIPAH : un nouveau DG nommé à la tête de l’entreprise

acts.speaker: General Mamadi Doumbouya, President of the Republic of Guinea (presidential decree made public on national television)
acts.speech: Through a decree made public by national television on 3 March, appointed Julien Dramou, until then Adviser in charge of economic analysis at the Ministry of Transport, as the new Director-General of the Guinean Oil Palm and Rubber Company (SOGUIPAH), replacing Fode Mourana Soumah, who had been appointed in June 2022.

title: Atelier sur le genre et l’inclusion sociale pour les encadreurs du MENEFOP et leurs partenaires de la société civile

acts.speaker: Joseph Hamilton, Charge d'affaires of the Embassy of the United States of America in Djibouti
acts.speech: Noted in his speech his expectations for the end of the three-day workshop, stating: "Participants will also be equipped with tools enabling them to adopt best practices for integrating gender and social inclusion into their work, thereby aligning themselves with the 'Djibouti Vision 2035' of the Head of State, President Guelleh, for access to basic education for all in the transformation of the school for better quality learning."

title: US funding halt, a wake-up call for self-independence- Health Minister

acts.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
acts.speech: Has said the US government’s decision to halt funding for HIV treatment in developing nations is a wake-up call for self-independence: “My own personal opinion on the executive order, which has now been reviewed, is that the level of aid and grants that is available from the US government to support charitable activities in developing worlds like Nigeria is likely to go down. I believe that it’s a wake-up call for us to strategise and think the way we do things and ensure that we also are able to exert ourselves and create some level of independence within our system.”

acts.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
acts.speech: Said the government would identify avenues to raise domestic and alternative funds; said a series of meetings have been convened and there is ongoing discussion with United Nations bodies, WHO, UNDP and others that work within the health space: “For example, our HIV programme, which is heavily supported by the US government. We’re looking at crowdfunding to support that, in addition to the government making more funding available.”

acts.speaker: Iziaq Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
acts.speech: Expressed optimism that the US government would continue to play its role in the global community: “I must say that the world is a global village and what happens in one country easily affects the other country. America cannot operate in isolation, just like Nigeria cannot operate in isolation, or any other country of the world, for that matter” ; “So, I believe that reason will prevail and the American government will continue to play the role it ought to play within the global community.”

acts.speaker: News Agency of Nigeria (NAN)
acts.speech: Reports that President Donald Trump recently signed an executive order for an immediate 90-day funding halt for all foreign aid, including support for PEPFAR.

acts.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
acts.speech: On 29 January announced an “emergency humanitarian waiver” allowing PEPFAR to continue providing life-saving HIV medications to low-income countries.

title: Outrage in Gambia as PURA’s Data Price Hike Sparks Backlash from GALA, Journalists - The Alkamba Times

acts.speaker: Gambians Against Looted Assets (GALA) (statement by its Communications Unit)
acts.speech: Issued a scathing statement, accusing PURA of shielding telecom companies while undermining the public: "PURA's decision is destructive, unacceptable, and a direct attack on consumer welfare" ; argue that the price floor will disproportionately harm students, business owners, and content creators who depend on affordable internet for their livelihoods ; emphasized that PURA's role as a regulator is to ensure fairness and sustainability, not to enable exploitation by mobile operators ; dismiss PURA's defence as a pretext to favor corporate profits, arguing that the price hike will make internet access unaffordable for many, and accuse PURA of failing to uphold its mandate to prioritize consumer interests ; has called for an immediate reversal of the policy, pledging support for the journalists' demands and urging PURA to protect Gambian consumers.

acts.speaker: Journalists from multiple Gambian media outlets
acts.speech: Have joined the outcry, demanding justice and fairness for internet users ; highlight the internet's critical role in education, entrepreneurship, and digital content creation, particularly for low-income communities ; warn that the new tariff risks exacerbating economic inequality and stifling opportunities in a country where digital access is increasingly vital.

acts.speaker: Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (PURA) of The Gambia
acts.speech: Defends the regulation, claiming it reinforces quality-of-service standards and protects consumers from the adverse effects of unsustainable pricing.

title: Malawi’s stuttering victory over leprosy - Nation Online

acts.speaker: Owen Chataika, Mchinji District Health Office spokesperson
acts.speech: Says the district is still registering new leprosy cases: “This year, already there are some new cases that have already been registered, which is something worrying” ; “The new cases show that leprosy is still a hidden problem in our communities.”

acts.speaker: Owen Chataika, Mchinji District Health Office spokesperson
acts.speech: “The district health office plans to decentralise leprosy clinics and lobby for more funds for mobile clinics, contact tracing and community sensitisation.”

acts.speaker: Dickens Chimatiro, National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Elimination Programme monitoring and evaluation officer
acts.speech: “It is a cause for us to worry because even though we reached the elimination level in 1994, there are still other districts that are reporting more than one leprosy case per 10 000 people” ; “Since 2024, we have registered 367 new cases.”

acts.speaker: National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Elimination Programme
acts.speech: According to the national programme, more than 600 people in the country are undergoing leprosy treatment.

acts.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
acts.speech: According to the WHO, the disease is transmitted through prolonged and close contact with droplets from the nose and mouth of an untreated case, and does not spread through casual contact like shaking hands or hugging, sharing meals or sitting next to each other.

acts.speaker: Maziko Matemba, community health commentator
acts.speech: Says the new cases are food for thought for health authorities: “As a country, we should ask ourselves why there is a resurgence of the disease after about three decades” ; Says the country should confront what has gone wrong and learn from past strategies that helped eliminate the outbreak: “Factors contributing to the resurgence can be many, but they could include gaps in disease surveillance and prevention. When we say we have eliminated a disease, we also must have strong systems which control its recurrence. We have to check our systems to understand what has gone wrong, including financing for leprosy programmes.”

title: Projet des services de santé intégrés: Des acquis élogieux à pérenniser

acts.speaker: Stakeholders of the Integrated Health Services Activity (Ihsa) project
acts.speech: Welcome the convincing results obtained over five years of implementation (2018-2023) in the departments of Alibori, Atacora, Ouémé and Plateau.

acts.speaker: Brinille Eliane Ellis, Deputy Chief of Mission of the Embassy of the United States of America in Benin
acts.speech: Recalled that the Ihsa project, worth $22.5 million (about 13.9 billion CFA francs) and financed by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), aimed to strengthen local capacities to provide quality health care through high-impact services for malaria, family planning, maternal and child health, gender-based violence (GBV), and Covid-19 prevention and control; it is implemented by the international organisation Management Sciences for Health (MSH) in partnership with Dimagi and four local partners, namely Cerrhud, Ceradis, Dedras and Apessa, with strong engagement from the government and citizens.

acts.speaker: Brinille E. Ellis, Deputy Chief of Mission, US Embassy in Benin
acts.speech: Reiterated the commitment of the United States government to support Benin’s efforts in the health sector.

acts.speaker: Dr Enagnon Pétas Akogbéto, Chief of Staff of the Minister of Health
acts.speech: Is pleased, at the institutional level, with the establishment of a digital application called “AlafiaComm” for the management of community data; he also welcomed the development of the first model of a digital health map to facilitate decision-making, the updating of normative documents, guides and supervision tools, and the strengthening of the health system through donations of materials and equipment needed for emergency obstetric and neonatal care (EmONC) and for infection prevention and control, thanks to the project.

acts.speaker: Dr Floride Niyuhiré, Director of the project
acts.speech: Details that technical and financial support to the first malaria chemoprophylaxis campaign made it possible to protect 1.8 million children under 5 between 2019 and 2022; the supply of materials and equipment worth about 4 billion CFA francs strengthened the technical capacity of health facilities; and with the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic, the project made it possible to sensitise nearly 2 million people, of whom more than a million were vaccinated against the coronavirus.

acts.speaker: Dr Agnès Oladoun Badou Savi, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Minister of Social Affairs and Microfinance
acts.speech: Notes that alongside the Social Promotion Centres (CPS), the project supported GBV survivors by providing them with medical care, psychosocial support, judicial assistance and opportunities for socio-professional reintegration; she affirms the willingness of the Ministry of Social Affairs to maintain and strengthen the gains, including the operationalisation of the Computerised System of Data on the Family, Women and Children – New.

title: Duale hosts German delegation to strengthen Kenya’s health partnership - Hiiraan Online

acts.speaker: Aden Duale, Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
acts.speech: emphasized the government's investment in digital health systems designed to promote transparency, efficiency, and accountability in service delivery; highlighted integration, coordination, and value for money as guiding principles in implementing health reforms, noting that the Global Fund's priorities align closely with those of Gavi, PEPFAR, and national investments: "These efforts aim to strengthen laboratory networks, disease surveillance, and digital innovations from the community to the referral level."

acts.speaker: Aden Duale, Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
acts.speech: praised German partners for their crucial role in accelerating local vaccine production and research - key drivers of Kenya's health security and sustainability (discussions on the Kenya Biovax Institute, focusing on equipment sharing, technology transfer, and capacity development).

acts.speaker: Aden Duale, Kenyan Health Cabinet Secretary
acts.speech: affirmed that Kenya continues to meet its 20% co-financing requirement under Global Fund guidelines, committing USD 593.3 million under the Fifth Administration to sustain HIV, TB, malaria, and community health programs; reaffirmed the Ministry's commitment to national and global health goals, citing Kenya's progress in reducing new HIV infections and expanding access to life-saving antiretroviral therapy.

title: 'The silent killer' : How Hepatitis puts millions at risk in South Sudan - Eye Radio

acts.speaker: Health experts
acts.speech: Are raising concerns over the growing threat of hepatitis in the country and warn that hepatitis remains a silent killer in South Sudan, despite being preventable through vaccination and treatable if detected early ; say Hepatitis B is mostly spread through blood contact, unprotected sex, mother-to-child transmission during delivery, and sharing sharp objects like needles and razors, while Hepatitis A and E are mainly linked to contaminated food and water and Hepatitis D only occurs alongside Hepatitis B.

acts.speaker: Matiok Anthony, Executive Director of Friends of Humanity
acts.speech: Says the disease is often unnoticed until it’s too late: “Hepatitis is a silent killer because its early signs like fatigue, abdominal pain, and loss of appetite are similar to common illnesses. The only way to know your status is through testing” ; warns that cultural practices such as traditional scarification, communal use of sharp objects, and poor infection control have fuelled transmission ; highlights that newborn babies from infected mothers face a 90% risk of developing chronic hepatitis without timely vaccination: “The first dose of Hepatitis B vaccine should be given within 24 hours of birth, but South Sudan still lacks this birth dose vaccine”.

acts.speaker: Matiok Anthony, Executive Director of Friends of Humanity
acts.speech: Urged, on the organisation’s $2 fundraising initiative to establish a Hepatitis Treatment Center at Juba Teaching Hospital: “Hepatitis doesn’t attract donor funding like HIV or malaria. We need citizens to take the lead know your status, get vaccinated, and support this initiative”.

acts.speaker: Global health reports (cited)
acts.speech: According to global health reports, South Sudan faces high prevalence rates of 9.9% for Hepatitis B and 9.1% for Hepatitis C.

acts.speaker: Dr. Ambrose Anthony, medical doctor
acts.speech: Explains that hepatitis primarily affects the liver and can go unnoticed until severe damage occurs: “Hepatitis is a disease of the liver and it’s like a silent killer. Most people don’t know they have it until symptoms appear” ; says the early signs include persistent fatigue and weakness, yellowing of the eyes (jaundice), dark-coloured urine, abdominal pain and sometimes fever: “These are the major symptoms that signal hepatitis infection” ; says hepatitis is a viral disease transmitted mainly through infected blood and body fluids, including unprotected sex, sharing needles, exposure to infected blood or vomit, and mother-to-child transmission during childbirth.

acts.speaker: Dr. Ambrose Anthony, medical doctor
acts.speech: Warns that “Some young people engage in unprotected sex or share sharp objects like needles. These behaviours make them highly vulnerable” ; explains that one of the biggest misconceptions is that a vaccine can cure hepatitis after infection: “If you already have hepatitis, taking a vaccine will not help. It only adds more load on your body. Vaccination is for prevention, not treatment” ; emphasizes early screening as the most effective preventive measure: “Know your status. If you test negative, take the vaccine. If positive, start treatment immediately to avoid complications” ; “Screen yourself. Know your status. Take the vaccine if negative, and if positive, seek treatment immediately. Hepatitis is dangerous, but together we can defeat it”.

acts.speaker: Dr. Ambrose Anthony, medical doctor
acts.speech: Calls for collaborative action between citizens, health workers, and the government: “If the community pushes for services, the government will prioritize them. Eliminating hepatitis needs strategy, planning, and awareness” ; appeals for behavioural change among youth: “Use condoms during sex and avoid sharing needles. Prevention is easier and cheaper than treatment” ; says “More than 95% of hepatitis cases can clear naturally if detected early and monitored. But late detection leads to chronic infection and complications”.

title: «Je suis viscéralement opposé à la révision de la Constitution» dixit Topanou sur zone franche

acts.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin and unsuccessful candidate in the 2011 presidential and legislative elections
acts.speech: “I am viscerally opposed to the revision of the Constitution.” According to him, nobody knows which articles of the December 1990 constitution one would wish to revise, and there is no major crisis requiring such an act ; “I agree that there are shortcomings, but none of them has led us into a deadlock.”

acts.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin
acts.speech: On the reforms undertaken by the Refoundation, notably the new-generation Import Verification Programme (PVI-ng), thinks the analysis must be carried out on two levels: the level of principles, where he states that the results are not in harmony with the reforms, and the political level. While for him there is no doubt as regards the politicisation of the PVI-ng, he does not appear to agree with those who think the 2016 election lies behind its tentacles. He proposes a mid-term evaluation of the PVI.

acts.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin
acts.speech: Says, concerning the reform on strikes, that it is not necessary to restrict workers' right to strike, even if agreement must be reached on a certain minimum in vital sectors such as health, and that social dialogue simply needs to be resumed.

acts.speaker: Victor Prudent Topanou, former Minister of Justice of Benin
acts.speech: Deplores the conditions under which the last presidential and legislative elections were organised and corrects statements made about him in public opinion: “I was never the spokesperson of the opposition, but rather the spokesperson of the candidates.” He says he came to the April 2011 elections not in order to win but in order to mark a date ; “Houngbedji did not proclaim himself President, but he claimed victory” — clarifying the rumours that President Houngbedji had proclaimed himself president after the last presidential elections.

title: Africa’s total public debt climbs to $1.86 trillion-UNECA Chief

acts.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
acts.speech: said more than 20 African countries are either already facing debt distress or on the brink ; said in 2024, Africa's total public debt shot up to US$1.86 trillion, with average debt-to-GDP ratios rising from 44.4% in 2015 to 66.7% today ; "When debt repayments outweigh investments in health and education combined, we must question the sustainability and human cost of our fiscal path." ; "Africa is not merely confronting a debt crisis; it is facing a development crisis – one where debt servicing competes directly with health, education, infrastructure and the fundamental right to development."

acts.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
acts.speech: said across Africa, access to concessional finance is narrowing, while tariff escalations are weakening market access for African goods ; said many African countries are facing higher borrowing costs, reduced export revenues and tighter budgets, at a time when fiscal expansion is essential for inclusive growth ; said the cost of capital has surged.

acts.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
acts.speech: said the international financial lifelines Africa once relied on, including Official Development Assistance, are fading; today, 83 percent of USAID programmes have been cancelled and traditional partners are tightening their budgets.

acts.speaker: Claver Gatete, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA)
acts.speech: said the G20 Common Framework, unfortunately, remains slow, opaque and creditor-biased.

title: THE WASTED MANDATE: TRACING A LEGACY OF NATIONAL DECLINE UNDER PRESIDENT LAZARUS CHAKWERA (2020–2025)

acts.speaker: Centre for Investigative Journalism Malawi
acts.speech: "Families forage for wild yams; hospitals turn away patients; youth sell bananas at intersections. Chakwera's 'New Malawi' is a graveyard of hope."

acts.speaker: Transparency International
acts.speech: Ranked Malawi 107/180 nations (CPI score: 34/100); "systemic rot" cited.

acts.speaker: UK National Crime Agency (NCA)
acts.speech: Implicated 80+ officials in the Sattar bribes; local prosecutions stalled.

title: I love China, I Love Malawi: China and Malawi jointly ‘run’ the Citrus Marathon

acts.speaker: Dr. Eviness Pemphero Nyalugwe, Malawi Government Focal Person for SSC, and Dr. Babagana, FAO Representative in Malawi
acts.speech: Visited and inspected the site and spoke highly of this achievement: "Advancing the citrus pilot observation [initiative] has laid the foundation for the subsequent introduction of mango and apple varieties," they noted.

acts.speaker: Liang Suiquan, senior agricultural expert from China's Hubei Province
acts.speech: "[The] Yichang citrus [fruit] has found a new home in Africa," Liang pointed out, his sentiments not only a testament to the transfer of technology but also the source of inspiration for the event.

acts.speaker: Liang Suiquan, senior agricultural expert from China's Hubei Province
acts.speech: "Thank you to my friends and family for helping me realise my dream. I love marathons and I love Malawi's citrus orchards even more," ; he hopes running can serve as a bridge that deepens the friendship between Chinese and Malawian technicians, as they work together toward meeting the 'Four Betters' goal which FAO advances ; described it as a "small, yet beautiful, initiative."

acts.speaker: Dr. Charles Malidadi, SSC Focal Person at the Ministry of Agriculture's research station
acts.speech: "This is the first time I've run on the experimental field with Chinese friends who taught us citrus-grafting techniques. Every step feels like stepping to the rhythm of cooperation."

title: President Hassan Sheikh Opens Second East African Community Conference (EACON 2025) in Mogadishu

acts.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of the Federal Republic of Somalia
acts.speech: "Somalia has come a long way to be one of the members of the EAC. After more than ten years, Somalia now celebrates its role in developing its economy and engaging with other member states" ; "The 2060 Vision of Somalia is a signpost for the Somali people."

acts.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of the Federal Republic of Somalia
acts.speech: Added that Somalia has adopted a private-driven economic system to enhance all sectors of the economy and highlighted the importance of technology: "Artificial intelligence is not the future — it is already here, and if used correctly, it can guide us toward progress."

acts.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of the Federal Republic of Somalia
acts.speech: On education, emphasized: "Education without financial support cannot be achieved. Our universities must begin teaching Arabic, as Somalia has joined the Arab League, and Swahili, as we are now part of the East African Community."

acts.speaker: Dr. Maxamed Maxamuud Maxamed, Rector of the Somali National University and Chairperson of the EACON 2025 Organizing Committee
acts.speech: Welcomed participants and underscored the importance of regional collaboration for sustainable development ; reiterated that EACON 2025 provides a platform for dialogue on accelerating economic integration, strengthening trade, and promoting political cooperation across East Africa.

acts.speaker: Ali Mohamed Omar (Ali Balcad), State Minister for Foreign Affairs of Somalia
acts.speech: Noted that the conference focuses on knowledge sharing, agricultural productivity, and leveraging modern technology, expressing optimism that it will produce tangible results.

acts.speaker: Farah Sheikh Abdikadir, Minister of Education of Somalia
acts.speech: Highlighted the need for education to guide production and innovation, ensuring strong links between education, trade, and agriculture across the region.

acts.speaker: Mohamed Abdi Hayir Maareeye, Minister of Agriculture of Somalia
acts.speech: "For a long time, our people depended on imported goods, but now, with increased domestic production, we are exporting Somali crops to the world. This is a key priority for boosting the economies of EAC member states."

acts.speaker: Dr. Mathew
acts.speech: Emphasized that regional communities have multiple avenues to benefit, making development and everyday life easier and more productive.

acts.speaker: Kamaal Guutaale, Permanent Secretary in the Prime Minister's Office
acts.speech: Said Somalia is investing in economic infrastructure and that educational institutions play a central role in EAC cooperation.

acts.speaker: Dr. Cabdikariin Muxudiin Axmed, Rector of SIMAD University
acts.speech: Welcomed Somalia's integration into the regional market, describing it as a milestone for the country.

acts.speaker: Björn Richter, representing the German Development Agency
acts.speech: Reaffirmed Germany's support: "Somalia is making remarkable strides, having recently joined the East African Community. We are ready to stand with Somalia."

title: Youth and Sports unveils $1 Million for Youth Service Program - Liberia news The New Dawn Liberia, premier resource for latest news

acts.speaker: Jeror Cole Banggalu, Minister of Youth and Sports of Liberia
acts.speech: Announced an allocation of US$1 million to reintroduce the National Youth Service Program and emphasized government's commitment to the Cadet Program, stating, “We are serious about this initiative and will ensure its successful implementation alongside UNDP Liberia.” ; “The government is dedicated to the welfare of young people; therefore, it is our responsibility to improve the lives of our citizens, especially our youth.”

acts.speaker: Press release (Ministry of Youth and Sports)
acts.speech: According to a press release, he highlighted the success of past cadets, many of whom have secured permanent roles in government following their internships, spoke of efforts to expand the program and expressed gratitude to UNDP for the partnership.

acts.speaker: Louis Kuukpen, Deputy Resident Representative for Programme, UNDP Liberia
acts.speech: Lauded the government's ongoing efforts in youth development, asserting that investing in youth is an investment in Liberia's future: “At UNDP, we strongly believe that investing in youth is investing in the future. Young people are not only the leaders of tomorrow, they are the changemakers of today. Yet across Africa, and here in Liberia, youth unemployment remains a pressing challenge. Programs like the NCP are essential to breaking that cycle by equipping young people with practical skills, professional exposure, and confidence to pursue dignified livelihoods.” ; said the cadet program is not a temporary placement but a launchpad for careers, innovation, and entrepreneurship, and urged cadets who will be recruited this year to take full advantage of the opportunity to learn, grow, contribute, and dream boldly.

acts.speaker: Kolubah Yekeh, speaking on behalf of the Commerce Minister of Liberia
acts.speech: Emphasized the importance of the program, calling for increased support from other partners for the next 5 years.

title: Nigeria Seeks Deeper BRICS Health Ties, Showcases Bold Healthcare Reforms At Brazil Meeting

acts.speaker: Federal Government of Nigeria
acts.speech: Has called for stronger South-South cooperation and deeper health partnerships within the BRICS bloc to tackle pressing global health challenges.

acts.speaker: Dr. Salako (Dr. Tunji Alausa), Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
acts.speech: Stressed that “global health is currently faced with several interconnected challenges,” including the burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), antimicrobial resistance (AMR), pandemic threats, shrinking health funding, climate change, and civil unrest ; called on BRICS nations to work in solidarity, saying, “These challenges call for stronger South-South cooperation and more global solidarity to share best practices and resources to achieve the UN Sustainable Development Goals and create a more equitable world.”

acts.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
acts.speech: Described Nigeria’s participation in the BRICS health platform as a strategic alignment with the country’s Renewed Hope Agenda, noting that the Tinubu administration had launched the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative (HSRII) ; “We are implementing the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative to operationalise the Renewed Hope Agenda of the President of the country.” “The initiative rests on four pillars: effective governance; efficient, equitable, and quality health systems; unlocking healthcare value chains; and ensuring health security.” ; said the government is driving reforms using cross-cutting strategies such as digitalisation, data management, strategic financing, smarter spending, and a new work culture.

acts.speaker: Dr. Salako, Nigerian Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare
