acts.speech: "It's the first time a pan-African institution has taken a clear position on the visual representation of Africa." ; This transforms a cultural and civic demand into a continental policy aimed at the entire world, he argued.

acts.speaker: "Correct The Map" petition (Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa)
acts.speech: "As Africa becomes increasingly central to solving global challenges, it is critical to represent its true scale. That's why the Correct The Map campaign calls on the United Nations, as the global leader in international cooperation, and the BBC, as a global leading international media organisation, to adopt the Equal Earth projection in their data, reports, and materials that include world maps" ; "With their influence, these institutions can set a new standard and encourage others to follow suit in ensuring Africa is represented accurately as a critical driver of global growth and development."

acts.speaker: Donald Porusingazi, political analyst
acts.speech: Said the map debate is emblematic of a broader postcolonial reckoning – a push to rewrite Africa's place in the world not just through policy but through perception. "Maps are instruments of power and Africa is ready to redraw the lines."

title: Italy, WFP partner to reduce malnutrition in eastern Sudan

acts.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) in Sudan (statement)
acts.speech: Welcomes a contribution of EUR6.55 million from the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS); according to a statement on Monday this vital funding will enable WFP to provide specialised nutritious foods and cash-based nutrition assistance to nearly 200,000 young children and pregnant or nursing women in Gedaref and Kassala states ; "This support will help prevent malnutrition in eastern Sudan, which is critical as some 3.7 million children under five and pregnant and breastfeeding mothers across the country are malnourished."

acts.speaker: Laurent Bukera, WFP Regional Director for Eastern Africa
acts.speech: "Amid Sudan's deepening hunger crisis, this generous contribution will help to improve diets among vulnerable women and children, which is key to reducing malnutrition. We are extremely grateful to the Government of Italy."

acts.speaker: Michele Tommasi, Ambassador of Italy to Sudan
acts.speech: "With this project, Italy is at the forefront in Sudan in supporting the most vulnerable populations. The partnership with WFP is a tangible example of our commitment in the fight against malnutrition, ensuring access to essential nutritional support for those most in need. This initiative also reflects Italy's broader strategy of humanitarian assistance and sustainable development, reinforcing long-term resilience and food security in the region."

acts.speaker: United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)
acts.speech: Said it is working tirelessly to expand food and nutrition assistance to millions more people across Sudan – aiming to triple the number of people it supports to 7 million.

title: Minneapolis school attacker 'obsessed with idea of killing children', officials say - Daily News

acts.speaker: Investigators
acts.speech: Say that the attacker who opened fire on pupils as they were praying at a church in Minneapolis was "obsessed with the idea of killing children".

acts.speaker: Brian O'Hara, Minneapolis Police Chief
acts.speech: Said Robin Westman, who killed two children and injured 18 others, did not seem to have any specific motive. The attacker "appeared to hate all of us", the chief said on Thursday, adding: "More than anything, the shooter wanted to kill children". ; He added that she, "like so many other mass shooters that we have seen in this country too often and around the world, had some deranged fascination with previous mass shootings".

acts.speaker: Brian O'Hara, Minneapolis Police Chief
acts.speech: Told reporters that news outlets should stop using the killer's name, because "the purpose of the shooter's actions was to obtain notoriety".

acts.speaker: Relative of Fletcher Merkel (unnamed)
acts.speech: "Fletcher loved his family, friends, fishing, cooking and any sport that he was allowed to play," he said. "Give your kids an extra hug and kiss today. We love you, Fletcher. You'll always be with us," he continued, choking back tears.

acts.speaker: Michael Moyski and Jackie Flavin, parents of Harper Moyski (statement)
acts.speech: Said in a statement that their daughter "was a bright, joyful, and deeply loved 10-year-old whose laughter, kindness, and spirit touched everyone who knew her". "As a family, we are shattered, and words cannot capture the depth of our pain," they said, adding that they hope "her memory fuels action" to stop gun violence. "No family should ever have to endure this kind of pain.... Change is possible, and it is necessary - so that Harper's story does not become yet another in a long line of tragedies."

acts.speaker: Joseph Thompson, acting US Attorney General for Minnesota
acts.speech: In a news conference on Thursday said "the shooter expressed hate towards many groups, including the Jewish community and towards President Trump". ; "I won't dignify the attacker's words by repeating them, they are horrific and vile," said Mr Thompson.

acts.speaker: Officials
acts.speech: Said the attacker, who died at the scene of a self-inflicted gunshot wound, left a note, but added that a definitive motive may never be known. ; In their news conference, officials confirmed that the attacker had previously attended the school, and that three residences associated with the attacker have been searched by police. They said that the church locked its doors before beginning its Mass service, likely saving many lives. Officials added that the guns used in the attack were all legally purchased, that the killer did not appear on any government watchlist, and that police are not aware of any mental health diagnoses or treatments that she was receiving.

acts.speaker: Judge in Westman's 2020 name-change case (court record)
acts.speech: Westman's name was legally changed from Robert to Robin in 2020, with the judge writing: "Minor child identifies as a female".

acts.speaker: US officials
acts.speech: Have warned for years that mass shooting can lead to copycat killings, as killers seek to become famous through their heinous crimes.

acts.speaker: Kash Patel, FBI Director
acts.speech: Has described the attack as "an act of domestic terrorism motivated by a hate-filled ideology". In a post on X, Patel said that the attacker "left multiple anti-Catholic, anti-religious references" written on guns and in notes uncovered by investigators. "Subject expressed hatred and violence toward Jewish people, writing Israel must fall,' 'Free Palestine,' and using explicit language related to the Holocaust," he wrote. The killer also "wrote an explicit call for violence against President Trump on a firearm magazine".

acts.speaker: Mary Grace Westman, the attacker's mother (non-response)
acts.speech: Her mother, Mary Grace Westman, previously worked at the school, and has so far not responded to law enforcement's attempts to contact her.

acts.speaker: Patrick Scallen, resident living near the church
acts.speech: Said that he saw three children fleeing the building - one of them a girl with a head wound. "She kept saying, 'please hold my hand, don't leave me', and I said I wasn't going anywhere."

acts.speaker: Vincent Francoual, father of an 11-year-old who was in the church
acts.speech: Said he tried not to panic after he heard the news. He called it "sick" that children in the US are trained to prepare for mass shootings. "We live in a country where we train kids what to do. And she did what she had to do," he said. "Here it's a pattern. It's no longer a freak accident," he said of school shootings in the US. "I told my wife that every morning, when we drop our kids, we don't know if she'd be back safe." ; Said that Chloe is afraid to return to school or church.

acts.speaker: Jacob Frey, Minneapolis Mayor
acts.speech: "There is no reason that someone should be able to reel off 30 shots before they even have to reload," said Mayor Jacob Frey, also calling for a ban on high-capacity ammo magazines. "We're not talking about your father's hunting rifle here. We're talking about guns that are built to pierce armour and kill people."

title: WBGs: Thousands of Raja returnees face dire humanitarian situation -Official - Eye Radio

acts.speaker: Authorities in Raja, Western Bahr el Ghazal State
acts.speech: According to authorities in Raja, over 24,000 returnees from Sudan are facing dire need of humanitarian assistance in different camps in the County.

acts.speaker: Gismallah Hassan Dahia, press secretary of the Raja County Commissioner
acts.speech: Said the returnees from conflict-torn Sudan are mainly children, women, and elderly; added the returnees are arriving from Sudan daily to the areas of Siri-Malaga, Boro el Madina, Tamsah and Raja, having fled from the Zamzum refugee camp in El Dein town of Eastern Darfur via Kafia Kengi.

acts.speaker: Gismallah Hassan Dahia, press secretary of the Raja County Commissioner
acts.speech: Said the returnees have been lacking food and medicines for months now; "The returnees are in big number and have been lacking food. The International Comitte of the Red Cross had given them food assistance since last year. Even (those) in Boro - al Madina now, don't have food. The new arrivals of more than 950 people came here without anything, they facing issue of shelters, food and something to sleep on," he said.

acts.speaker: Gismallah Hassan Dahia, press secretary of the Raja County Commissioner
acts.speech: According to him, the ongoing humanitarian challenges faced by returnees and displaced populations in South Sudan have been worsened by limited resources and support infrastructure.

acts.speaker: United Nations (registration figures)
acts.speech: Since the fighting erupted in Khartoum, Sudan, the UN has registered more than 1 million people who have crossed into South Sudan, with 90% of them South Sudanese.

title: Africa needs to increase internet penetration as COVID-19 disrupts trade condition, says UNECA

acts.speaker: United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA/ECA)
acts.speech: Said on Tuesday that much still needs to be done for Africa to increase internet penetration as the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the continent's trade and socioeconomic condition.

acts.speaker: UN Economic Commission for Africa (ECA figures)
acts.speech: According to figures from the ECA, Kenya, Mauritius, Namibia and South Africa are the only countries where the share of online shoppers exceeds 8 percent, while the trend is below 5 percent in “most other countries” in Africa.

acts.speaker: Mama Keita, director of ECA's Eastern Africa region
acts.speech: “The COVID-19 pandemic changed the way we do business, and this should be an accelerator for digital transformation. Sectors like education, health, trade, food delivery, events and conferencing experienced unprecedented demand for technology.”

acts.speaker: Mama Keita, director of ECA's Eastern Africa region
acts.speech: Stressed that Africa's projected GDP growth of 3.2 percent for 2020 is now expected to be a sharp contraction ; emphasized how the COVID-19 crisis and containment measures have upended almost every aspect of life, affecting big and small enterprises, disrupting supply chains, causing the decline of export revenues and interrupting the tourism, transport and logistics sectors significantly ; noted that East Africa's economic growth, although highly impacted too, is expected to remain the largest in Africa ; “COVID-19 pandemic should be used as a game-changer. It should serve as a wakeup call underscoring the urgency to turn Africa's structural vulnerabilities into opportunities.”

acts.speaker: Mama Keita, director of ECA's Eastern Africa region
acts.speech: Said that the over reliance on imports from the rest of the world of essential goods such as medical, pharmaceutical and food items should be reduced considerably and gradually be replaced with local production.

acts.speaker: International Telecommunication Union (ITU) figures
acts.speech: Recent figures from the ITU showed that only 28 percent of Africans used the internet in 2019, while online shoppers are relatively still few in the continent.

acts.speaker: Experts attending the virtual dialogue
acts.speech: Stressed that in the wake of COVID-19, there is an urgent need for African enterprises to digitalize and tap into enormous opportunities offered by e-commerce.

acts.speaker: Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC)
acts.speech: Said that as of Tuesday, the number of confirmed COVID-19 cases across the African continent reached 736,288 while the number of deaths related to the pandemic rose to 15,418 ; said 391,898 patients who tested positive for COVID-19 have recovered across the continent.

title: Lutte contre la faim et la malnutrition: Les nouveaux engagements du Pam en faveur des pays pauvres

acts.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP) Executive Board, first regular session of 2024 (decision/recommendations)
acts.speech: Recommended that WFP increase the support provided to the least developed countries in the fight against vulnerability, poverty, food insecurity, malnutrition and inequality, and that it support social protection programmes in rural and urban areas and the redistribution of resources that help people meet their essential needs. Under the decision, WFP will pay particular attention to the implementation of the Doha Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries, within the framework of the support it provides to them and in accordance with its mandate.

acts.speaker: Youssef Balla, President of the WFP Executive Board (and other board members)
acts.speech: Stress that the UN institution will rely on its 2022-2025 Strategic Plan and its normative framework, which are consistent with the Doha Programme of Action and its priority areas of action.

acts.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP) Executive Board decision
acts.speech: States that the opportunities offered by global and local partnerships will be explored, drawing for example on UNICEF's specialised expertise on matters concerning children, families and essential services, and on that of the World Bank in reforming social protection systems and developing policies.

title: PM welcomes new U.S. Chargé d’Affaires

acts.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
acts.speech: Expressed his pleasure in receiving the new U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Marc Weinstock, describing him as a person who “radiates a pleasant personality and vibrant energy”; acknowledged the commendable work of Weinstock’s predecessor, Caitlin Piper, noting that she “worked well with the current Administration of the Government of the Kingdom of Eswatini and successfully strengthened the relations between the two countries”, and wished Piper success in her new assignment.

acts.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
acts.speech: Emphasised that their discussions focused on “the opportunities that we can seize working together to serve our countries as well as to further strengthen our relations”, with key areas for collaboration including food security, border surveillance, and disaster risk management.

acts.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
acts.speech: Touched on the recent reinstatement of critical health programs funded by USAID and PEPFAR, which are vital for HIV/AIDS prevention, care, and treatment in Eswatini, highlighting the importance of these programs in safeguarding public health, and noted the arrival of third-country migrants from the U.S.

acts.speaker: Russell Dlamini, Prime Minister of Eswatini
acts.speech: Described the United States as “one of the country’s most valuable diplomatic partners” and underscored that the relationship is “based on mutual trust and respect for one another”, reaffirming Eswatini’s commitment to deeper cooperation ; Addressed Weinstock directly: “To you, Chargé d’Affaires, seize the opportunity because time and chance have happened. Welcome to the Kingdom of Eswatini, the palace of Africa.”

title: L'aide médicale marocaine arrive à Gaza en pleine crise de famine

acts.speaker: Bayt Mal Al-Quds agency (video and photos published)
acts.speech: A video released on Monday by the Bayt Mal Al-Quds agency shows trucks loaded with supplies travelling through the streets of Gaza. The trucks bore the Moroccan flag and the logo of the Mohammed V Foundation for Solidarity. The agency then published photos showing Moroccan food aid, including baby food, canned goods, flour and fruit, reaching storage centres in Deir el-Balah, a city in central Gaza.

acts.speaker: Many Palestinians
acts.speech: This aid was welcomed by many Palestinians, who say it helps meet urgent needs.

acts.speaker: Humanitarian organisations
acts.speech: warn that the volume of aid is still far from sufficient.

acts.speaker: Gaza government press service
acts.speech: indicated that only 85 trucks of humanitarian aid had entered the enclave yesterday, and that many of them had been looted before reaching people in need. The press service and the United Nations both indicated that between 500 and 600 trucks were needed each day to provide adequate aid to the population, reduce looting and bring down the high prices caused by shortages.

acts.speaker: United Nations
acts.speech: indicated that between 500 and 600 trucks were needed each day to bring adequate aid to the population, reduce looting and lower the high prices caused by shortages.

acts.speaker: Gaza Ministry of Health
acts.speech: According to the Gaza Ministry of Health, at least 135 Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks over the last 24 hours, including 87 people who were waiting for aid. These attacks also left 771 wounded. The ministry indicated that five people died of hunger during the same period, bringing the total number of hunger-related deaths to 193, including 96 children.

title: LNDC campaign continues to progress

acts.speaker: Molise Ramaili, LNDC Interim CEO
acts.speech: highlighted that sometime last year Ace Apparel faced a closure bringing a challenge of unemployment to so many Basotho; the worst-case scenario was its closure during the Christmas holidays where employees would have been left without their salaries. Ramaili mentioned that they sat down and figured a way out. He said they approached Joans Enterprise bringing along investors from South Africa noting to them that Basotho are experts in sewing and are always ready to do a great job. He said if it were not for Basotho's hard work, investors would not stay and would have searched for market elsewhere. "We promised investors to give them a firm that will do a great job and in return we pleaded with them to give the same firm work so as to grow. This is a huge change in terms of opening factories to see to it that Basotho are employed through this campaign," he said ; highlighted that their journey with the investors and Joans was a success as the factory grew from 180 employees to 350 and now it has employed 700 Basotho.

acts.speaker: Molise Ramaili, LNDC Interim CEO
acts.speech: noted that the management has informed that they have not stopped employing and it is their wish to expand once again and employ more Basotho; the issue of expansion is important especially in factories, adding they attract investors. "We are already selecting another factory that was called CMT where Joans Enterprise will expand and be able to employ 700 more Basotho. The issue of opening factories has been taken into serious consideration and this will go a long way so that Basotho are employed. I urge workers and management to continue working hard, as the LNDC we will continue supporting them and where they have challenges we are ready to solve them together so that the factory stays sustainable," he said.

acts.speaker: Mokhethi Shelile, Trade Minister
acts.speech: noted that there are challenges such as unemployment which lead to Basotho leaving the country and seeking work elsewhere. He said one example was the sudden closure of the Ace Apparel which left many factory workers stranded without work. The minister was appreciative Joans came along and assisted ; he urged workers to work hard all the time and to be a part of unions because the ministry of trade and the ministry of labour usually work together with unions ; exchanged a vote of thanks to Joans Management for their efforts to continue employing Basotho and alleviating the high unemployment rate.

acts.speaker: Mokhethi Shelile, Trade Minister
acts.speech: said the government is waiting for tariffs announcement at least until September after doing all the necessary requirements to be a part of the Southern African countries that can work with the United States in terms of market. He also spoke about the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) which he cautioned will be ending, adding that government is working towards finding tariffs agreement that does not exceed 10 percent to enable market access in USA. Shelile also noted that the government is in search of alternative market access in other countries.

acts.speaker: Manoj Rooplall, Joans Enterprise Cutting Room Manager
acts.speech: exchanged a vote of thanks to the ministry for assisting with the building so that the company could grow and increase employment. He said they look forward to the future growth with the support of the Lesotho government in the textile industry. He likewise thanked customers, and stakeholders.

acts.speaker: Selinah Mpakathe, Joans Enterprise Floor Manager
acts.speech: added that for a firm which commenced as an SME with only 180 employees, moving to 700 by March this year is a huge step and it is promising for many other Basotho in terms of employment opportunities. She noted with appreciation the Management for continuing to search for investors to create jobs in Lesotho.

acts.speaker: 'Makatleho Mothae, an employee
acts.speech: highlighted that she was an employee at Ace Apparel and was part of those who were retrenched. She noted that through Joans Enterprise she is now back to work. She hoped more factories will be opened so that those on queues outside also receive the opportunity to be able to feed their families as employees.

title: Énergie : La Côte d’Ivoire et les Etats-Unis signent un Compact régional de 322 millions de dollars

acts.speaker: Dr Robert Beugré Mambé, Prime Minister of Côte d'Ivoire
acts.speech: Welcomed the quality and dynamism of the relationship between Côte d'Ivoire and the United States, describing it as a “relationship built on trust, nurtured by rigour and consolidated by concrete results on the projects from which our country benefits” ; “the bilateral compact that is now ending is a perfect illustration of what can be produced by cooperation founded on four things: mutual respect, transparency, responsibility and mutual trust” ; “the results on the ground, beyond the physical infrastructure achievements and the figures, are even more eloquent in terms of the improvement of living conditions and the retreat of poverty.”

acts.speaker: Dr Robert Beugré Mambé, Prime Minister of Côte d'Ivoire
acts.speech: Promised that what he described as “the diplomacy of the concrete, which does not only promise but acts and delivers results” would be implemented to make this new partnership an even more resounding success.

acts.speaker: Alassane Ouattara, President of Côte d'Ivoire (vision cited by the Prime Minister)
acts.speech: “Development is not decreed. Development is built with methods, with solid partners and with a constant political will.”

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
acts.speech: “America is proud of its friendship with the nations that share its will to build a better world. It aspires, like us, to a future in which every people can prosper in dignity and freedom.”

acts.speaker: Fidèle Sarassoro, Minister-Director of Cabinet of the President of the Republic and Chairman of the Board of the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA Côte d'Ivoire)
acts.speech: Reiterated the commitment of the teams to work towards achieving more significant results: “We are convinced that the experience and the lessons learned from the bilateral compact will allow us in future to avoid the shortcomings observed during its implementation. Likewise, the MCC's eligibility criteria through the Scorecard will continue to guide our efforts to improve our country's performance in matters of governance.”

acts.speaker: Jason Small, MCC Vice-President for Operations
acts.speech: Congratulated Fidèle Sarassoro and the staff of MCA Côte d'Ivoire, welcomed a model that works and the shared belief that economic growth makes itself felt beyond borders, and saluted in particular the numerous road infrastructures, the three technical and vocational training centres, the 40 neighbourhood secondary schools, the two annexes of the École normale supérieure and two campuses built under the bilateral Compact.

acts.speaker: Jessica Davis Ba, United States Ambassador to Côte d'Ivoire
acts.speech: Highlighted the special character of relations between the Ivorian and American governments, pointing out that the regional Compact is the first partnership of this level within the MCC framework that the United States has entered into since President Donald Trump's return to the White House.

acts.speaker: Christopher Landau, US Deputy Secretary of State (quoted by the Ambassador)
acts.speech: “This pact reflects President Trump's attachment to intelligent and responsible development serving the interests of the United States. A more robust energy sector in West Africa makes it possible to create new markets for American companies, to support employment in the United States and to contribute to regional stability, which is beneficial for all of us.”

acts.speaker: Mamadou Sangafowa Coulibaly, Minister of Mines, Petroleum and Energy
acts.speech: Requested further support from the American government in the energy field: “We hope to be able to explore new investment opportunities, notably through an additional Compact aligned with the strategic priorities of our electricity sector”, to cover the “investment needs to modernise our infrastructure, optimise energy distribution and integrate alternative energies” ; undertook to “do everything possible to guarantee a rigorous, transparent and exemplary implementation of this project under the vigilant eye of the head of government.”

title: Former Peace Corps volunteer to Malawi advocates use music in diplomacy

acts.speaker: Jack Allison, former Peace Corps volunteer in Malawi (1967-69) and music diplomat
acts.speech: “From a lifetime of practicing music diplomacy, I urge that music be highlighted as a powerful means of promulgating peace and goodwill.” ; “Music diplomacy is essential at a time like this to be utilized whenever possible to foster peace and crosscultural sharing for the common good.”

title: NBE leader rolls out new reforms

acts.speaker: National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE)
acts.speech: Announced that, despite the foreign currency shortage, there have been significant reforms in the financial sector.

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Said that since he came to NBE there have been many changes ; “About eight months ago our situation was very difficult. The reserve had significantly dropped and the situation regarding settling foreign debts was dire. We were at the edge of defaulting on our external loan settlements” ; “The coming of Abiy has led to new bilateral and multilateral partners who have provided hard currency. This will provide short term relief and enable us to think about further reform plans so that we can solve structural economic problems, hard currency earnings and exports” ; He added that even though there have been delays in payments the government is now settling its loans properly, and providing hard currency to the manufacturing industry, although not as much as needed ; The foreign reserve has also improved, according to the Governor, but he declined to give a specific amount of available forex.

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Stated the economy was on the brink of a bad fate when the new government came in, but now things have improved, and he expects the country’s economy will register a similar rate as last year ; “If we can provide what the manufacturing industry demands and the agriculture sector is able to meet its targets then economic growth will reach double digits” ; He stated that the government is doing its best to provide foreign currency to the manufacturing sector but it is still less than they need, and amplified that the manufacturing sector also faces other problems like power and skilled labour.

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: “We have worked on several things, and we are undergoing transitions, for instance in the past few months we have worked hard on remittances” ; Said the bank is improving the capacity of staff and establishing groups of experts from local and external professionals for applying several new businesses like bonds and capital markets in the financial sector, and that they are also working on a ten year roadmap.

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: According to the governor the volume of loans in local banks has become quite high: “Due to the instability in the past few years some investors were unable to settle their debt properly so to do so, NBE has been working for extension of the loan settlement period with banks.”

acts.speaker: Ethiopian investors engaged in similar businesses
acts.speech: Said the NBE suppliers’ credit scheme created a problem.

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Said that local investors are supposed to be given priority but the foreign investors believed the country’s law and they have also invested a huge sum so it would be bad if they are not able to make their products because of a hard currency shortage, which can affect the country’s image ; “It is not against the country’s forex law” ; For local investors we are doing our best to help the manufacturing sector get hard currency via a letter of credit (LC), he added.

acts.speaker: Experts / legal experts
acts.speech: Experts are arguing that the directive goes against the investment proclamation amended in 2012 ; Legal experts argued that the 769/2012 investment proclamation erroneously mentioned on the central bank directive FXD/47/2017 as ‘679/2012’ on its part one article 2/4 stated that investor means a domestic or a foreign investor that invests in Ethiopia.

acts.speaker: A business consultant
acts.speech: “The proclamation indicated that it has not divided local and foreign investors in relation to acquiring external loans,” a business consultant said, “but they claim the central bank directive goes against it.”

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Said that he is informed about the selling of hard currency by exporters via banks that is illegal ; “The basic problem is the shortage of foreign currency but to tackle illegal activities we are working our hardest and we are also meeting with banks’ presidents to improve the financial sector. If we find someone involved in an illegal act in the foreign market, the actors and the bank will be punished” ; “We have suspicions on illegality in hard currency allocation but have not been able to prove it and we will solve problems if we see any.”

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: “Regarding first come first serve we have not gotten a better option than applying,” he said, regarding the allocation of foreign currency at banks ; “We are working with relevant body that gives licenses to the importers or exporters to solve the problem and identify the real market actors” ; He confirmed that there is a high burden at banks to provide foreign currency.

acts.speaker: Bankers / bank officials
acts.speech: In the past banks wanted the regulatory body to ease the new directive that controlled the way banks handle hard currency; they asked the central bank to give them the responsibility of managing the LC process ; During a meeting between NBE leaders and bank officials in November 2018 bankers expressed their concern about the directive which they claim does not benefit banks or customers; they said illegal actors are still accessing the hard currency and distributing it unfairly.

acts.speaker: Central bank leaders (NBE)
acts.speech: The central bank leaders argued that they applied the directive to create fairness. “NBE has told bankers to come up with a proposal to replace the directive.”

acts.speaker: Business actors and some bankers
acts.speech: Told Capital that individuals who are not seeking hard currency for legitimate reasons, lined up at banks to access foreign currency based on the directive, then they sell their place in line to others.

acts.speaker: Experts and the private sector / sector actors
acts.speech: Expressed their concern regarding the growing loan interest at banks; the sector actors said that the interest rate has gone up to 25 percent on some types of loans; while the minimum rate which is mainly given to the export business is not small, according to experts in banks. They expressed their concern that it may have lead to inflation and pressure borrowers into debt stress.

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: “Even though it is free for banks and a free market scheme, we shall see if it becomes a problem. But the issue will be answered after a relevant and adequate study” ; “In this regard we have to speak with banks,” he added ; He said that banks, mainly private banks are now providing loans without any challenge.

acts.speaker: The private sector
acts.speech: Stated that loans particularly from state owned financial firms is lagging.

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Stated that loan approval from Development Bank of Ethiopia (DBE) is not as much as is being requested ; “The problem at DBE is very high in relation to debt given for investors mainly for those engaged in rain fed farms” ; He said that agriculture loans amounting to 6.3 billion birr could be repossessed but NBE has ordered DBE to settle the matter legally ; “We did not allow the birr or foreign currency that it wants until it normalizes non-performing loans” ; “Even though they received the loan legally, they took it in an organized manner even calculating how they will not settle the loan.”

acts.speaker: Yinager Dessie, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Said that in the coming year vast irrigation mainly in low land areas will be applied in the coming years; said the manufacturing sector like textiles and agro processing is growing in the country which will be fed by local input ; “The government has given serious attention to developing the agriculture sector to support the overall economy including solving the hard currency shortage” ; The governor has hinted that irrigation will be a priority for the coming budget year.

acts.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Prime Minister of Ethiopia
acts.speech: In his meeting with government leaders and prominent international businesspeople, he spoke about the support with irrigation development.

title: Mca-Bénin II : Le Conseil d'Administration fait le point et formule des résolutions pour la suite

acts.speaker: Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, Minister of State in charge of development, Chairman of the Board of Directors of MCA-Benin II
acts.speech: According to him, the resolutions adopted will enable the MCA-Benin II coordination team to move surely and on schedule through the next steps towards the entry into force of this second compact ; In opening the session, he recalled how important this compact is, saying that, entirely devoted to energy, it constitutes a key means for development in Benin: "Today, the number one obstacle to economic growth is energy."

acts.speaker: Samuel Batcho, National Coordinator of MCA-Benin II
acts.speech: Said the team he leads is certain that, with the support of the Board of Directors and the MCC country team, the entry into force will be a success, envisaged for the first quarter of 2017 ; He recalled that in the process, the coordination team has, since the 3rd ordinary session of the Board, continued the preparatory activities for entry into force and the setting up of staff and their working framework.

title: U.S. government celebrates partnership with Mozambique to prevent, treat and eliminate malaria

acts.speaker: U.S. Government (statement marking World Malaria Day)
acts.speech: Celebrates the advances Mozambique has made in preventing and treating malaria and recommits to continue supporting Mozambique's efforts at eliminating the disease, noting it has invested more than $416 million since 2007 and provides more than $500 million in annual assistance to Mozambique.

acts.speaker: Peter H. Vrooman, U.S. Ambassador to Mozambique
acts.speech: "The United States is proud of its more than 15-year partnership with Mozambique to combat malaria. Investments we make together with the goal of ending malaria-related deaths not only save lives now, but also help prepare to respond to future health threats."

acts.speaker: World Health Organization
acts.speech: Reported more than 600,000 people died of malaria in 2020, 96 percent of which were in Africa.

title: CREAKY GEARS

acts.speaker: Ethiopian federal government
acts.speech: Has claimed that Ethiopia has become a net wheat exporter despite the bread price nearly doubling in two years.

title: Le ministre des affaires étrangères et de la coopération internationale participe à la 1218e réunion du Conseil de Paix et de Sécurité

acts.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Djiboutian Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation
acts.speech: Represented President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh at the 1218th meeting of the Peace and Security Council and, on his behalf, read out and conveyed a stirring message to the assembly concerning the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

acts.speaker: Chairperson of the African Union Commission (report)
acts.speech: Report on the situation in the Republic of Sudan, examined by the Council during the meeting.

acts.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti (message read to the Council)
acts.speech: In his message, expressed his gratitude to President Museveni for having convened this crucial meeting on Sudan, as well as to the Chairperson of the African Union Commission and the Executive Secretary of IGAD for their reports and their constant efforts to resolve the Sudanese crisis.

acts.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti (message read to the Council)
acts.speech: Stressed that Sudan has been plunged into a destructive war since April 2023, with fighting between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) causing great suffering to the Sudanese people. Thousands of civilians have been killed and millions displaced. The humanitarian situation is disastrous, with numerous human rights violations reported.

acts.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti (message read to the Council)
acts.speech: Announced that Djibouti will host a meeting of all mediators in July, aimed at working on a coordinated approach focused on concrete results, notably the immediate cessation of hostilities.

acts.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti (message read to the Council)
acts.speech: Made several recommendations to the Council to promote a cessation of hostilities in Sudan, notably: 1. Call on the RSF and the SAF to immediately cease fighting in Darfur and other regions of Sudan. 2. Invite the RSF and the commander of the Supreme Council to meet under the auspices of the IGAD-African Union platform without delay. 3. Allow unconditional access to humanitarian aid for the Sudanese people. 4. Prepare the ground for an inclusive dialogue in Sudan in July. 5. Insist on accountability and launch investigations into the reported human rights violations.

acts.speaker: Ismaïl Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti (message read to the Council)
acts.speech: Concluded by affirming that Sudan has reached a critical point where it risks breaking apart if the war continues unpredictably. The Peace and Security Council must not wait for this scenario to materialise, because the consequences could be disastrous.

acts.speaker: Djibouti, as Chair of IGAD
acts.speech: Has repeatedly called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the face of the crisis.

title: USAID : Donald Trump supprime la quasi-totalité des financements à l’étranger

acts.speaker: Trump administration
acts.speech: Announced on Wednesday 26 February 2025 that it was making massive cuts to American international aid, in particular through the elimination of 92% of the funding of overseas programmes by USAID, boasting of “saving American taxpayers nearly 60 billion dollars”.

acts.speaker: Federal judge (US, unnamed)
acts.speech: Suspended the decision to freeze expenditure approved by Congress, after being seized by two organisations grouping together companies, NGOs and other beneficiaries of American aid funds.

acts.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
acts.speech: Decided, following a review of these programmes carried out by his services, to definitively eliminate nearly 5,800 of the funding grants awarded around the world by the agency, with a remaining cost of 54 billion dollars, keeping only a little over 500, according to the State Department.

acts.speaker: Spokesperson for American diplomacy (US State Department, unnamed)
acts.speech: Specified that of more than 9,100 grants awarded by the State Department, for a total amount of 15.9 billion dollars, 4,100 – at an estimated cost of 4.4 billion – have been cancelled.

acts.speaker: US State Department
acts.speech: Assures that USAID is maintaining “vital” grants such as food assistance and treatments for patients suffering from AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria, as well as for countries such as Lebanon, Haiti, Venezuela and Cuba.

acts.speaker: USAID
acts.speech: Announced on 23 February 2025 the dismissal of 1,600 of its employees in the United States and the placement of the majority of its personnel on administrative leave.

title: Serikali yasisitiza udhibiti magonjwa ya wanyama kuhamia kwa binadamu

acts.speaker: Professor Riziki Shemdoe, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries of Tanzania
acts.speech: called on livestock professionals in the country to be at the forefront of preventing the spread of livestock diseases to humans in order to help the Government avoid spending large sums of money treating preventable diseases; said preventing animal diseases from passing to humans is easier than treatment, which requires a lot of money and time ; “This training is very important for livestock professionals; treating livestock diseases in humans costs us far more money than tackling these diseases early. It is important to be at the forefront of preventing these diseases from passing to humans; by doing so we will have helped save a great deal of Government money that would have been spent on treatment.”

acts.speaker: Professor Riziki Shemdoe, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries of Tanzania
acts.speech: urged the professionals to use the training they received to vaccinate livestock so that Tanzania can continue to grow its international meat market, as there is already a country looking into the possibility of importing 54,000 tonnes of meat from the country.

acts.speaker: Dr Rogath Kishimba, Coordinator of Epidemiology and Laboratory Management Training, Ministry of Health of Tanzania
acts.speech: said the cost of livestock vaccination is small, but when a disease passes from an animal to a human the cost of treatment is high; giving the example of rabies, said a dog is vaccinated for Sh2,000, but a person bitten by a dog with the disease must receive four vaccine doses costing between Sh30,000 and Sh60,000 per dose.

acts.speaker: Dr Rogath Kishimba, Coordinator of Epidemiology and Laboratory Management Training, Ministry of Health of Tanzania
acts.speech: said that when a person contracts rabies and begins to show symptoms, the chance of recovery is small: “If you have 100 patients, on average only two can recover, or none at all recover; that is why we stress the importance of control - when it is in animals it is cheaper to treat and prevent.”

acts.speaker: Dr Benezeth Lutege, Director of veterinary services, Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries of Tanzania
acts.speech: said that in order to increase better availability of vaccines the Government has removed tax on livestock vaccines imported from abroad: “Vaccines and veterinary medicines in the country are imported free of tax, so we expect vaccine costs to be lower. Also, we have a dog vaccine we expect to produce and it is at various stages of production, and possibly by 2030 we will have begun production; we have also prepared a strategy to eliminate rabies from 2024 to 2028 and we have submitted it to the World Organisation for Animal Health.”

acts.speaker: Innocent Mrope, livestock expert from Masasi
acts.speech: said that among 300 people aged 18 and above surveyed in 15 villages in the district, 54.6 percent have no understanding of rabies and 32.3 percent had a negative attitude about the problem; said it is important that the district focuses on providing education to citizens about rabies because only 14 percent have a positive attitude about the disease, and most of them, when they face a problem related to the disease, do not believe in recovering through treatment or in vaccinating their dogs.

acts.speaker: Mosses Ole Neselle, FAO Programme Coordinator
acts.speech: said the livestock professionals enabled by the training number 30 - 20 from mainland Tanzania and 10 from Zanzibar; said the training is important because animal diseases endanger world food security and undermine countries’ economies.

acts.speaker: World Organisation for Animal Health
acts.speech: according to it, more than 70 percent of diseases occurring in the world come from animals to humans.

acts.speaker: United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
acts.speech: according to it, there are more than 200 diseases associated with transmission from animals to humans, meaning that 6 out of 10 infectious diseases that affect people are spread by animals, including domestic animals.

acts.speaker: National Library of Medicine website (United States)
acts.speech: shows that for diseases passing from animals to humans, 2.5 billion cases have been reported with 2.7 million deaths witnessed.

title: BUSINESS TODAY | NAMCOR still struggling despite N$1.9 billion government bailout

acts.speaker: Ebson Uanguta, NAMCOR interim managing director
acts.speech: Highlighted that the company has put in place strategies and policies to address its financial instability; while some of its debts have been paid, he added that the company still has a lot of work to do in ensuring it does not sink. "We need the suppliers of NAMCOR because we trade in oil. As we know, Namibia does not produce oil or petroleum products. We need to import this from other nations where oil is found. And when we import this, we trade it now in a domestic economy to supply the demand. And that is possibly where things went wrong, and hence NAMCOR found itself having significant debts. Because of that debt, we needed some kind of support from the government as shareholders. We really want to thank the government for coming in fully to support NAMCOR at that difficult time. They came up with a guarantee of N$1.2 billion; it was a sovereign guarantee, and the money was given by the commercial banks. So that has really enabled us somehow to stabilise the entity. It helped us to restructure some of our debts and almost brought us back to business."

acts.speaker: Ebson Uanguta, NAMCOR interim managing director
acts.speech: Acknowledges that the company stood to lose credibility with creditors and suppliers and says Namcor has had to re-strategise and come up with a recovery plan. "Part of that recovery plan was focused on how to stabilise the company and making sure to introduce efficiency measures to be able to ensure that there have been unnecessary expenses and that these expenses are contained and also strengthen the processes and bring about policies that are addressing some of the challenges that we found. Because in many cases, when companies governance lapses. It requires that some of the policies need to be re-updated or strengthened. So that whatever was done does not happen again."

acts.speaker: Ebson Uanguta, NAMCOR interim managing director
acts.speech: Said income from recent oil discoveries in the Orange Basin, which are anticipated to become operational in the future, should greatly help in solving NAMCOR's cash flow troubles.

title: UN reports grave atrocities in Sudan's El Fasher

acts.speaker: UN human rights office (OHCHR) reports
acts.speech: There are reports reaching the UN human rights office (OHCHR) of summary executions of civilians trying to escape the violence in El Fasher, some of it ethnically motivated. The reports say the killings are mostly committed by the Rapid Support Forces, targeting former combatants who have put down their weapons. Graphic reports said RSF had summarily executed five men who were attempting to bring food supplies into the Darfuri regional capital, which has been blockaded by the militia for 18 months. They were accused of supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).

acts.speaker: Volker Türk, UN human rights chief
acts.speech: “The risk of further large-scale, ethnically motivated violations and atrocities in El Fasher is mounting by the day,” warned UN human rights chief Volker Türk, who said urgent and concrete action is needed to ensure the protection of civilians in El Fasher and safe passage for those trying to leave. ; Mr. Türk enjoined RSF commanders to an obligation under international law to protect civilians and ensure the safe passage of humanitarian assistance.

acts.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
acts.speech: has told journalists that the “terrible escalation” necessitates the international community to exert pressure on countries taking sides in Sudan’s internal conflict by “providing weapons” to one of the warring sides, urging them to agree a ceasefire.

acts.speaker: Denise Brown, UN humanitarian coordinator for Sudan
acts.speech: at a press briefing on Monday said civilians including adults and children fleeing El Fasher often appear “dehydrated, malnourished, some injured and all traumatised.”

acts.speaker: United Nations / Denise Brown, UN humanitarian coordinator for Sudan
acts.speech: According to the UN some 130 aid workers have been killed since the conflict erupted more than two years ago, with reports of volunteers being killed in El Fasher, Ms. Brown said. “These people are the backbone of the humanitarian response in the most difficult areas and they are also protected under international humanitarian law,” she added.

title: I see them as second-class citizens.

acts.speaker: United Nations
acts.speech: The United Nations estimates that more people will live in towns and cities than in rural areas by 2026.

acts.speaker: Refugees International (report)
acts.speech: According to a report by the US-based rights group Refugees International, most of the millions of people fleeing from rural to urban areas in Somalia are not going home, not now and not ever.

acts.speaker: Refugees International (report)
acts.speech: Says "Many long-standing IDPs more closely resemble urban poor and have a different set of needs than new arrivals."

acts.speaker: Fatima Mohamed Iise, 31, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: "We had a very good life as pastoralists. We had about 40 cows. Now we have none so I had no choice but to come to Mogadishu with my children." ; "My nine-year-old daughter and I go out early every morning to look for work. The only jobs we can find are laundry work and tidying up construction sites which pay between $1 and $1.50 a day. This is not enough to pay for basic necessities but it's better than nothing at all." ; "We only have countryside skills and nobody needs these in the city." ; "I use my earnings to buy rice, beans or maize meal. We eat once a day at lunchtime. The rest of the time we drink tea. My children and I go to sleep on empty stomachs."

acts.speaker: Fatima Mohamed Iise, 31, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: On harassment: "Men come to me offering to help me find a job or get some food. Then they say they want something in return. They either want sex or to marry my daughters."

acts.speaker: Hawa (name changed), 70, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: "No sex, no food. The circumstances of my life now are beyond anyone's imagination. It is hard to believe the reason why I no longer receive food aid but that is the truth." ; "The camp manager asked me to engage in some misbehaviour if I wanted food. I asked what he meant and he said he wanted sex. I was shocked and angrily I rejected him. Since then I haven't received a single grain of food." ; says demands for sexual favours are becoming increasingly common in Mogadishu's IDP camps: "Some girls and women agree to have sex with these men. It is so sad."

acts.speaker: Hawa (name changed), 70, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: On harassment at work: "The male shopkeepers and their staff offer women food and extra money in return for sexual favours. The situation is better for IDPs who work in people's houses because it's women who stay at home while men go out to work." ; "The employers who are kindest to us are older women. They sometimes give us extra money."

acts.speaker: S'iido Hassan Moalim, 66, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: "I live here alone. I believe I am the poorest person in this camp. I cannot see, I cannot work and I have received no voucher cards for food aid." ; "The weak have no rights."

acts.speaker: S'iido Hassan Moalim, 66, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: On exploitation in the camp: "The residents of this camp who benefit are those who accept the demands of the men in charge. I cannot do that because I am old and I respect my culture which forbids such activities." ; "Nobody respects young girls and women. The men call on them anytime they want. When their needs are satisfied they give them money or food."

acts.speaker: Iisho Mukhtar Adam, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: "I wash the clothes and clean the houses of people who are better off than me. I earn between $1 and $2 a day. I work long hours in order to manage the life of my family as best I can." ; explains how IDPs who work in people's houses are occasionally beaten by their employers who sometimes accuse them of stealing their property: "At the end of the day, some people say they don't have money to pay us and that we should come back to following day to collect it. Others don't pay us at all. They have no respect for us. Most employers look down on us but some more educated people treat us as humans."

acts.speaker: Iisho Mukhtar Adam, displaced woman in Asal IDP camp
acts.speech: Says there is nobody to call on for help, as the police tend to be busy dealing with Mogadishu's endless security threats and many are corrupt: "Nobody listens to us. The only thing to do is tell the media about our plight and hope that somebody with the power and resources to do so will help us." ; on sexual abuse in the camp: "I have not yet been asked for sexual favours. Most people keep silent about it because they know that if they complain they will be expelled from the camp."

acts.speaker: Rahma Mohamed, displaced woman in Allah-dhowr IDP camp
acts.speech: "Often the people I work for pay me less than what we agreed on. We might agree on $5 but at the end of the day they only pay me $3."

acts.speaker: Rahma Mohamed, displaced woman in Allah-dhowr IDP camp
acts.speech: "Despite being viewed as a refugee by the people of Mogadishu, I want to establish my own small business here to support my family."

acts.speaker: Asmo Abdi Farah Ahmed, 15, displaced girl working as a maid
acts.speech: "The children in neighbourhoods surrounding our camp go to school and play together. Sometimes they make fun of me for not going to school. They say I am just a 'village kid'."

acts.speaker: Sayid Omar, Mogadishu resident
acts.speech: "Although some have lived in the city for years, I hesitate to consider them as full residents. I see them as second-class citizens, even if they settle permanently and integrate into city life. It's true that people in the capital come from different backgrounds but this doesn't automatically grant them equal status or opportunities within the city."

acts.speaker: Mukhtar Abdalla Abdow, 60, displaced man living in Mogadishu
acts.speech: "People here still consider me a displaced person, a refugee, even though I have lived here for 16 years." ; "I consider myself a local resident."

acts.speaker: Juweeriya Mohamed Ibrahim, Mogadishu resident
acts.speech: "I see them as normal people who came here because their lives were threatened by floods, drought and conflict. For me, if they have lived in Mogadishu for more than five years, I consider them to be residents just like me." ; "Others often say they are second-class citizens. I firmly believe they are not."

title: Clinics short-staffed after Pepfar funding cuts

acts.speaker: Ritshidze (South African community-led clinic monitoring organisation), three-month report
acts.speech: A report over three months shows that Pepfar cuts to HIV programmes have led to reduced staff and longer waiting times for ARV medicines; found that in areas with a high number of people with HIV, US funding cuts have led to staff shortages and overburdened clinics, and that disorganised filing systems frequently caused delays and increased waiting times.

acts.speaker: Clinic staff surveyed by Ritshidze
acts.speech: Nearly half the staff surveyed reported capacity in clinics had been reduced, because Pepfar-funded health workers were not working there anymore or were working less; 20% of surveyed staff said that following Pepfar cuts, there were fewer staff to provide testing and not enough test kits were available.

acts.speaker: Clinic managers surveyed by Ritshidze
acts.speech: 85% of managers reported that their clinics faced staffing shortages, though only one in five blamed shortages on Pepfar staff cuts.

acts.speaker: Patients and healthcare users surveyed by Ritshidze
acts.speech: Over 60% reported that there were too few staff and that these shortages have got worse since Pepfar cuts; a fifth of healthcare users said waiting times were longer than usual (72% in Mangaung, 34% in Buffalo City), and about 35% said it had taken longer to collect ARVs since February.

acts.speaker: Ritshidze
acts.speech: Said with less testing, it becomes harder to identify people with HIV who need to start or restart treatment.

acts.speaker: South African health department
acts.speech: About 1.1 million people with HIV are not receiving treatment, according to the health department.

acts.speaker: TAC (Treatment Action Campaign) and Ritshidze
acts.speech: Have recommended people be given a six-month supply of ARVs in all provinces, instead of the current one- or three-month supply.

acts.speaker: Foster Mohale, Health department spokesperson
acts.speech: Had not responded by the time of publication.

title: USAID staff told to shred and burn classified documents

acts.speaker: Erica Y Carr, Acting Executive Secretary, USAID (email)
acts.speech: Sent an email that thanked staff for clearing out classified safes and personnel documents from a Washington DC office and told them to meet in the building's lobby for an all-day disposal event on Tuesday: "Shred as many documents first, and reserve the burn bags for when the shredder becomes available or needs a break" ; the email asked staff not to overfill the burn bags and label them with the words "SECRET" and "USAID (B/IO)" using permanent markers.

acts.speaker: US State Department
acts.speech: Did not immediately return a request for comment.

acts.speaker: Nikki Gamer, spokesperson, American Foreign Service Association (AFSA)
acts.speech: Told the BBC that the union, which represents USAID staff, was aware employees had been asked to shred documents.

acts.speaker: American Foreign Service Association (AFSA)
acts.speech: Said it was "alarmed" by the reports and warned that such documents "may be relevant to ongoing litigation regarding the termination of USAID employees and the cessation of USAID grants" ; noted that federal law dictates that government records must be preserved as they are "essential to transparency, accountability, and the integrity of the legal process" ; warned that "the unlawful destruction of federal records could carry serious legal consequences for anyone directed to act in violation of the law."

acts.speaker: Experts (unnamed, speaking to the BBC)
acts.speech: Said the email sent by Carr did not contain some of the details traditionally found in a records disposal request, raising concerns about procedure.

acts.speaker: Kel McClanahan, executive director of the National Security Counselors
acts.speech: "There is no indication in this email order that any thought is being given to proper retention or even identifying which records can be destroyed and which records cannot" ; filed a complaint with the National Archives and Records Administration, asking them to "take immediate measures" to stop the destruction of records.

acts.speaker: Elon Musk
acts.speech: Referred to the agency as "evil."

acts.speaker: The White House
acts.speech: Has argued that the agency's international programmes were a wasteful use of taxpayer dollars.

acts.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State and acting head of USAID (post on X)
acts.speech: Announced on X that the administration was cancelling "83% of the programmes at USAID" ; "The 5200 contracts that are now cancelled spent tens of billions of dollars in ways that did not serve, (and in some cases even harmed), the core national interests of the United States."

title: Au Coin du feu avec Jérémie Ngendakumana

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: On his main quality and main fault: said the question embarrasses him because it is difficult to judge oneself, and that “I forgive easily, but I forget with difficulty,” adding that others know his qualities and faults better than he does.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said the quality he prefers in others is honesty - “I like an honest person who makes his thinking clearly known” - which is even more important for a leader ; and that the fault he cannot bear is resentment, because “the resentful man is unpredictable” and “hatred, sourness, bitterness and resentment are more deadly than the venom of a cobra.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said the woman he admires most is Wangari Maathai, the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, known as “the one who plants trees,” who created the Green Belt Movement ; and that he also admires the courage of his wife, Mpawenayo Gertrude, for her resilience during his long period in the bush, devoting herself to the education of their children.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Spoke with pride of his daughters' education - one with a Master's in Finance from Shanghai, one with a Master's in Computer Science from Bordeaux, and a jurist admitted as a lawyer by the Supreme Court of New South Wales in Australia.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said the man he admires most is Mwalimu Julius Kambarage Nyerere, who “had a vision for his country” and whose sobriety and pan-Africanism made him a respected and great political figure in Africa and the world.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said his happiest memory was the announcement that he had passed the inter-diocesan examination giving him access to the minor seminary of Kanyosha - “extraordinary news for me, for my parents and for the whole village.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said his saddest memory was the assassination of President Melchior Ndadaye on 21 October 1993: “We were beginning to taste the benefits of democracy and one morning... everything fell apart. We were going to live once again in fear and uncertainty about the next day.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said his greatest misfortune would be never returning to his native country: “I love my motherland dearly and I feel deeply unhappy without it.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Described 1 June 1993 as a historic date for Burundi, when for the first time a figure acceded to the supreme office through the ballot box and a Hutu was elevated to the presidency to the surprise of the former holders of power, with power shifting from Bururi to Muramvya province.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said he was in Bujumbura that day, where reactions were varied: in majority-Tutsi neighbourhoods disappointment was total and young university students demonstrated against what they called “an ethnic census,” while in working-class Hutu neighbourhoods such as Kamenge and Kinama Ndadaye's victory was welcomed with enthusiasm ; added that Ndadaye delivered a historic, unifying and reassuring speech, and yet some never stopped gnashing their teeth.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said the greatest feat in Burundi's history was the resistance to and victory over the slave trader Mohammed Ben Khalfan, known as Rumaliza, when King Mwezi Gisabo mobilised his troops to safeguard his people's dignity, adding that present and future generations should keep in mind that human life and dignity are priceless.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Named 1 July 1962 (independence) and 1 June 1993 (the victory of democracy) as the two unforgettable dates of Burundi's history.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said the most terrible dates for him were 13 October 1961, the assassination of Prince Rwagasore, which “left the people orphaned,” and 21 October 1993, the assassination of President Ndadaye, which plunged the country into a fratricidal war ; said that had they not been killed, Burundi's present trajectory would have been different.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Recounted as his worst war memory, besides the daily loss of comrades, being attacked by bees from a hive while withdrawing after a military operation, and being saved only by smearing his body with crushed cassava leaves.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said his memory retained no positive event from the bush - “Hunger, fatigue, the loss of friends, a permanent state of alert, that is life in the bush” - quoting Napoleon that “poverty, privation and misery are the school of the good soldier.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Corrected the premise that he returned to the country, saying the fighters never left national territory and only returned to Bujumbura ; recounted being reunited with his family on 31 December 2003 after seven years, returning “like heroes,” holding a press conference as FDD spokesman that astonished people who did not expect a bush fighter to speak French, Kirundi and Swahili so easily, and believing at the war's end in a pacified, reconciled Burundi committed to development.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Described his rapid rise within the CNDD-FDD: elected MP for Muramvya in 2005, appointed Head of State Protocol and then Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Kenya, and recalled on 7 February 2007 to head the party.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said he was proudest, as Head of State Protocol and chairman of the celebrations committee, of having established punctuality and respect for timing at official ceremonies, which ended within five minutes of the scheduled time - “That was new.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said he was glad of the good rapport with the presidents of the chambers of parliament, Pie Ntavyohanyuma and Gervais Rufyikiri, and of having initiated permanent dialogue with the leaders of the other political parties in the National Assembly ; and glad to have avoided interfering in the Executive, describing his role as adviser rather than order-giver and addressing the Head of State directly to avoid two-headedness at the summit of the State.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said that if he had to do it again he would avoid no mistake: “I think I did what I could, as best I could, and I am proud of it.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Declined to say what decisions he would take as CNDD-FDD president, noting he was expelled from the party and that wisdom recommends speaking to those concerned directly rather than through the media.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said he took philosophically being blocked in Kampala when he tried to return for the May 2020 elections, calling it fair game in a period of electoral fever, but argued that after the elections there is no longer anything at stake and he should be allowed to return freely to his native country: “I keep hoping.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said that as president of Burundi his three urgent measures would be good governance (putting the right man in the right place, with a cult of excellence), effective implementation of the legal dividing line between technical and political posts, and a merciless fight against corruption and economic malpractice, quoting Shakespeare's “The Merchant of Venice” as a warning against corruption.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Defined democracy as a mode of government guaranteeing freedom of thought and opinion, free political and religious affiliation and participation through elected representatives, insisting it “is not reduced to the election period alone” but is a way of life and a culture, and that citizens must keep watch so the Republic does not become the property of a few individuals, quoting Maurizio Viroli: “Defective as it might be, a democratic republic is preferable to any other political system.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Defined independence as the right of peoples to self-determination and the capacity of leaders to decide freely and sovereignly, adding that a people is economically independent when citizens can meet basic needs without resorting to any assistance, that economic independence guarantees political independence, and quoting the English saying “who feeds you controls you” - concluding “We still have a big step to take before reaching true independence.”

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Gave as his motto “Be the best whatever you are,” an extract from a poem by Douglas Malloch.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Named his native commune of Bukeye and the view from Mount Saga as his favourite place in Burundi, recalling with emotion a childhood song about the country's beauty.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said his favourite song is Burundi's national anthem, which constitutes a political ideology and basic patriotic education ; that he listens attentively to “Yaramenje” by Nimbona alias Kidumu and “Umugabo w'ukuri” by Canjo Amissi, noting that such great men have often been lacking and Burundi has often sunk ; and that as a Catholic he listens with emotion to the “Adoro te devote” of Saint Thomas Aquinas.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said his favourite dish is wheat paste with a piece of well-cooked meat, without many ingredients, and that the journey he would like to make is to Mauritius, to learn the secret that makes it the most prosperous country in Africa.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said he is firmly convinced that man is born with a great potential to do good but also a propensity for harm, like a tree with two branches in which the best-watered branch grows best, quoting the Italian writer Fabrizio Caramagna that life is an invisible vase which overflows with anxiety or serenity according to what one pours in.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said death is an obligatory passage and the common denominator of the human species, quoting Francois de Malherbe on death's harshness, and that it is wise to think of it with serenity without making it an obsession.

acts.speaker: Jeremie Ngendakumana, former president of the CNDD-FDD party (Burundi), in interview
acts.speech: Said that before God he would give thanks for being kept alive in the most difficult moments, ask forgiveness for his failings, and ask Him to help the country find peace, stability and reconciliation.

title: Ethiopia to Introduce Green Court

acts.speaker: Ayele Hegena (PhD), director general for policy, law and standards research development at the Environment, Forest & Climate Change Commission
acts.speech: Said lack of environmental technical expertise of both judges and prosecutors is one of the major difficulties for the effective enforcement of environmental laws in Ethiopia. "This led the courts to be reluctant to engage with environmental matters," Ayele told Fortune, "and prosecute violations that require the use of technical reports and scientific understanding."

acts.speaker: Ayele Hegena (PhD), director general for policy, law and standards research development at the Environment, Forest & Climate Change Commission
acts.speech: Said the current police force does not have the knowledge nor the capacity to be entrusted with these cases; that the judges and all of the legal professionals under this establishment are expected to be vigilant and sensitive toward environmental issues and develop environmental law, compliance and enforcement consistency through the cases that come before the courts; and that as a start the green tribunal will be established at a federal level, with regional states able to form their own if they have the capacity.

acts.speaker: Andualem Mekonnen (PhD), environmentalist and assistant professor at the School of Natural Science, Addis Abeba University
acts.speech: Said that at a glance this might be deemed a profound move to address environmental issues, but it falls into doubt when looking at the capacity of the regulatory institutions; "Designing programmes or approaches just for the sake of being established will not solve the current environmental problems." "I highly doubt the execution of these kinds of programmes," he said. "Instead, the government should work on the grassroots issues from proper studies to proper assessments before jumping into anything."

title: Trump met fin à l'initiative américaine visant à améliorer l'accès à l'électricité en Afrique, rapporte Bloomberg News

acts.speaker: Bloomberg News, citing people familiar with the matter
acts.speech: Reported on Wednesday that a United States initiative aimed at increasing the electricity supply in Africa had been dismantled by the administration of President Donald Trump after more than a decade of work; the report adds, citing anonymous sources, that almost all Power Africa programmes are on the list of programmes to be discontinued and the majority of its staff have been laid off, and that some remaining programmes, notably those aimed at connecting projects with American companies, could be retained under the responsibility of other US agencies.

acts.speaker: US State Department spokesperson (cited by Bloomberg)
acts.speech: "Every programme is under review with the goal of restructuring aid to serve American interests."

acts.speaker: US State Department official (anonymous, to Bloomberg)
acts.speech: "Programmes that serve our nation's interests will continue. By contrast, those that are not aligned with our national interests will not," a department official told Bloomberg in response to questions.

acts.speaker: US State Department
acts.speech: An email sent to the US State Department's office seeking comment did not receive an immediate response.

title: Understanding African solutions to African problems

acts.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Prime Minister of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Used the phrase "African solutions to African problems" seven times during his speech delivered on February 18, and offered the suggestion that existing conflicts and disputes on the continent must be resolved through collective efforts and "must be confined to this continent and quarantined from the contamination of non-African interference."

acts.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Prime Minister of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia
