acts.speech: Saluted "the government's efforts to establish a climate of peace and security allowing our operations to continue in the field, despite certain constraints that should be noted" ; "Whether elsewhere in the world or here in Niger, significant challenges remain to be met" ; "this requires increased mobilisation and strengthened engagement from our bilateral and multilateral partners, as well as from all our traditional or emerging donors" ; "affected populations need our help right now; we will only be able to meet all humanitarian needs if the humanitarian community and international donors invest in supporting and empowering local and national humanitarian action."

title: Bepc session 2025 : Les filles surclassent les garçons

acts.speaker: Kadidiata Diarra Badji, Director of Examinations and Competitions (DECO), Cote d'Ivoire
acts.speech: Announced on Tuesday 17 June 2025 in Abidjan the results of the 2025 session of the Brevet d'etudes du premier cycle (BEPC): in total 312,041 candidates were declared successful, a national pass rate of 51.41%, against 40.18% in 2024, an increase of 11.23 points.

acts.speaker: Kadidiata Diarra Badji, Director of Examinations and Competitions (DECO), Cote d'Ivoire
acts.speech: "The progressive improvement of pass rates is a promising indication of the revival of our education system towards greater performance and competitiveness. At the same time it is a source of satisfaction in view of the massive investments made by the State of Cote d'Ivoire," she said with satisfaction ; according to her, these convincing results of the 2025 BEPC, already perceptible at the CEPE session, are the fruit of the vision of the Minister of National Education, of her quest for a quality school and of the reforms stemming from the General Assembly on National Education and Literacy (EGENA).

acts.speaker: Kadidiata Diarra Badji, Director of Examinations and Competitions (DECO), Cote d'Ivoire
acts.speech: Also welcomed the awareness shown by candidates and the remobilisation of all the actors of the educational community around the values of work, merit and transparency: "I congratulate all those who passed. They can be proud of the work accomplished during the 2024-2025 school year, today crowned by these results. I associate with these congratulations the supervisors and the parents of pupils, true architects of this success," she declared.

acts.speaker: Kadidiata Diarra Badji, Director of Examinations and Competitions (DECO), Cote d'Ivoire
acts.speech: Expressed satisfaction at the smooth running of the examinations: "As for the CEPE, no major incident likely to compromise the credibility of the examinations was reported in the various examination centres."

acts.speaker: Kadidiata Diarra Badji, Director of Examinations and Competitions (DECO), Cote d'Ivoire
acts.speech: "I recall and I insist on the fact that appeals and the issuing of transcripts of marks are entirely free of charge in all the centres," she specified.

title: Somalia, Ethiopia agree to work together to resolve Somaliland port dispute

acts.speaker: Somalia and Ethiopia (joint statement)
acts.speech: Said they would work together to resolve a dispute over Addis Ababa's plan to build a port in the breakaway region of Somaliland; the two countries' leaders said they had agreed to find commercial arrangements to allow landlocked Ethiopia “reliable, secure and sustainable access to and from the sea” ; in a joint statement released late on Wednesday, said they had agreed to start technical negotiations by the end of February next year, and to conclude them within four months, without going into detail.

acts.speaker: Tayyip Erdogan, Turkish President
acts.speech: “This joint declaration focuses on the future, not the past,” Erdogan said at a press conference in Ankara afterwards.

acts.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, President of Somalia
acts.speech: Said he was ready to work with Ethiopia.

acts.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopian Prime Minister
acts.speech: Welcomed Turkish efforts to resolve the dispute.

acts.speaker: Government of Ethiopia
acts.speech: Said in January that it would lease a port in Somalia's breakaway northern region of Somaliland in exchange for recognising the area's independence.

acts.speaker: Mogadishu (Somali government)
acts.speech: Rejected the deal and threatened to expel Ethiopian troops who were stationed in Somalia to fight Islamist insurgents.

title: Centre Roi Salman pour le secours et les actions humanitaires : La Grande mosquée "Roi Fayçal" et le quartier de Sabalibougou dotés de forages artésiens !

acts.speaker: Notables of the Bagadadji neighbourhood and Muslim faithful, including Imam Amadou Kallé
acts.speech: According to them, this borehole comes at just the right time since it will serve to relieve the faithful during prayer hours.

acts.speaker: Dr. Abdullah Al Mouhalim, representative of the King Salman Centre
acts.speech: For Dr. Abdullah Al Mouhalim, this act is purely humanitarian and aims to improve the living conditions of the Malian people; it is also about further strengthening the fraternal ties between the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Mali.

acts.speaker: Dr. Mahamadou Koné, Malian Minister of Religious Affairs, Worship and Customs
acts.speech: Expressed all his gratitude to the Saudi authorities for their commitment and determination on Mali’s behalf in this crucial period; he said King Salman’s efforts reinforce the concrete actions carried out by the President of the Transition, Army General Assimi Goïta, to provide the Malian people with boreholes financed entirely from the national sovereignty fund.

acts.speaker: Abdallah Saleh Saber, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to Mali
acts.speech: Said this borehole construction project is one of many programmes carried out for Mali in various sectors such as health, sanitation and above all education; he specified that these initiatives reflect the depth of the relations between the two friendly and brotherly countries.

acts.speaker: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (official commitment statement)
acts.speech: The Kingdom has been committed for decades “to promoting sustainable development in middle- and low-income countries and to reducing the economic gap that keeps countries under the yoke of poverty, undermines their capacity to meet the needs of vulnerable groups, and prevents their equal access to resources.”

acts.speaker: King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (statement)
acts.speech: “Acting on behalf of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the Centre has helped to relieve the suffering of millions of people in need across the world.”

title: Single window for decent trade opens

acts.speaker: Walinase Msiska, cross-border trader from Chitipa District
acts.speech: Admits she has been running the business without export permits, hence the use of uncharted routes ; "It is very risky, sometimes we lose it all when we are caught by Police who patrol these routes regularly together with MRA [Malawi Revenue Authority]."

acts.speaker: Steve Yohane, President of the Crossborder Traders Association (CBTA)
acts.speech: Confirms that cross-border trading has a myriad of challenges that put off potential traders while pushing many into smuggling, many of them involving processes of obtaining various permits ; "We have been engaging authorities to iron out issues cross border traders face every day but not much is changing."

acts.speaker: Project brief on the National Single Window facility (document)
acts.speech: "Single Window solution is a one-stop platform for information exchange between traders and government agencies involved in international trade, integrating customs, ports, maritime authority and other government agencies through electronic ICT platform." ; "The NSW is a highly convenient tool for private sector stakeholders since all information associated with trade or related transport transactions is submitted and retrieved from a single system. Private sector stakeholders reap the benefits of electronic access: savings in time and resources since physical submission and collection of documents are eliminated." ; further explains that border control agencies are linked to the NSW platform to process transactions but operate in the background, with workflow management of their organizations integrated into the NSW.

acts.speaker: Christina Chatima, Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Trade
acts.speech: Said cross-border traders from all corners of the country will be able to apply and obtain permits online once the national single window is operational.

title: Ciclone Tropical Chido: Governo norte-americano disponibiliza 450 mil dólares para ajudar na recuperação - O País - A verdade como notícia

acts.speaker: Embassy of the United States of America in Mozambique (press release)
acts.speech: According to a press release from the US Embassy in Mozambique, the critical funding will help meet the urgent needs of affected populations in Cabo Delgado province, with a focus on shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); one of the grants will be implemented by the Adventist Development and Relief Agency (ADRA) and the other rapid response actions by CARE International; other USAID humanitarian partners are mobilising existing resources to respond to immediate needs; initial reports indicate that the greatest human and material losses occurred in the south of Cabo Delgado province and surrounding areas; assessments are under way to determine the full impact of the disaster, and the US Government will continue to work closely with the National Institute for Disaster Risk Management and Reduction to coordinate the cyclone response.

acts.speaker: Peter H. Vrooman, United States Ambassador to Mozambique
acts.speech: stressed the importance of rapid action to help those affected by Cyclone Chido: "The United States Government recognises the enormous challenges faced by the affected people and wants to reaffirm our solidarity. Our assistance will provide vital help to the people most impacted by the cyclone, helping to alleviate human suffering and to support recovery efforts," said Ambassador Vrooman, quoted in the same press release.

title: Aid cuts threaten fragile progress in ending maternal deaths, UN agencies warn

acts.speaker: UN report, Trends in maternal mortality (WHO on behalf of the UN Maternal Mortality Estimation Inter-Agency Group)
acts.speech: Shows a 40% global decline in maternal deaths between 2000 and 2023 - largely due to improved access to essential health services; reveals that the pace of improvement has slowed significantly since 2016, and that an estimated 260 000 women died in 2023 as a result of complications from pregnancy or childbirth - roughly equivalent to one maternal death every two minutes ; provides the first global account of the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on maternal survival, with an estimated 40 000 more women dying in 2021 due to pregnancy or childbirth, increasing to 322 000 from 282 000 the previous year ; highlights persistent inequalities between regions and countries, with sub-Saharan Africa still accounting for approximately 70% of the global burden of maternal deaths in 2023, and nearly two-thirds of global maternal deaths now occurring in countries affected by fragility or conflict, where a 15-year-old girl faces a 1 in 51 risk of dying from a maternal cause compared to 1 in 593 in more stable countries.

acts.speaker: United Nations (UN) agencies
acts.speech: Highlight the threat of major backsliding as unprecedented aid cuts take effect around the world; warn that without urgent action pregnant women in multiple countries will face severe repercussions - particularly those in humanitarian settings where maternal deaths are already alarmingly high.

acts.speaker: Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: "While this report shows glimmers of hope, the data also highlights how dangerous pregnancy still is in much of the world today despite the fact that solutions exist to prevent and treat the complications that cause the vast majority of maternal deaths." ; "In addition to ensuring access to quality maternity care, it will be critical to strengthen the underlying health and reproductive rights of women and girls - factors that underpin their prospects of healthy outcomes during pregnancy and beyond."

acts.speaker: Catherine Russell, UNICEF Executive Director
acts.speech: "When a mother dies in pregnancy or childbirth, her baby's life is also at risk. Too often, both are lost to causes we know how to prevent." ; "Global funding cuts to health services are putting more pregnant women at risk, especially in the most fragile settings, by limiting their access to essential care during pregnancy and the support they need when giving birth. The world must urgently invest in midwives, nurses, and community health workers to ensure every mother and baby has a chance to survive and thrive."

acts.speaker: Dr Natalia Kanem, UNFPA's Executive Director
acts.speech: "Access to quality maternal health services is a right, not a privilege, and we all share the urgent responsibility to build well-resourced health systems that safeguard the life of every pregnant woman and newborn." ; "By boosting supply chains, the midwifery workforce, and the disaggregated data needed to pinpoint those most at risk, we can and must end the tragedy of preventable maternal deaths and their enormous toll on families and societies."

title: Editorial: Galamsey: IGP Yohuno’s promise is very refreshing - The Ghanaian Chronicle

acts.speaker: Christian Tetteh Yohuno, COP, Inspector General of Police of Ghana
acts.speech: Declared an all-out war on illegal mining, also known as ‘galamsey’, because it poses a serious threat to national security and the environment ; revealed that armed criminals linked to illegal mining operations have carried out brutal attacks on innocent civilians, including forest guards, without justification: “This lawlessness must not be allowed to continue” ; stressed that urgent action was needed to combat the problem: “We are declaring war on illegal mining, and I expect every regional commander to take decisive action, to bring perpetrators to justice.”

acts.speaker: myjoyonline.com (report)
acts.speech: Reported that the Inspector General of Police has declared an all-out war on illegal mining because it poses a serious threat to national security and the environment.

acts.speaker: Emmanuel Armah Kofi Buah, Minister for Lands and Natural Resources of Ghana
acts.speech: Said that last year alone, excavators worth GHS6.2billion were imported into the country, making it the third largest import into the country within the period being referenced.

title: L'armée soudanaise rejette l'appel des Émirats à un cessez-le-feu durant le Ramadan - Mali 24

acts.speaker: United Arab Emirates official (anonymous)
acts.speech: Declared: "As the holy month of Ramadan approaches, a time conducive to mercy and compassion, the United Arab Emirates calls on all parties to honour this sacred period with a humanitarian ceasefire."

acts.speaker: Senior Sudanese military source (anonymous), speaking to Reuters
acts.speech: Stated: "We do not accept a ceasefire for Ramadan as long as the siege is not lifted in all besieged towns and areas."

acts.speaker: Sudanese army
acts.speech: Considers the UAE a hostile actor in the conflict, accusing it of supplying weapons to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary militia.

acts.speaker: UN experts and US lawmakers
acts.speech: Deemed these accusations credible.

acts.speaker: United Arab Emirates
acts.speech: Denied any military support to the RSF.

acts.speaker: United Arab Emirates (government)
acts.speech: Announced their intention to organise a summit on Friday in Addis Ababa, in collaboration with the African Union, to attract funding for humanitarian aid to Sudan; the UAE said it would announce $200 million in funding.

acts.speaker: Government of Sudan
acts.speech: Rejected the initiative, describing it as a "crime and an aggression against an African nation seeking to protect its land and its sovereignty."

acts.speaker: Malik Agar, deputy to Abdel Fattah al-Burhan on Sudan's Sovereign Council
acts.speech: Stressed the UAE's alleged complicity in the conflict.

acts.speaker: Emirati representative (anonymous)
acts.speech: Declared in response: "Unfortunately, the Sudanese army has sought to distort the role of the United Arab Emirates by falsifying the facts [...]. These allegations will not divert the United Arab Emirates from its main objective, which is to promote stability."

title: L'Afrique face au carrefour financier : Entre coupes d'aide, dette accrue et quête d'autonomie

acts.speaker: Barclays (new report by the British bank)
acts.speech: According to a new report by Barclays, Senegal's public debt now reaches 119% of its GDP, nearly double the regional average in sub-Saharan Africa, significantly higher than the 99.7% cited in a recent national audit.

acts.speaker: Recent Senegalese national audit (report)
acts.speech: Cited a public debt figure of 99.7% of GDP.

acts.speaker: Bassirou Diomaye Faye, President of Senegal
acts.speech: Ordered a general audit of the hidden debts of the previous administration.

title: USAID, Tanzania join forces in fight against rabies - Daily News

acts.speaker: Dr Stanford Ndibalema, Assistant Director of Veterinary Services at the Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries (Tanzania)
acts.speech: Emphasized the importance of collaboration in combating rabies: “The partnership between USAID and the Tanzanian government is crucial in our fight against rabies. By working together, we can ensure that communities are not only educated about the risks but also empowered to take proactive steps in protecting themselves and their pets.” ; Underscored the critical need for vaccination and community awareness campaigns, highlighting that “every vaccinated dog is a step toward a rabies-free community.”

acts.speaker: Revina, a mother of three from Mwanza
acts.speech: Recounted her experience: “Before the campaign, I had no idea how dangerous rabies could be. Once we learned about the importance of vaccinating our dogs, we took immediate action. Now, I feel much safer allowing my children to play outside.”

title: Money trials: Teddy Bear Clinic gets creative to raise cash amid NGO funding crisis | News24

acts.speaker: Shaheda Omar, clinical director of The Teddy Bear Clinic
acts.speech: "I think we in the NGO sector have been struggling for a long time. Unfortunately, it's not a new phenomenon, but it has become bleak. Look at the financial landscape, not only of South Africa but globally. We can see how the USAID funding has impacted so many service providers globally and, even in South Africa, where services have been shut down."

acts.speaker: Shaheda Omar, clinical director of The Teddy Bear Clinic
acts.speech: Lamented the dwindling resources and its impact on collaboration among civil society organisations, noting that the competition brewing among NGOs often resulted in secrecy and a lack of unity ; "Instead of us standing united, holding hands, and trying to work together, that's not what we are finding on the ground or in practice."

acts.speaker: Shaheda Omar, clinical director of The Teddy Bear Clinic
acts.speech: Shared the heart-wrenching story of a young girl impregnated twice by a teacher: "She ingested rat poison to terminate the first pregnancy and contracted HIV following the second. These are victims who are so helpless in their fight against the scourge inflicted on them."

acts.speaker: Shaheda Omar, clinical director of The Teddy Bear Clinic
acts.speech: Stressed how limited funding affects the clinic's operations and the well-being of its staff: "We are overloaded. Caseloads are high, and the work comes at a price. It affects the human resources of the foundation, increasing stress levels and volumes, and there is always the risk of compassion fatigue and burnout."

acts.speaker: Shaheda Omar, clinical director of The Teddy Bear Clinic
acts.speech: "Every rand makes a difference in the journey to healing a child. Our mission is about promoting healing, support, and providing these children with a voice."

acts.speaker: News24 (January report)
acts.speech: Reported that the Gauteng Care Crisis Committee (GCCC) approached the courts after the department failed to comply with court orders related to the funding of NPOs.

acts.speaker: Gauteng High Court (May 2024 order)
acts.speech: Ordered the Gauteng Department of Social Development to pay NPOs, to finalise funding applications for NPOs, issue service-level agreements, and pay NPOs within seven days of signing the agreements.

acts.speaker: Lisa Vetten, GCCC chairperson
acts.speech: Said there was a need for "accountability and transparency" regarding the funding decisions made by the department ; "The impact of funding delays on NGOs and their communities is severe, and it is urgent to resolve these issues to uphold socio-economic rights." ; said some organisations faced closure "with reports of suicides due to lack of services" ; "There are firm deadlines to settle these outstanding issues as the end of the financial year approaches."

title: Development partners mark Int Day of Education

acts.speaker: Osama Makkawi, UNICEF Representative to Ghana
acts.speech: Said painting classrooms alongside the students was his first time of doing such an activity.

acts.speaker: Osama Makkawi, UNICEF Representative to Ghana
acts.speech: In an interview, stated that TVET was the best way to reach the most vulnerable adolescents and young people to impart skills, and emphasised the need to modernise TVET in the 21st century to fit the purpose and the needs of the market and the people.

acts.speaker: Christin Lucille McConnell, Chair, Development Partners in Education Group (speech read on her behalf by Christopher Nkrumah, education specialist of UNICEF Ghana)
acts.speech: Said at least in 2024, 242 million students worldwide from pre-primary to upper secondary experienced school disruptions due to climate events, and that in Africa an additional 20 million children were at risk of dropping out of school due to climate-related challenges, highlighting the urgent need to address the intersection of education and climate resilience; said for Ghana approximately 1.2 million children, predominantly in rural areas, were still out of school and vulnerable to risks such as child labour, early marriage and violence, and that climate-induced disruptions in 2023, including flooding that affected over 30,000 children and heatwave that rendered classrooms uncomfortable, further underscored the need for action ; "We are particularly optimistic about Ghana's potential to address these challenges through home-grown solutions. TVET institutions stand out as strategic partners in championing innovative approaches to solving problems in schools, workplaces and communities. By leveraging their expertise, we can design and implement climate-smart and disaster-resilient learning facilities, while addressing broader infrastructural and environmental challenges" ; urged all stakeholders including the government, development partners, private sector and community members to take concrete actions to strengthen partnerships between TVET and non-TVET institutions to address infrastructural and environmental challenges effectively.

acts.speaker: Dr Eric Kofi Adzroe, Director of Infrastructural Planning and Development at the Ghana TVET Service
acts.speech: Called on parents to encourage their children to take the path of TVET for the nation to develop.

acts.speaker: Awo Yaa Otwiwa, queen mother of Agyemanti
acts.speech: Said education held the key to improving the lives of their children such that going forward, it would be difficult for one to get a good employment opportunity if one was not educated.

acts.speaker: Elizabeth Afriyie, Akuapem South Municipal Director of Education
acts.speech: Called on all to work together to ensure that every child had access to quality education and the opportunity to reach their full learning potential.

title: WHO recommends twice-a-year HIV prevention shot

acts.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: Is now recommending that countries include an HIV drug newly approved for prevention, lenacapavir, as a tool in their efforts to fight HIV infections – especially for groups most at risk and in areas where the burden of HIV remains high; the global recommendation was issued Monday at the International AIDS Conference in Kigali, Rwanda. According to WHO, about 40 million people globally were living with HIV at the end of 2023.

acts.speaker: Dr. Meg Doherty, director of WHO's Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections Programmes
acts.speech: “These new recommendations are designed for real-world use. WHO is working closely with countries and partners to support the implementation” ; “The first recommendation is that a long-acting injectable, lenacapavir, should be offered as an additional prevention choice for people at risk for HIV and as part of combination prevention. With that, we call it a strong recommendation with moderate to high certainty of the evidence” ; “LEN is a six-monthly injectable option, and it may be particularly attractive for people who prefer fewer clinic visits or have challenges with daily oral PrEP. … It could improve adherence and reach more people who need HIV prevention and can be used in pregnant and breastfeeding women” ; “WHO is providing technical assistance to countries interested in adopting LEN and simplified testing strategies, in coordination with global partners like the Global Fund, UNAIDS and several other partners and donors” ; “We call on governments, funders, implementers and civil society to work together for implementing and integrating LEN into the HIV programs. And we believe time to act is now.”

acts.speaker: United Nations
acts.speech: International assistance accounts for 80% of prevention programs in low- and middle-income countries, according to the United Nations.

acts.speaker: Gilead Sciences
acts.speech: Announced Wednesday that it has reached an agreement with the nonprofit Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria to supply lenacapavir for HIV prevention at no profit to the company; the company added that the cost of lenacapavir under this agreement remains confidential, and that the US annual list price of $28,218 for prevention is similar to the price of other prevention medicine options.

acts.speaker: Daniel O'Day, Gilead Chairman and CEO
acts.speech: “We are providing the medicine at no profit to Gilead, and in enough supply to reach up to two million people in low- and lower-middle-income countries ahead of generic lenacapavir becoming available.”

acts.speaker: Peter Sands, executive director of the Global Fund
acts.speech: Said lenacapavir can “fundamentally change the trajectory of the HIV epidemic,” but only if it reaches the people who need it most ; “Our ambition is to reach 2 million people with long-acting PrEP. But we can only do that if the world steps up with the resources required” ; “This is a pivotal moment — not just for the fight against HIV, but for the fundamental principle that lifesaving innovations must reach those who need them most — whoever they are, and wherever they live.”

acts.speaker: United Nations report released Thursday
acts.speech: Warned that millions more people could die from HIV-related causes by 2029 if funding for HIV programs permanently disappears; among the 60 low- and middle-income countries included in the report, 25 have indicated increasing their domestic budgets for HIV response efforts next year, but the report noted that may not be sufficient to replace the scale of international funding that these countries have been heavily reliant on.

acts.speaker: Mary Mahy, director of UNAIDS's Data for Impact department
acts.speech: “We know that PEPFAR had committed $4.3 billion to over 50 countries in 2025, and that support was suddenly ended in January of 2025” ; “If none of the PEPFAR funding is replaced, we'd expect something like 4 million additional deaths between 2025 and 2029, and another 6 million additional new infections” ; “We also know that drug resistance would likely occur with some of those people going off treatment.” According to Mahy, some countries already have seen effects of the rollback of funding for HIV programs.

acts.speaker: UNAIDS data
acts.speech: In Nigeria, facilities reported about 40,000 people who received PrEP at least once during the later part of last year, a number that dropped to fewer than 7,000 in April; in Kenya, about 3,000 women already received medications and nearly 900 initiated medications in October 2024, but those numbers fell to only about 300 already receiving and 100 starting medications in April.

acts.speaker: Winnie Byanyima, UNAIDS Executive Director
acts.speech: “This is not just a funding gap — it's a ticking time bomb. … We have seen services vanish overnight. Health workers have been sent home. And people — especially children and key populations — are being pushed out of care” ; “There is still time to transform this crisis into an opportunity” ; “Countries are stepping up with domestic funding. Communities are showing what works. We now need global solidarity to match their courage and resilience.”

title: Adopt flexible trade approach with US, AfDB boss urges Africa

acts.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
acts.speech: Warned that the higher US tariffs could trigger significant economic disruptions across Africa, affecting numerous nations and accelerating a strategic shift in global partnerships; in an exclusive interview with CNN's Christiane Amanpour revealed that 47 of Africa's 54 countries will be impacted directly by the new U.S. trade policies, with potential declines in export revenues and foreign exchange reserves ; "When those currencies weaken, two things will happen: first, you will find that most of these countries are import-dependent. So, you're going to find that high inflation becomes a problem" ; "And secondly, you find that the cost of actually servicing a lot of their debt, which is foreign currency debt, but in local currencies, is going to get worse."

acts.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
acts.speech: Emphasized that Africa cannot afford a trade confrontation with the United States, noting that the continent accounts for only 1.2 per cent (approximately $34 billion) of America's global trade, with a trade surplus of just $7.2 billion; proposed a pragmatic three-point strategy for the continent: engage the U.S. through flexible and constructive trade negotiations, diversify export markets to reduce dependency on any single partner, and accelerate the African Continental Free Trade Area implementation to unlock the potential $3.4 trillion market; stressed the need to expand Africa's domestic market and boost domestic savings to develop consumption as a bigger share of its GDP, and said the continent must take advantage of increasing external interest in its natural resources, such as cobalt and lithium, to negotiate a better trade and investment deal.

acts.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
acts.speech: Dismissed any notion of binary alignment between the U.S. and China: "U.S is a key ally of Africa—and so is China," he stated. "Africa is building bridges, not isolating itself." ; stressed that Africa seeks balanced, transparent, and mutually beneficial partnerships with all major global players, including the U.S., China, the European Union, and the Gulf states: "I think at the end of the day, we want to make sure that whatever deals that are being done with Africa are transparent, fair, equitable, and led by Africa and in Africa's interests."

acts.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
acts.speech: Firmly rejected the long-standing paradigm of foreign aid dependency: "The era of aid as we've known it is completely gone," he declared, calling instead for bold investments in domestic resource mobilization, infrastructure, and value-added industrialization; said aid must be turned into concessional financing to allow multilateral financial institutions like the African Development Bank to do more for the continent by mobilizing more private capital to develop and derisk projects.

acts.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
acts.speech: Pointed to a resilient and transformative growth narrative: ten of the world's twenty fastest-growing economies are in Africa; highlighted flagship initiatives under the Bank's "High 5" agenda that have impacted more than 565 million people through investments in power, food security, industrialization, regional integration, and initiatives to improve the quality of life of the people of Africa.

acts.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
acts.speech: Cited the great potential of Mission 300, a joint initiative by the World Bank and the African Development Bank to connect 300 million people in Africa to electricity by 2030: "Because without electricity, what can you do? You can't industrialize, you can't add value, you can't be competitive in the dark," he said; highlighted the achievements of the Africa Investment Forum, launched in 2018 by the Bank and eight other partners, saying it has since mobilized more than $225 billion in investment interest to the continent.

acts.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank Group
acts.speech: Believes that despite its challenges, Africa is the largest greenfield investment destination in the world, and it remains "the investor's dream" ; "We got hydropower. We have a massive youth population that can become the labor force of the world. Sixty-five percent of the arable land left in the world to feed almost 9.5 billion people by 2050 is in Africa, so what Africa does with it will determine the future of food in the world," he added.

acts.speaker: Report distributed by the APO Group on behalf of the African Development Bank Group (AfDB)
acts.speech: According to the report, Adesina believes that despite its challenges, Africa is the largest greenfield investment destination in the world, and it remains "the investor's dream."

title: "Confiscation" de terres: le président sud-africain rejette les accusations de Trump

acts.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
acts.speech: Rejected on Monday the accusations of his American counterpart Donald Trump according to which South Africa is "confiscating" land following the promulgation of an expropriation law. "The South African government has not confiscated any land," Mr Ramaphosa stated in a communiqué ; "The recently adopted expropriation law is not an instrument of confiscation. It is a legal procedure that guarantees access to land in a just and equitable manner, in accordance with the Constitution" ; "We look forward to discussing our land reform policy and other issues with the Trump administration," he added, hoping that following these exchanges the two countries would have a "better common understanding."

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States (Truth Social post)
acts.speech: "South Africa is confiscating land and treating certain classes of people VERY BADLY," Donald Trump wrote on his Truth Social network. "I will cut all future funding to South Africa until a full investigation of this situation has been completed!"

acts.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa
acts.speech: Regarding the threat to suspend American aid, specified that apart from aid coming from the American Pepfar programme to fight HIV/AIDS, "there is no other significant funding from the United States to South Africa" ; "The United States remains a strategic political and trade partner for South Africa," he nevertheless stressed.

acts.speaker: Pretoria (South African government)
acts.speech: Maintains that the text does not allow the authorities to carry out expropriations arbitrarily, and that they must first attempt to reach an agreement with the owner.

acts.speaker: Certain critics of the law
acts.speech: Say they fear a situation similar to what neighbouring Zimbabwe experienced after its independence, when in the early 2000s some 4,000 of the then 4,500 large white landowners were forcibly expelled from their land in favour of black farmers on the orders of Robert Mugabe's government.

title: UN calls for protection of aid workers, civilians in Somalia

acts.speaker: George Conway, UN Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator for Somalia
acts.speech: called on all parties to protect civilians and humanitarian workers in the country's conflict areas; said the country has recorded 124 incidents affecting humanitarian access in 2024, with 12 aid workers injured and 13 incidents of physical assault, harassment, and intimidation.

acts.speaker: George Conway, UN Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator for Somalia
acts.speech: said in a statement issued in Mogadishu to mark World Humanitarian Day: "I pay particular tribute to Somali aid workers who, despite immense challenges, have demonstrated their commitment to serve those in most need of assistance and protection." ; said the theme of this year's WHD, #ActForHumanity, urges the world to do a better job of protecting civilians and humanitarian workers, especially in conflict zones.

acts.speaker: United Nations
acts.speech: According to the UN, Somalia is experiencing one of the world's most serious humanitarian crises, with millions of people exposed to incredible suffering due to recurring and intensifying climate shocks, protracted conflicts, disease outbreaks, and economic turmoils.

acts.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
acts.speech: said these conditions have led to widespread food shortages and water scarcity, displacement, and proliferation of diseases, and that the need for lifesaving humanitarian assistance and resilience building remains high, despite the number of people in need of assistance having decreased to 6.9 million from 8.3 million in 2023 ; said that aid worker security is a major concern because humanitarian personnel are frequently subjected to violence, both directly and indirectly.

title: One-year-olds among those raped during Sudan civil war, UN says

acts.speaker: Unicef, the UN children’s agency (report)
acts.speech: Says armed men are raping and sexually assaulting children as young as one during Sudan’s civil war; says that, although 221 rape cases against children have been officially reported since the start of 2024, the true number is likely to be much higher; reports that a third of the victims were boys, who typically face “unique challenges” in reporting such crimes and seeking the help they need, and that 16 of the victims were under the age of five years, including four infants; does not say who is responsible.

acts.speaker: Other UN investigations
acts.speech: Have blamed the majority of rapes on the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), saying RSF fighters had a pattern of using sexual violence to terrorise civilians and suppress opposition to their advances.

acts.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
acts.speech: Has denied any wrongdoing.

acts.speaker: Mohamed Chande Othman, chair of the UN’s fact-finding mission
acts.speech: “The sheer scale of sexual violence we have documented in Sudan is staggering.”

acts.speaker: International human rights groups (evidence presented)
acts.speech: According to evidence presented, victims in the RSF’s stronghold of Darfur were often targeted because they were black African rather than Arab, apparently with the aim of driving them out of Sudan.

acts.speaker: Omnia (not her real name), adult female survivor held by armed men
acts.speech: “After nine at night, someone opens the door, carrying a whip, selects one of the girls, and takes her to another room. I could hear the little girl crying and screaming. They were raping her” ; “Every time they raped her, this girl would come back covered in blood. She is still just a young child. They only release these girls at dawn, and they return almost unconscious. Each of them cries and speaks incoherently. During the 19 days I spent there, I reached a point where I wanted to end my life.”

acts.speaker: The UN
acts.speech: Says three out of four school-age girls are out of school.

acts.speaker: Sudanese coordinating committee that monitors the Emergency Response Rooms
acts.speech: Said the activists relied quite heavily on US aid, and most have been forced to shut down.

acts.speaker: UN organization dedicated to protecting women’s rights
acts.speech: Says local organisations led by women are vital in delivering support to survivors of sexual violence, but they receive less than 2% of the total funding of the UN’s Sudan Humanitarian Fund.

acts.speaker: Sulaima Elkhalifa, Sudanese human rights defender who runs a government unit on combatting violence against women
acts.speech: Said the local group known as “She Leads” was not a big expense, measured in the tens of thousands of dollars, but enabled case workers to reach around 35 survivors a month; told the BBC that those who have been raped by armed men “don’t have the luxury of being depressed”, adding that the demands of war – finding food, needing to flee – leave no space to deal with trauma.

title: Embaixador de Cabo Verde nos EUA confirma existência de cabo-verdianos que já receberam ordem de deportação

acts.speaker: Jose Luis Livramento de Brito, Ambassador of Cabo Verde to the United States
acts.speech: Clarified this fact when contacted by Inforpress about a list circulating on social media claiming that 314 Cape Verdeans are to be sent to the country in the coming days. According to the diplomat, there is no immediate deportation list; however, many Cape Verdeans already have a judge's order and have only not been deported because they have not yet been detained by the American police. As he explained, the number has been accumulating over the years and what can be confirmed is that they will only be deported if they are caught committing some crime.

acts.speaker: Jose Filomeno Monteiro, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Cabo Verde
acts.speech: Said on Friday the 24th that the Government is working on a contingency plan to support the Cape Verdean community in the United States with regard to a possible deportation of illegal immigrants. As he stated, a large proportion of Cape Verdean citizens residing in the USA have legalised status, stressing that the Government views the choices made by the United States with "naturalness", respecting the country's sovereignty.

acts.speaker: Ulisses Correia e Silva, Prime Minister of Cabo Verde
acts.speech: Acknowledged in an interview with RCV that the measures announced by the new administration regarding illegal deportation raise some concern on the part of the authorities, but assured that the country is prepared to receive the possible repatriates.

acts.speaker: United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement
acts.speech: According to the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement service, on Thursday the 23rd a total of 538 foreigners were arrested and 373 were placed in detention in the first actions following Trump's decree.

acts.speaker: United States Department of Homeland Security (data)
acts.speech: According to data from the United States Department of Homeland Security, the goal of one million deportations a year set by the Republican is considered double the maximum number of deportations carried out in a single year in recent decades.

title: Ethiopie: Le Tigré s’enfonce dans une crise humanitaire grave

acts.speaker: United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR)
acts.speech: Is extremely concerned about the fate of thousands of Eritreans currently trapped between the two camps, as fighting intensifies in Tigray.

acts.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: Estimates that 3.8 million people in the region need emergency health assistance.

acts.speaker: Babar Balloch, spokesperson of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Geneva
acts.speech: Said around 24,000 Eritrean refugees, grouped in the camps of Mai Aini and Adi Harush near Mai Tsebri in Tigray, are currently victims of intimidation and harassment by unidentified armed groups.

acts.speaker: Information coming from Mai Aini (unattributed reports)
acts.speech: According to information from Mai Aini, at least one refugee is reported to have been killed by armed elements operating inside the camp, a death that comes in addition to the murder of another refugee on 14 July.

acts.speaker: UNHCR (statement)
acts.speech: “Implores all parties involved in the conflict to fulfil their obligations under international law, in particular by respecting the civilian character of refugee camps, the rights of refugees and of all civilians to be protected from hostilities.”

acts.speaker: David Beasley, head of the World Food Programme (WFP)
acts.speech: Issued a cry of alarm so that the 170 trucks loaded with food and other essential items currently blocked can leave immediately, because by 30 July Tigray will have no more food.

acts.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
acts.speech: Acknowledges having extremely limited means in the Tigray region, so that hundreds of thousands of people, including victims of the fighting, pregnant women and survivors of sexual violence, have no access to basic care and essential medicines.

acts.speaker: Humanitarian agencies
acts.speech: Are deeply concerned by the growing risk of severe acute malnutrition in Tigray.

acts.speaker: Ethiopian agency in charge of refugees (ARRA)
acts.speech: According to ARRA, 92,000 Eritrean refugees lived in this region before the war, including 19,200 in Hitsats and Shimelba.

title: Self Help Africa banks on carbon finance project to improve social relations, conserve environment

acts.speaker: Self Help Africa
acts.speech: Says that the Programme of Activities (PoA) aims to support local organisations and companies to participate in the Carbon Market which will help tackle financial challenges, reduce carbon emissions, conserve the environment, and promote health and economic development towards Malawians.

acts.speaker: Charles Matewere, Self Help Africa Project Manager
acts.speech: Said engaging stakeholders meaningfully is important in enhancing project design and outcomes. Matewere explained that the consultation aims to inform stakeholders about the project, discuss its potential positive and negative impacts, and establish a continuous engagement process for stakeholders to provide input and raise concerns throughout the project's lifecycle. He noted that the Programme of Activities allows for the registration of multiple similar carbon projects as a single programme, reducing transaction costs and increasing management efficiency ; "We are establishing a Programme of Activities and need to consult various stakeholders to gather their views, which will be essential for our registration process. We want to hear the thoughts and expectations of those involved in this initiative."

acts.speaker: Charles Matewere, Self Help Africa Project Manager
acts.speech: Added that participating in the carbon market presents huge financial opportunities. He mentioned the need to support people and projects aimed at mitigating carbon emissions, noting that current participation levels are low ; "Self Help Africa is committed to opening doors for those lacking financial and technical capacity."

acts.speaker: Benson Chidaomba, Lilongwe City Council's Environment Health Officer
acts.speech: Welcomed the Programme of Activities citing the council's responsibility to address environmental and health issues in the community ; "It is crucial to consider projects like this, especially since health concerns are often overlooked. Cooking activities produce harmful emissions, such as carbon dioxide from the smoke, which can lead to health issues like tuberculosis. The Lilongwe City Council will play a role in disseminating information to improve community health during the project's implementation."

title: Mozambique protest leader vows to return home

acts.speaker: Venancio Mondlane, Mozambique opposition leader
acts.speech: Announced on Sunday that he would return ahead of the new president’s inauguration, saying in a Facebook live address he would arrive at Maputo’s Mavalane airport on Thursday; called for demonstrations against the results of the 9 October election, which he says were rigged in favour of the ruling Frelimo party ; “If they are killing my brothers, they are murdering my brothers, then I will be there. If it’s for me, if it’s because of Venancio, then Venancio will be today at Mavalane International Airport.” ; insists the election was stolen from him and that another count said he was the winner.

acts.speaker: Venancio Mondlane, Mozambique opposition leader
acts.speech: Appeared to shrug off criminal and civil charges laid against him: “You can do whatever you want,” he said, apparently addressing the authorities. He added: “If you want to murder, murder. If you want to arrest, arrest too. I will be there.” ; has previously claimed there had been attempts to assassinate him.

acts.speaker: Local rights group (tally)
acts.speech: The violence has left around 300 people dead, according to a tally by a local rights group, with authorities also reporting looting and vandalism.

acts.speaker: Final official results of the poll
acts.speech: Said Mondlane took 24% of the presidential vote compared to 65% for the Frelimo candidate, Daniel Chapo.

acts.speaker: International observer missions
acts.speech: Several international observer missions have also said there were irregularities.

acts.speaker: Filipe Nyusi, President of Mozambique
acts.speech: Has called for dialogue among the parties to resolve the dispute.

acts.speaker: Daniel Chapo, Frelimo president-elect
acts.speech: On 27 December last year called for “non-violence” and “unity”, saying several police officers had died during the clashes.

acts.speaker: Samia Hassan, President of Tanzania (chairing the SADC security troika)
acts.speech: Said the regional grouping SADC was concerned that the situation “may jeopardise peace and security for the country concerned and the region as a whole” ; “For the last couple of weeks, we have witnessed the spread of violent protests that have caused massive harm to human life, affected economic activities and disrupted cross-border trade.”

acts.speaker: Chansa Kapaya, UNHCR regional director for southern Africa
acts.speech: “Refugees and civilians are facing immense risks, losing their livelihoods and relying on humanitarian assistance” ; “While we are grateful for the generosity of Malawi and Eswatini, immediate support is crucial to tackle the worsening crisis and prevent further suffering.”

title: Nach 70 Jahren Geschichte

acts.speaker: David Muwonge, spokesperson for Elso Holdings
acts.speech: Said that Elso Holdings currently manufactures 27 cleaning products at one production facility, distributes them through a single sales branch and employs thirty staff, of whom 21 are women and nine men.

acts.speaker: David Muwonge, spokesperson for Elso Holdings
acts.speech: Said that employees are currently paid only part of their salary immediately, with the rest within a period of up to two weeks; he explained this unfortunate circumstance as being due to restrictions in the payout procedures.

acts.speaker: Employees of Elso Holdings (complaints)
acts.speech: Complained of a lack of safety equipment and frequent work stoppages due to a lack of input materials.

acts.speaker: An employee who wishes to remain anonymous
acts.speech: Reported that numerous workers were dismissed in November, before the factory moved from Prosperita to Lafrenz in Windhoek: “The problems began to become serious this year, but we have been struggling for two to three years already, for example in the area of overalls.”

acts.speaker: David Muwonge, spokesperson for Elso Holdings
acts.speech: Denies that there are unsafe working conditions; on the contrary, he insists that overalls as well as boots and aprons are always provided in all necessary situations: “The most dangerous product is not produced regularly, but only at the request of a particular customer. During the period of procuring the [raw materials necessary for the product] and manufacturing this product, it is ensured that both masks and gloves are worn. When hazardous chemicals are purchased, they are generally used directly and not stored, so that at no point are hazardous chemicals permanently stored.” ; However, he admitted that in May of this year an employee was injured on duty, although according to him this was the only workplace accident this year.

title: Nigerian States Spend Peanuts On Flood, Erosion Control Amid Flood Warnings For 30 States, But Splurge On SUVs, Govt Houses

acts.speaker: Federal Accounts Allocation Committee (data)
acts.speech: A SaharaReporters reporter's review of the Federal Accounts Allocation Committee data has shown that state and local governments received N96 billion as ecology funds between December 2023 and November 2024.

acts.speaker: Nigerian Government
acts.speech: Recently, the Nigerian Government warned of flooding in 30 states of the country and the FCT.

acts.speaker: Office of the Accountant General of the Federation (published data)
acts.speech: According to data published by the Office of the Accountant General of the Federation, in November 2024, states received N4.607 billion, while local governments across the country received N3.839 billion as an ecology fund.

acts.speaker: United Nations Children's Education Fund (UNICEF) (statement on its website)
acts.speech: In 2022, the United Nations Children's Education Fund noted that 2.5 million people in Nigeria needed humanitarian assistance due to flooding. Sixty per cent of these were children. ; "The floods, which have affected 34 out of the 36 states in the country, have displaced 1.3 million people. Over 600 people have lost their lives and over 200,000 houses have either been partially or fully damaged," a statement on UNICEF's website read.

acts.speaker: Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP)
acts.speech: In 2022, the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) urged then President Muhammadu Buhari to "direct the Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice Mr Abubakar Malami, SAN, and appropriate anti-corruption agencies to promptly and thoroughly investigate the spending of Ecological Fund by governments at all levels - federal, state and local governments from 2001 to 2022."

title: Extremist-Linked Somali PM Hamza Barre Visits China Amid Expanding CCP Influence

acts.speaker: Office of Somali Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre (statement on X)
acts.speech: confirmed Hamza's Saturday meeting with Wang, where the two discussed "strengthening the deep-rooted relations and cooperation" between Somalia and China ; claimed Hamza thanked Beijing for its "multifaceted support" in politics, security, economic development, and humanitarian assistance.

acts.speaker: Office of Somali Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre
acts.speech: said the Expo will focus on trade, investment, technology, and energy - areas where Somalia seeks Chinese capital.

acts.speaker: Hamza Abdi Barre, Somali Prime Minister
acts.speech: once called the Jewish, "Children of pigs and monkeys."

acts.speaker: Wang Yu, Chinese Ambassador to Somalia
acts.speech: pledged that China would continue backing the Somali government, describing relations as "longstanding and cooperative."

acts.speaker: Diplomatic sources in Mogadishu (anonymous)
acts.speech: told our reporter that Wang's visit was about more than pleasantries. He not only extended the Expo invitation but also pressed Mogadishu on Beijing's growing concerns over "Somaliland's ties with Taiwan" - a partnership China views as a direct threat to its influence in the Horn of Africa.

acts.speaker: China
acts.speech: has denounced the partnership [between Somaliland and Taiwan] as a violation of its sovereignty and vowed to counter it.

acts.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President
acts.speech: recent remarks suggesting Washington was "looking into the Somaliland proposal" for recognition.

acts.speaker: Analysts
acts.speech: warn that Hodan's political ties and access to sensitive Somali security and diplomatic files could give Beijing unparalleled insight into Western intelligence cooperation in the Horn of Africa - a strategic prize for China's regional ambitions.

title: Bien-être des populations de Banikoara: Relais et agents de santé communautaires qualifiés, maîtres du terrain

acts.speaker: Noélie Guézo, community health officer at UNICEF
acts.speech: “The role of the community relays and the ASCQs is to help promote all the themes relating to the field of children and community well-being.”

acts.speaker: Noélie Guézo, community health officer at UNICEF
acts.speech: “After a year and a half of implementation of the community health policy, we have observed that attendance at health centres by communities has increased, certain pathologies have regressed and the question of hygiene is taken seriously.”

acts.speaker: Noélie Guézo, community health officer at UNICEF
acts.speech: “UNICEF positioned itself very early to support the government. From six communes at the start (Malanville, Banikoara, Bembèrèkè, Sinendé, Nikki and Kalalé), UNICEF today supports the government throughout Borgou and Alibori and in four communes of Zou, with the help of other partners.”

acts.speaker: Farouk Taïrou, father of a family, octogenarian resident
acts.speech: “We thank the government for all its efforts through its new community health policy, thanks to which the community relays come into our households to give us valuable health advice. In the past we spent a lot of money on health, but thanks to their presence things have changed” ; “Since they have been here, we have fewer difficulties following our hospital care. Sometimes they themselves take us to the health centres, explaining to us the course to follow for the follow-up of care. They are genuinely involved in promoting our well-being.”

acts.speaker: A woman participant in the educational talk at Kégamarou (unnamed)
acts.speech: “The relay showed us the frequency and the position mothers should adopt to breastfeed their babies. The baby must suckle as often as it wishes,” explains a woman in the local language.

acts.speaker: Aliou Sabi Bassè, qualified community health agent (ASCQ) of the district of Sompérékou
acts.speech: “I am a nurse. My work consists of supervising the community relays. We ensure the smooth progression of the continuum of care in health centres and in the community. We take charge of simple cases of illness among children under five in the community on the basis of the community relay's observation (diagnosis)” ; “I sometimes make unannounced visits to certain houses to observe the work of the community relays while assessing their quality.”

acts.speaker: Katoumi Séko Yo, community relay in Kégamarou, district of Sompérékou
acts.speech: “The group follow-up strengthens our capacities. At this meeting, we take an inventory of our activities and list the difficulties we encounter in the field as well as the approaches to solutions.”

title: LE CHEF DE L’ÉTAT REÇOIT UN ÉMISSAIRE DU PRÉSIDENT ALGÉRIEN ABDELMADJID TEBBOUNE

acts.speaker: Abdelmadjid Tebboune, President of Algeria (message delivered by emissary)
acts.speech: The message handed to the Head of State concerns an official invitation from President Tebboune inviting his Djiboutian counterpart to take part in the 31st general meeting of the League of Arab States, which will be held next November in Algeria.

acts.speaker: Kamal Rezig, Algerian Minister of Trade and Export Promotion, and Mohamed Warsama Dirieh, his Djiboutian counterpart
acts.speech: At the end of the audience, they spoke to the Djiboutian press. They indicated in their remarks that the meeting provided a framework for discussing ways and means of increasing the level of exchange and cooperation between the two countries and the two brotherly peoples — in particular the merits of setting up a joint parity commission between the two countries, whose mission would be to define projects of shared economic interest for the two nations.

title: Increase in internet restrictions across Africa this year - report | News24

acts.speaker: Surfshark (report by the Netherlands-based internet monitor)
acts.speech: According to a report by Surfshark, there were nine internet restrictions in eight African countries in the first half of 2023 - double the number of restrictions the same time last year.

acts.speaker: Surfshark (statement)
acts.speech: Said the restrictions were related to political turmoil and protests ; "All of Africa's new restrictions were imposed amid protests or other political turmoil, highlighting the critical role the internet plays during periods of civil unrest," the organisation said in a statement.

acts.speaker: Gabriele Racaityte-Krasauske, spokesperson for Surfshark
acts.speech: Said there would likely be more internet restrictions across Africa because of elections and military involvement in civilian affairs.

acts.speaker: Gabriele Racaityte-Krasauske, spokesperson for Surfshark
acts.speech: Said the shutdowns left people with no means to communicate with the outside world: "When the internet is restricted, people are left with limited opportunities to spread information to the rest of the world, organising protests, medical aid for people in need, and contacting friends and loved ones. It's important to spread the word on this because the people affected often have limited opportunity to do so themselves."

title: Conjoncture économique au Bénin: La dynamique entrepreneuriale ralentit au 2e trimestre

acts.speaker: Observatory of Trade, Industry and Services (Ocis) of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Benin (Cci-Benin)
acts.speech: According to Ocis, the economic situation remains broadly favourable thanks to price stability and the resilience of several productive sectors.

acts.speaker: Benin Agency for the Promotion of Investment and Exports (Apiex) (figures)
acts.speech: According to Apiex figures, 14,863 businesses were registered in Benin between April and June 2025, a 2 per cent decline compared with the first quarter, when 15,166 new entities were recorded; sole proprietorships account for 89 per cent of creations against 11 per cent for companies, women head 37 per cent of new entities and young entrepreneurs aged 21 to 45 account for 86 per cent of registrations.

acts.speaker: National Institute of Statistics and Demography (Instad) (data)
acts.speech: According to Instad data, the annual average inflation rate came to 1.1 per cent at the end of June against 1.2 per cent in April, a decline of 8.33 per cent; over three months the general level of consumer prices rose by 0.4 per cent, driven by housing, water, electricity and fuel (+4.1 per cent), food products (+0.7 per cent) and energy products (+1.4 per cent), offset by falls in transport (-1.9 per cent), alcoholic beverages (-0.7 per cent) and financial services (-0.7 per cent).

acts.speaker: OCIS report, July 2025 (based on APIEx data, Monentreprise.bj)
acts.speech: Cited as the source of the key figures on the evolution of business registrations in the second quarter of 2025.

title: Province de Kirundo: Lancement officiel du projet «Mpore activity»

acts.speaker: Cléophile Akindavyi, Director General, Burundi Ministry of Public Health and the Fight against AIDS (speaking on behalf of the Minister)
acts.speech: Thanked the United States, via USAID, for its continuous multifaceted support in public health and other sectors. Recalled that Mpore activity builds on two prior USAID-funded projects (Giriteka and GBV-Bridge activity). Stressed that "GBV remains a gateway to HIV/AIDS." Promised the Ministry of Health will provide full support for the project's implementation.

acts.speaker: Lisa Peterson, US Ambassador to Burundi
acts.speech: Stated that the Mpore activity project's overall objective is to improve and integrate gender-based violence (GBV) prevention into HIV and family-planning services and to strengthen the health system, at a cost of $6,350,000, covering Bujumbura Mairie, Bujumbura, Gitega, Rumonge and Makamba provinces.

acts.speaker: Spès Caritas Bishoboye, deputy legal representative of Swaa-Burundi
acts.speech: Thanked the US Embassy for entrusting her organization, via USAID, with implementing the Mpore activity project with two sub-partners. Commended the Government of Burundi for its multifaceted support. Called for the involvement of everyone — administration, police, justice, and GBV care structures — in the fight against GBV. Promised that Swaa-Burundi "will spare no effort" to achieve the project's objectives.

acts.speaker: Jean Bosco Uwimana, GBV sensitization worker (Giriteka project), Busoni commune
acts.speech: Testified that the predecessor Giriteka project bore fruit. Described helping a family with malnourished children get care, after the mother revealed she was a victim of sexual harassment by her husband; said he helped the couple access family-planning services, and concluded that the family now leads a normal life.

acts.speaker: Victor Segasago, Governor of Kirundo province
acts.speech: In his welcome address, welcomed the Mpore activity project, which includes his province in its area of operation, saying he expects many results and hopes it will contribute to the good health of the population so they can devote themselves to development work towards the 2040-2060 vision. Invited the administrative authorities to contribute to the implementation and success of the project.

title: PAICV diz que falta de informação sobre deportação dos cabo-verdianos dos EUA é motivo de preocupação

acts.speaker: Rui Semedo, President of the PAICV party (Cabo Verde)
acts.speech: At a press conference in Praia, recommended that the country organise itself to respond to the mass deportation of undocumented Cape Verdeans from the United States, by creating the conditions for deportees to receive the necessary support, such as access to mechanisms allowing them to be covered by lawyers and to defend legality and their rights; stressed that the country must inform itself better about the situation, make the necessary contacts with the American authorities and set up an organisation for the reception, welcoming, follow-up and support of these immigrants ; “It is a matter of extended deportation that requires special care, even if the Government has previously taken care to receive deportees; at this moment there will have to be special concerns because it is a new situation,” reiterating the need to know the scale and number of those threatened with expulsion.

acts.speaker: Rui Semedo, President of the PAICV party (Cabo Verde)
acts.speech: On the suspension of United States foreign aid, specifically the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) package, said he hoped negotiations would be resumed and that Cabo Verde would not be removed from the list of beneficiaries of the cooperation ; “As a party we express the wish that the issue be restored and that Cabo Verde benefit from this important financing,” adding that the Government should use every means of influence and negotiation to continue to have access to this source of financing.

acts.speaker: United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement
acts.speech: According to the service, on Thursday the 23rd a total of 538 foreigners were arrested and 373 were placed in detention in the first actions following Trump's decree.

acts.speaker: United States Department of Homeland Security (data)
acts.speech: According to its data, Trump's goal of accelerating deportations to one million per year is considered double the maximum number of deportations carried out in a single year in recent decades.

title: #InsideTheBox with Dr Andy Gray | Who can prescribe medicines in SA? | News24

acts.speaker: Dr Andy Gray, pharmaceutical sciences expert, senior lecturer at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and co-director of the WHO Collaborating Centre on Pharmaceutical Policy and Evidence Based Practice
acts.speech: In his latest #InsideTheBox column, explains how the system of medicine scheduling and prescribing authority works now and sets out how it might be improved ; argues that the corollary of making medicines prescription-only must be that those authorised to prescribe must be competent to do so, regardless of their professional registration; that the enabling provisions exist in South African law and are working; but that in the case of public sector nurses and clinical associates, the "back door" approach has been too easy, and expediency has won over principle.

acts.speaker: Statistics South Africa, General Household Survey
acts.speech: Every year, Statistics South Africa asks participants in the General Household Survey where they would first seek care if someone in their family is ill or injured. Two-thirds respond their first port of call would be a public sector clinic.

acts.speaker: South Africa's National Drug Policy (1996)
acts.speech: One of the short policy statements in the document still informs current legislation and practice; it states simply: "At primary level, prescribing will be competency, not occupation, based."

title: DOGE shuttering Millennium Challenge Corp aid agency, staff told

acts.speaker: Kyeh Kim, senior MCC official
acts.speech: “Foreign aid is not a priority for the administration and so MCC’s work needs to wind down,” Kyeh Kim, a senior MCC official, told staff. Said officials from DOGE arrived at the agency early last week and entered talks with leadership, who were attempting to save the agency.

acts.speaker: Kyeh Kim, senior MCC official (advice to staff)
acts.speech: “I would encourage you to think very hard of what makes sense for you and your family at this time, and that is more important than your commitment to this organization,” Kim said in the meeting on Wednesday, warning that the organization’s future “looks very stark.”

acts.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
acts.speech: The MCC did not respond to an email requesting comment.

acts.speaker: President Donald Trump and adviser Elon Musk
acts.speech: Saying U.S. taxpayer money is misspent, in an unprecedented push to shrink the federal government.

acts.speaker: MCC employee (anonymous)
acts.speech: Told Reuters all the agency’s work had been ordered halted apart from a small number of active construction projects, including a wastewater treatment plant in Mongolia, electrical power grids in Senegal and Nepal, and schools in Ivory Coast. “This is very much a business- and infrastructure-focused way of doing development. It’s very much in America’s interest,” said the employee, who requested anonymity.

acts.speaker: MCC recording of staff meeting
acts.speech: MCC staff were told in a meeting on Wednesday that all of the agency’s programs will be closed and staff numbers would be minimized, according to a recording of the meeting.

acts.speaker: Politico
acts.speech: First reported the move, citing an email sent to staff at the agency on Tuesday, which Reuters has also reviewed.

acts.speaker: Email to MCC staff
acts.speech: Gives the agency’s 300 or so staff until April 29 to decide whether to take voluntary early retirement or a deferred resignation under which they will receive pay until the end of September, or face being placed on administrative leave.

acts.speaker: MCC website
acts.speech: It partners with developing countries on projects like improving electricity supply for businesses and improving roads for farmers to get their goods to market, according to its website.

title: Amnesty International Warns Of Deepening Global Human Rights Crisis Fuelled By ‘Trump Effect’

acts.speaker: Amnesty International
acts.speech: Issued a stark warning about a rapidly worsening global human rights crisis, attributing the acceleration of repressive global trends to what it describes as the "Trump effect" - a broad and deliberate assault on international law and human rights by the United States under President Donald Trump's second administration.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International, annual report "The State of the World's Human Rights"
acts.speech: Reviewing conditions in 150 countries throughout 2024, depicts a world sliding deeper into authoritarianism, saying governments are increasingly silencing dissent, curtailing fundamental freedoms and undermining accountability mechanisms while multilateral systems built to protect human rights are being steadily dismantled: "Year after year, we have warned of the dangers of human rights backsliding. But events of the past 12 months - not least Israel's livestreamed but unheeded genocide of Palestinians in Gaza - have laid bare just how hellish the world can be for so many when the most powerful states jettison international law and disregard multilateral institutions."

acts.speaker: Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International Secretary General
acts.speech: Described Trump's return to power as a catalyst for global regression, saying his administration has exhibited outright contempt for universal rights and has deliberately dismantled key institutions meant to safeguard justice, equality and the environment; by attacking racial and gender justice, rolling back climate action, defunding global health efforts and undermining asylum systems, Trump has created a permissive atmosphere for other anti-rights actors around the world to intensify their own crackdowns.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International
acts.speech: "One hundred days into his second term, President Trump has shown only utter contempt for universal human rights."

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Emphasised that the crisis cannot be blamed on one leader alone, saying the world has been witnessing a long, creeping rise in authoritarian practices driven by both aspiring and elected leaders who view power as a means to crush dissent and enrich elites, and warning that entire governments are now weaponizing the law to sow fear and evade scrutiny; documented widespread suppression of civil society through arbitrary arrests, censorship and criminalization of activists, human rights defenders and journalists.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Documented violent responses to public protests and unrest across numerous countries, describing brutal state-led crackdowns and abuses including excessive and often lethal force against demonstrators; noted that security forces used repression as a tool to crush civil disobedience, leaving thousands dead or injured, while peaceful protestors faced indefinite detention under vaguely worded anti-terror laws.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Accused powerful states of allowing war crimes and other serious violations of international law - particularly atrocities in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan and Myanmar - to persist unchecked, while international responses remained inconsistent and in many cases absent; said the Trump administration's suspension of foreign aid and its imposition of sanctions on international justice bodies exacerbated humanitarian conditions in multiple regions and undermined global efforts to hold perpetrators accountable.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Highlighted how collective failures to address the climate crisis, growing inequality and corporate excess are condemning future generations to greater hardship; described the 2024 COP29 summit as a failure, with fossil fuel interests dominating the agenda and wealthy nations pushing through inadequate financing deals that left poorer countries vulnerable, and saw Trump's withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and his aggressive promotion of fossil fuel extraction as not only regressive but dangerously influential.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Said rising economic inequality was another major theme, as governments allowed unchecked corporate power, failed to regulate financial abuses and scapegoated migrants and refugees to deflect blame for deepening poverty and stagnation, and said such rhetoric, often laced with racism and xenophobia, is helping normalize exclusionary politics while deflecting from the real drivers of inequality.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Expressed grave concern over attacks on women, girls and LGBTI people, noting a worsening global backlash against gender rights, and said the Trump administration has played a central role in this trend by dismantling gender-focused programs, attacking transgender rights and halting funding for services benefiting women and girls worldwide.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Warned of the growing misuse of technology by states and corporations, with surveillance tools entrenching discrimination and artificial intelligence systems reinforcing existing inequalities, and criticised the Trump administration's cozy relationship with tech billionaires, accusing it of rolling back regulatory safeguards and encouraging platforms to weaken content moderation and allow disinformation, hate speech and corporate influence to proliferate.

acts.speaker: Amnesty International (report)
acts.speech: Commended the resilience of multilateral bodies like the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice, which took significant steps in 2024 to pursue accountability for war crimes and other serious violations, and noted growing leadership from countries in the Global South, including legal challenges, arms embargo initiatives and international cooperation aimed at restoring the rule of law; concluded by urging governments to act boldly and collectively to reverse the damage, restore international justice and protect the fundamental rights of all people.

acts.speaker: Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International Secretary General
acts.speech: Emphasised that while the current landscape is bleak, the erosion of human rights is not irreversible, noting that around the world people continue to resist, mobilize and vote against anti-rights regimes and that civil society, despite facing threats and restrictions, remains a powerful force.

title: U.S. Ambassador reaffirms equal partnership and ongoing support to Ghana

acts.speaker: Virginia Palmer, United States Ambassador to Ghana
acts.speech: Underscored the importance of maintaining a respectful and balanced partnership between Ghana and the United States, stressing that despite differences in economic scale and historical timelines, the two nations must continue working together as equals: “I think we are equals. Your economy is smaller than mine, and you have been independent for less time than the U.S., but I think we must work together as equals. That is number one.”

acts.speaker: Virginia Palmer, United States Ambassador to Ghana
